Asgard archaea are an archaeal group important in studies of eukaryotic origins. Molecular comparisons connect their genes to the nuclear lineage of eukaryotes, rather than making modern Asgard archaea the direct ancestors of modern animals or plants. See the original analysis cited under two-domain system.

Eukaryote

Words: 2k Articles: 19
Organism OurBigBook.com
A eukaryote is an organism belonging to the lineage characterized by a membrane-bounded cell nucleus and extensive cellular compartmentalization. A nuclear envelope surrounds the nuclear genome; nuclear chromosomes are typically linear. Ribosomes perform biological translation outside the cell nucleus. See OpenStax Microbiology, 3.4: nuclear organization and protein synthesis. Specialized biological cells can lose their cell nucleus, as mature mammalian red blood cells do, while remaining parts of eukaryotic organisms; see OpenStax Biology 2e, 40.2: mature red blood cells.
Yeasts, plants and animals are all eukaryotes. Typical cells in these groups have mitochondria, but chloroplasts belong to photosynthetic plant and algae lineages, not to every eukaryote. A cell wall occurs in typical plant and fungus cells but is absent from animal cells. These are comparisons of representative cells, not a checklist every specialized cell must satisfy. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 4.3: nucleus, organelles and representative cells.
The interesting feature is controlled separation: cell membranes and organelle membranes let different cellular processes occupy distinct compartments while membrane transport connects them. The evolution of eukaryotes also involved partnership: mitochondria descend from a bacterial endosymbiosis. Modern phylogenetics supports an archaeal ancestry for the nuclear lineage, alongside this bacterial contribution; see two-domain system. Thus the history of a whole eukaryote cannot be read as the history of just one of its genes.

Fungus

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Eukaryote OurBigBook.com
A fungus is a eukaryote that obtains nutrients by absorption rather than photosynthesis. Fungi include unicellular yeasts and multicellular forms. Their cell walls differ from bacterial peptidoglycan walls; having a cell wall does not make a fungus a plant. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 24.1: fungal nutrition and organization.
Yeast
Words: 1k Articles: 2
Fungus OurBigBook.com
Yeasts are fungi whose growth is predominantly unicellular, commonly through budding or division into two cells. The word describes a growth form across different fungal lineages, rather than one species or an exclusive clade; some fungi can switch between unicellular and filamentous growth. Thus Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a yeast, but yeast is not another name for that one species. See Kurtzman, Fell and Boekhout, The Yeasts, chapter 1 (2011): definition and classification.
A yeast cell has eukaryotic organization, including a cell nucleus, mitochondria and a cell wall. Small size and a unicellular lifestyle do not make it a member of bacteria. These compartments let an experimentally accessible biological cell retain much of the organization shared with other eukaryotes. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 24.1: fungal cells and yeast growth.
A motivating experiment: can fermentation continue without intact yeast cells? In 1897, Eduard Buchner ground brewers' yeast with quartz sand and diatomite, added water, and pressed out a liquid extract. Adding concentrated cane sugar produced carbon dioxide after 15–60 minutes. A cell-retaining filter still yielded an active filtrate: with sterilized cane sugar in an icebox, fermentation began after about a day. Saturated lactose gave no observed fermentation. These are reported observations, not invented control results. See Buchner, Alcoholic fermentation without yeast cells (1897), translated excerpt hosted by Carmen Giunta.
The filtration comparison addresses the objection that surviving intact yeast cells caused the activity. The lactose comparison tests substrate dependence; it is not a no-sugar blank, nor a comparison at matched sugar concentrations. A proposed modern follow-up would also compare the same extract with and without added sugar, accounting for material already in the extract. That is an experimental suggestion, not a result attributed to Buchner. His report specifies brewers' yeast; it does not identify the preparation here as a pure Saccharomyces cerevisiae strain.
Heat treatment asks a different question: does destroying activity in the extract stop fermentation? Buchner's preliminary report described weak or absent activity after heating and filtration, rather than one clean universal threshold. Harden's 1914 account of the subsequent work summarized loss of activity on heating the juice to 50∘C. Harden also described requirements for both enzymes and coenzymes. Cell-free therefore means neither chemical-free nor a preparation containing one purified enzyme. See Arthur Harden, Alcoholic Fermentation (1914), chapters II and VI: cell-free activity and the fermenting complex.
The inference is that extracted cellular machinery can sustain these chemical reactions without an intact living biological cell. This does not show that the extract reproduces, grows or maintains itself like a yeast. Moreover, gas evolution alone does not identify ethanol: cellular respiration can also release carbon dioxide. Product identification is a separate measurement; Harden's account describes both ethanol and carbon dioxide as products of cell-free alcoholic fermentation. The beautiful separation is between the organism that produces and maintains the machinery and the machinery that catalyzes a particular transformation.
Schizosaccharomyces pombe
Words: 17
Yeast OurBigBook.com
Schizosaccharomyces pombe is a yeast species used as a model organism. It supplies the candidate genes in the yeast cross-species complementation experiment; the recipient remains Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
Saccharomyces cerevisiae
Words: 589
Yeast OurBigBook.com
Saccharomyces cerevisiae is a particular species of yeast, used in baking, brewing and laboratory research. During ordinary vegetative growth it reproduces by budding: a smaller daughter grows from the mother before separation. Laboratory strains can be maintained as either haploid or diploid biological cells. This makes it possible to investigate genes in a single eukaryote, then use controlled crosses and meiosis to connect a genotype to a phenotype. See Burgess, Powers and Mell, Budding Yeast Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a Model Genetic Organism (2017), pp. 1–2.
The practical value of Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a model organism is the combination of easy laboratory cultivation, accessible genetics, and cellular functions shared with other eukaryotes. A haploid strain has one set of chromosomes, so a changed allele is not accompanied by a second copy at that genetic locus. But a mutation need not produce an observable phenotype under every condition. The yeast is also a whole organism, not a miniature human: transferring a result requires evidence that the relevant function is shared in the target system. See Duina, Miller and Keeney, Budding Yeast for Budding Geneticists (2014): cultivation, genetic tools and conserved functions.
For a concrete example, Hartwell, Culotti and Reid's 1970 work followed temperature-sensitive Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains with successive microscope photographs. Failure to complete a particular part of the cell cycle helped identify required gene functions. Their distinction between when a function is required and where a cell finally stops is especially instructive: the visible endpoint need not be the time of the underlying defect. See Hartwell, Culotti and Reid, Genetic control of the cell-division cycle in yeast. I. Detection of mutants (1970): primary abstract. This is a useful way to turn an observable change in a biological cell into a question about genes and causal order.
In alcoholic fermentation, Saccharomyces cerevisiae converts sugars into ethanol and carbon dioxide. The carbon dioxide helps dough rise; the ethanol is useful in alcoholic drinks. The metabolism also supports production of ATP, a usable cellular energy carrier. This is one metabolic ability of one species, not the definition of every yeast. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 7.5: alcohol fermentation and the Burgess, Powers and Mell account above.
For glucose, the ideal net stoichiometry is
C6​H12​O6​⟶2C2​H5​OH+2CO2​.
(30)
One molecule of glucose supplies six carbon chemical atoms: four end up in the two ethanol molecules and two in the two carbon dioxide molecules. The twelve hydrogen and six oxygen chemical atoms also balance. This is a net material balance across several enzyme-catalyzed steps, not a single chemical reaction step or the complete bookkeeping for cellular energy carriers. The standard pathway accounting yields a net two ATP per glucose: the initial breakdown produces the ATP, while the later conversion to ethanol regenerates a coenzyme needed to keep the breakdown going. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 7.2: net ATP accounting and the section 7.5 cited above.
At complete conversion, this toy gives 20mmol of ethanol and 20mmol of carbon dioxide. The carbon balance is 6×10=2×20+1×20=60mmol of carbon chemical atoms. A real culture also builds cellular material, can use other metabolic routes, and may retain dissolved carbon dioxide; the toy is a reference balance rather than a prediction of collected gas or beverage yield.
Although alcoholic fermentation does not require molecular oxygen as a reactant, the presence of molecular oxygen does not force Saccharomyces cerevisiae to stop fermenting. De Deken's 1966 experiments reported predominantly fermentative glucose use during exponential growth in air. Consequently, bubbles do not establish either absence of molecular oxygen or an exclusively fermentative metabolism. See De Deken, The Crabtree Effect: A Regulatory System in Yeast (1966): primary abstract.

Taxonomy (biology)

Words: 1k Articles: 10
Biology OurBigBook.com
Taxonomy names and classifies organisms. Classification can organize known diversity and make comparisons useful, but ranks and names are not themselves evidence of ancestry. Phylogenetics infers that ancestry; a clade includes an ancestor and all its descendants. A shared feature such as lacking a cell nucleus need not identify an exclusive clade. The organism branch here organizes cell types for reading and is not a proposed phylogenetic tree. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 20.1: classification and evolutionary history.

Domain (biology)

Words: 247 Articles: 2
Taxonomy (biology) OurBigBook.com
A biological domain is a high-level rank used to classify organisms in the three-domain system. Distinguish a taxonomic rank from a primary branch in an inferred phylogenetic tree: retaining familiar names does not settle the branching relationships.

Three-domain system

Words: 87
Domain (biology) OurBigBook.com
The three-domain system recognizes bacteria, archaea and eukaryotes as three domains. In 1990, Woese, Kandler and Wheelis proposed the domain rank and the names Bacteria, Archaea and Eucarya, using molecular comparisons to argue that the older prokaryote/eukaryote division hid important differences. See Woese, Kandler and Wheelis, 1990: Towards a natural system of organisms.
The associated three-domain ancestry model places the nuclear lineage of eukaryotes alongside archaea, rather than within them. This historically influential interpretation should be distinguished from the two-domain system; listing three familiar groups does not establish three independent primary branches.

Two-domain system

Words: 127
Domain (biology) OurBigBook.com
The two-domain system recognizes bacteria and archaea as the two primary lineages, placing the nuclear ancestry of eukaryotes within archaea. In this model, archaea as a complete clade includes that eukaryotic lineage; restricting the name to prokaryotic members describes a different grouping. Williams and colleagues' study, published online in 2019 and in a 2020 journal issue, found support for this model and a close relationship to Asgard archaea. See Williams et al., 2020: Phylogenomics provides robust support for a two-domains tree of life.
This updates the interpretation of the 1977 and 1990 classifications rather than undoing their discovery of deep differences between bacteria and archaea. Deep phylogenetic trees depend on the sampled genes, organisms and inference model; the precise closest archaeal relatives and early sequence of events require further evidence. Bacterial ancestry of mitochondria through endosymbiosis is a separate part of eukaryotic history.

Species

Words: 778 Articles: 6
Taxonomy (biology) OurBigBook.com
A species is a named unit of biological classification. The useful criteria vary among groups: reproductive compatibility can inform classification in many animals, while microbial comparisons also use genomes and other characters. Escherichia coli is a species; K-12 MG1655 identifies a particular strain within it. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 18.2: species concepts.

Species concept

Words: 397 Articles: 3
Species OurBigBook.com
A species concept states what should make organisms members of the same species; an operational criterion states what observations will test that claim. Reproductive isolation, distinguishable morphology and ancestry inferred through phylogenetics answer different questions. In a lineage-based interpretation, they are evidence for separation of evolving biological populations, and need not appear together. [ref]
Biological species concept
Words: 117
Species concept OurBigBook.com
The biological species concept groups naturally interbreeding biological populations with viable, fertile offspring, distinguished from other such groups by reproductive isolation. An operational test examines mating, fertilization, offspring survival and offspring reproduction, rather than only whether two adults can be paired. Sexual reproduction is its scope: fossils and organisms studied only through asexual reproduction cannot supply the same mating evidence. [ref]
For an original hypothetical example, imagine two separated biological populations that reproduce successfully after contact. The separation alone did not demonstrate reproductive isolation. Conversely, failure to mate in one unfamiliar chamber could reflect the assay conditions. Field observations of gene flow and tests under suitable conditions address the biological question more directly. A successful laboratory pairing does not establish frequent interbreeding in nature.
Morphological species concept
Words: 121
Species concept OurBigBook.com
A morphological species concept distinguishes species using morphology: measurable differences in form or structure. It can be applied to preserved specimens and fossils when mating cannot be observed. Similar appearance need not imply the same species, and different appearance need not imply different species. [ref]
An original operational example is to compare a chosen structure in specimens of comparable age, sex and rearing conditions. Suppose two apparent groups differ in size, but one group contains only juveniles. The observed difference does not yet diagnose two species. Specify the measured phenotype, variation within each sample, and whether the distinction persists across comparable specimens. A single striking specimen is a poor substitute for that comparison.
Phylogenetic species concept
Words: 97
Species concept OurBigBook.com
Phylogenetic species concepts use ancestry and diagnostic inherited differences; versions differ over requiring a clade, an exclusive ancestry pattern at genetic loci, or a distinguishable character combination. State which criterion is intended. [ref]
For an original operational example, suppose a phylogenetic tree inferred from one genetic locus separates two sampled biological populations. Compare further genetic loci and additional local samples before interpreting that branch as a species boundary. Otherwise the test may merely identify the particular ancestry of the sampled alleles. Adding more sites from the same genetic locus improves that locus's evidence without creating an independent ancestry test.

Species delimitation

Words: 233
Species OurBigBook.com
Species delimitation infers the boundaries and number of species from evidence. No single arbitrary percentage of nucleotide sequence difference is a universal boundary. Divergence within an old, widespread species can exceed divergence between recently separated species; geography and multiple kinds of evidence matter. [ref]
An original counterexample to a universal percentage rule: an assay could examine a strongly conserved gene in one comparison and a rapidly changing nucleotide sequence in another. Equal percentages then answer different historical questions. Even the denominator needs specifying: all sites, aligned sites, or only a filtered region? A threshold is an operational rule for a stated assay and group of organisms, whose errors need evaluating. It is not a definition that automatically transfers to every species.
The diagram's hypothetical pair B has similar morphology but reduced mating and distinct ancestry evidence. A morphological species concept could miss that distinction. Pair C instead has different morphology but compatible mating and ancestry that fails to separate the samples. That combination calls for checking variation in phenotype within a species. Pair A has only a structural difference observed: the other criteria remain untested. These examples show why missing evidence, disagreeing evidence and agreeing evidence require different interpretations.

Species, populations and strains

Words: 99
Species OurBigBook.com
A species can encompass many biological populations. A biological population specifies a set of organisms in a place and time; a biological strain identifies a maintained variant or lineage, often in a laboratory. A species name, a local census and a biological strain designation therefore describe different things. Multiple independently maintained cultures can also share the same biological strain designation.
For example, a culture identified as Escherichia coli K-12 MG1655 specifies more than the species alone. Two flasks inoculated from that culture are separate experimental biological populations; the separate containers do not establish two species or two different biological strains. This is an original experimental bookkeeping example, not a claim that every biological strain name encodes a complete genotype.

Ecology

Words: 3k Articles: 26
Biology OurBigBook.com
The goal of ecology is to explain where organisms live, how many there are, and how their interactions with one another and their surroundings change those patterns. Living partners include prey, predators and parasites; nonliving conditions include light, temperature and water. An ecosystem brings these interacting parts into one study system. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 44.1: the scope of ecology.
Start with an invented aquatic food web: photosynthetic algae feed zooplankton, which feed small fish, which feed large fish. That food chain has four feeding positions and three feeding arrows. Dead material also reaches decomposers through detritus, so the food web branches rather than forming a single ladder.
The appeal of ecology is that an organism's surroundings include other organisms that change those surroundings. Photosynthesis links light to living material; predation transfers that material between organisms; decomposers return its constituent chemical elements to forms that can be used again. These connections help explain why changing one part of an ecosystem can affect distant parts of its food web, although an arrow alone does not predict the size or even the direction of an indirect change. Population dynamics supplies quantitative tools when the question concerns changing counts.
In 1866, Ernst Haeckel's Generelle Morphologie der Organismen included a section titled Oecologie und Chorologie in volume 2, beginning on page 286. This places the terminology of ecology in an early systematic treatment of organisms and their relationships. See Haeckel, Generelle Morphologie der Organismen, volume 2 (1866), contents and p. 286. A later quantitative landmark is Raymond L. Lindeman's 1942 treatment of ecosystems through feeding relationships and energy flow. See Lindeman, The Trophic-Dynamic Aspect of Ecology, Ecology 23 (1942), 399–417.

Population (biology)

Words: 46
Ecology OurBigBook.com
A biological population is a set of organisms of a species occupying a specified area or experimental setting at a specified time. State the boundary for the question being studied: a flask, a breeding locality, or a wider region connected by gene flow. A biological population need not be perfectly mixed or isolated.

Ecosystem

Words: 911 Articles: 8
Ecology OurBigBook.com
An ecosystem is a system of interacting organisms and their nonliving surroundings. A pond study might include algae, fish, bacteria, water, dissolved chemical compounds and incoming light. The useful step is to state the boundary and time interval: the pond surface, bottom and shoreline might enclose the study region, but water, organisms and energy can cross them. The chosen boundary specifies what counts as internal storage, input or output; it does not make the ecosystem sealed. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 46.1: ecosystems and their components.
For a toy pond water budget over one day, begin with 1000m3, add 120m3 crossing inward, and remove 90m3 crossing outward. With all other transfers omitted by assumption, the final amount is 1000+120−90=1030m3. The same bookkeeping asks whether a change inside an ecosystem came from internal processes or exchanges with its surroundings. Changing the boundary to include an upstream reservoir changes which transfers are internal, while preserving the accounting.

Primary producer

Words: 33
Ecosystem OurBigBook.com
A primary producer builds organic chemical compounds from inorganic sources. Photosynthetic algae, plants and cyanobacteria use light energy for this role through photosynthesis and carbon fixation. The role supplies new living material to a food web; it does not mean that the organism creates energy.

Consumer (food chain)

Words: 114 Articles: 2
Ecosystem OurBigBook.com
A consumer obtains organic material by feeding on other organisms or their products. A consumer feeding on primary producers is a primary consumer; one feeding on primary consumers is a secondary consumer. These names describe positions in a food chain, rather than permanent labels for a species.
Decomposer
Words: 48
Consumer (food chain) OurBigBook.com
A decomposer breaks down dead organic material and absorbs products of that breakdown; many bacteria and fungi perform this role. Decomposers connect detritus from different trophic levels to material recycling, so placing all decomposers at one final step of every food chain is misleading. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 46.1: grazing and detrital food webs.
Omnivore
Words: 26
Consumer (food chain) OurBigBook.com
An omnivore feeds on both primary producers and consumers. Its mixed diet explains why a trophic level need not be a whole number or a fixed label throughout an organism's life.

Detritus

Words: 43
Ecosystem OurBigBook.com
Detritus is nonliving organic material, including dead remains and organic wastes. It is a resource for decomposers, not itself an organism or a predator. In the illustrative food web, the dashed arrow from algae to detritus denotes a material transfer; the solid arrow from detritus to decomposers denotes resource use.

Trophic level (TL)

Words: 139
Ecosystem OurBigBook.com
A trophic level describes feeding position relative to primary producers. Assign primary producers level 1; in the illustrated food chain, zooplankton occupy level 2, small fish level 3, and large fish level 4. Following a single feeding path adds one level at each step. The labels make dependence on the initial resource visible, but a branching food web can give an organism several feeding paths. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 46.1: feeding positions and branching food webs.
An omnivore can obtain food from more than one trophic level. As an explicitly assumed diet-weighted example, suppose an omnivore gets half its assimilated food energy from level-1 primary producers and half from level-2 consumers. Define its trophic level as one plus the weighted mean level of its food: 1+(1/2)1+(1/2)2=2.5. This computed position depends on the specified diet and weighting convention; it is not an immutable property of the species. A different life stage or diet can change it.

Energy flow (ecology)

Words: 398
Ecosystem OurBigBook.com
Energy flow tracks energy entering an ecosystem, passing through organisms and leaving its boundary. To see its quantitative effect, assume net production at one trophic level is P1​=1000kJm−2day−1 and assume a transfer efficiency ε=0.10 at each of two successive steps. Here Pi​ measures the energy incorporated into new living material per unit area per day, after that level's own cellular respiration; it is not a count of organisms or a standing stock. The joule supplies the energy unit, with 1kJ=1000J.
Pi+1​=εPi​,P2​=100,P3​=10kJm−2day−1.
(31)
Only 10/1000=0.01, or one percent, of the initial production reaches level 3 in this toy food chain. The first step leaves 1000−100=900 and the second 100−10=90 outside the next level's new production. These differences can include uneaten material, wastes, and energy released as heat during cellular respiration; their separate amounts have not been assigned. Detritus can still carry energy to decomposers. The 10 percent efficiency is an assumption, not a universal law: transfer efficiencies vary with the organisms, food and conditions. The production ratio Pi+1​/Pi​ also differs from the fraction of an individual meal converted into growth. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 46.2: production and transfer efficiency.
The shrinking budget explains why supporting another trophic level requires enough production below it. It does not prove an exact maximum length for every food chain, particularly when a food web imports resources or has branching diets. Lindeman's 1942 paper grouped feeding relationships into trophic levels, compared transfers and cellular respiration, and emphasized the ecosystem as a unit connecting living and nonliving components. That viewpoint made different organisms comparable through a common energy budget. See Lindeman, The Trophic-Dynamic Aspect of Ecology (1942).
Material recycling and energy flow describe different bookkeeping. Carbon, nitrogen and phosphorus can be reused through chemical reactions and transfers between organisms and their surroundings. Energy transferred as heat is conserved, but is no longer the same store of chemical energy available to a consumer; photosynthetic primary producers need continuing light input. A decomposer helps recycle material and also releases heat through metabolism. Thus loss from one feeding budget means transfer into other forms or routes, never destruction of energy. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 46.3: material cycles. Conservation of energy applies to the whole accounting.

Zooplankton

Words: 33
Ecosystem OurBigBook.com
Zooplankton are drifting aquatic consumers, including small animals. In the illustrative food web, the chosen zooplankton feed on algae and serve as prey for small fish; this assumed diet is not a claim about every kind of zooplankton.

Endosymbiosis

Words: 1k Articles: 5
Ecology OurBigBook.com
Endosymbiosis is an ecological association in which one organism, the endosymbiont, lives inside another. The definition specifies location, not that both partners benefit, nor that the internal partner has become an organelle. An intracellular association can remain an association between distinct organisms. Endosymbiotic theory addresses a different question: how particular ancestral bacteria became inherited, functionally integrated organelles during evolution.
The striking consequence is that a eukaryotic biological cell can combine histories: its nuclear lineage and its mitochondria need not have the same ancestry. Mitochondria have bacterial ancestry related to Alphaproteobacteria; the plastids of plants and many algae, including chloroplasts, have ancestry within cyanobacteria. These are ancestral lineages, not a claim that a named living bacterial species is the literal ancestor. Present-day bacteria and organelles have both evolved since their shared ancestors. [ref]

Endosymbiont

Words: 25
Endosymbiosis OurBigBook.com
An endosymbiont is the internal partner in an endosymbiosis. Calling an organism an endosymbiont does not by itself classify it as an organelle or imply an irreversible evolutionary transition.

Endosymbiotic theory

Words: 890 Articles: 3
Endosymbiosis OurBigBook.com
Endosymbiotic theory explains the bacterial origins of mitochondria and plastids through enduring internal associations and subsequent integration. Survival inside a biological cell is only part of the problem: exchange through membrane transport, inherited division, gene expression and delivery of required proteins must work together. The elegance is evolutionary reuse of an existing cellular capability, followed by changes that make the partners operate as one system. [ref]
The historical On the origin of mitosing cells by Lynn Sagan (1967, abstract and Introduction, pp. 225–226) synthesized a symbiotic account of eukaryotic origins and proposed tests using molecular evidence. Its Introduction explicitly acknowledged earlier proposals. It also hypothesized origins for other structures; the modern evidence for mitochondria and plastids should be assessed separately from the rest of that historical scheme.
Evidence for bacterial ancestry of organelles
Words: 331
Endosymbiotic theory OurBigBook.com
Resemblance is a clue, not sufficient evidence of common descent. A small size, two surrounding membranes, division, retained DNA or bacterial-looking ribosomes does not uniquely identify an ancestor. Internal membranes exist outside these organelles, and a similar function can favor similar structures. The stronger question is whether independently examined molecular characters support the same historical relationship.
A concrete genomic observation is the mitochondrial sequence reported in 1997 for Reclinomonas americana: 69,034 base pairs containing 97 identified genes, including four for a bacterial-type multisubunit RNA polymerase. This is a reported genome inventory, not a calculation from the pictured shape of a mitochondrion. Retention of such bacterial features strengthens the ancestry argument; a living Reclinomonas americana is not itself an ancestral eukaryote. The inspected abstract supplies these observations but not the detailed sequencing protocol or contamination controls, so those details are not attributed to this report here. [ref]
A sequence-based investigation obtains nucleotide sequences by DNA sequencing, identifies comparable genes, makes a sequence alignment and uses phylogenetics to infer relationships. The readout is a proposed relationship with support and uncertainty, not a photograph of an ancient encounter. Comparisons of plastid sequences with bacterial sequences support cyanobacterial ancestry, while the exact closest sampled cyanobacterial group has depended on the chosen data and inference. A bacterial affinity in one gene is weaker than coherent evidence across several genes and cellular systems. [ref]
For such an analysis, useful checks include distinguishing organelle DNA from bacterial contamination, verifying sequence quality, comparing corresponding rather than unrelated genes, sampling several bacterial groups and testing sensitivity to the sequence alignment and evolutionary mathematical model. These are methodological requirements, not a claim that this article has rerun a particular published analysis. Horizontal gene transfer, gene loss and unequal evolutionary change can make an individual gene's history differ from a whole organism's history. A supported bacterial origin therefore need not identify an extant donor species, an exact date or the original mode of entry. [ref]
Endosymbiotic gene transfer
Words: 443 Articles: 1
Endosymbiotic theory OurBigBook.com
Endosymbiotic gene transfer moves genetic material from an endosymbiont or its descendant organelle into the host genome, notably the nuclear genome. A transferred DNA segment can remain silent. For a transferred gene to replace an organelle-encoded function, nuclear gene expression must work and its protein must reach the right compartment through organelle protein import. Transfer of DNA and transport of proteins are distinct processes in opposite directions. [ref]
Gene loss and endosymbiotic gene transfer are different: absence from an organelle genome does not by itself show that a functional nuclear copy exists. Conversely, an imported protein may derive from a host gene rather than a transferred gene. The surviving organelle genome is therefore a partial record, not a complete inventory of either ancestral bacteria or the modern organelle's machinery. [ref]
Functional plastid-to-nucleus gene transfer experiment
Words: 313
Endosymbiotic gene transfer OurBigBook.com
Experimental Reconstruction of Functional Gene Transfer from the Tobacco Plastid Genome to the Nucleus by Sandra Stegemann and Ralph Bock (2006, Results, pp. 2870–2874) separated relocation of DNA from activation of a relocated gene. Engineered tobacco chloroplasts carried an nptII gene with nuclear expression signals beside an aadA gene with plastid expression signals. Selection on kanamycin recovered plants with the segment in the nuclear genome. Crosses then replaced the engineered chloroplasts with ordinary chloroplasts: the nuclear segment remained, but the plants were initially sensitive to spectinomycin and streptomycin. The transferred aadA gene was not yet functional in its new setting.
Leaf pieces were cultured on regeneration medium containing both drugs. Resistant regenerated plants supplied the functional readout. Using both drugs reduced selection of spontaneous plastid mutations conferring resistance mainly to one drug. Reciprocal crosses and selfing distinguished maternal plastid inheritance from nuclear Mendelian segregation; eight of sixteen initial candidates had the latter pattern. [ref]
The molecular readout came from RNA hybridization and DNA sequencing. A Northern blot detected aadA messenger RNA in activated lines, with different transcript sizes. Thermal asymmetric interlaced polymerase chain reaction recovered upstream DNA; products present in activated lines but absent in original-line and ordinary-plant controls were sequenced. The mapped rearrangements connected aadA to the upstream nuclear gene promoter. Thus resistance, inheritance, RNA detection and changed nucleotide sequences supported activation of the transferred nuclear gene, rather than resistance alone. [ref]
This engineered test demonstrates one route to functional nuclear gene expression after plastid DNA transfer. It does not establish a natural transfer rate, replay ancient endosymbiosis or demonstrate that the resulting protein is imported into a chloroplast. The authors explicitly identify acquisition of targeting information as an additional step not reproduced by this experiment. [ref]

Ecology OurBigBook.com
Parasitism is an interaction in which a parasite obtains resources from a host, reducing some component of the host's performance. Its demographic effects depend on exposure, within-host processes and transmission opportunities.

Parasitism OurBigBook.com
A parasitoid develops on or in a host and eventually kills it. Host-parasitoid transmission therefore has different offspring accounting from ordinary predation or a nonlethal parasite-burden model.

Host (biology)

Parasitism OurBigBook.com
A biological host provides the environment or resources used by a parasite or other associated organism.

Parasite

Parasitism OurBigBook.com
A parasite is an organism benefiting from parasitism. Microparasite and macroparasite distinguish useful transmission-model descriptions of within-host multiplication and distributed parasite burden.
Macroparasite

Parasite OurBigBook.com
A macroparasite is typically modelled using the number of parasites carried by each host. Adult parasitic worms illustrate why within-host parasite burden, developmental stages, mating and host exposure heterogeneity matter beyond an infected/not-infected classification.
Within-host parasite burden (j)
Words: 28
Macroparasite OurBigBook.com
The within-host parasite burden is the number of parasites, or a specified parasite-load measure, carried by one host. A population's mean burden and its infected-host prevalence are different summaries of the burden distribution.
Microparasite

Parasite OurBigBook.com
A microparasite is typically modelled as multiplying rapidly within a host, so infection status rather than the exact organism count is the first between-host state variable. SIS model, SIR model and SEIR model descriptions are examples. Additional within-host structure can still be required.

Predation

Words: 292 Articles: 2
Ecology OurBigBook.com
Predation is the consumption of prey by a predator, affecting the demographic rates of both populations.
In the usual animal-feeding sense, a predator kills and eats its prey. This distinguishes the interaction from feeding on already-dead material and from the prolonged exploitation of a living host in parasitism. In the illustrative food web, a small fish eating zooplankton is a predator; a large fish eating that small fish makes the same small fish its prey. These roles belong to a particular interaction. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 45.6: predation and community interactions.
For a toy count, suppose 50 small fish begin a day and 8 are eaten by large fish. With births, other deaths and movement explicitly omitted, 42 small fish remain, and the fraction removed by predation is 8/50=0.16. This measures removal of prey, not production of new predators. Food intake can support survival and reproduction, but eight meals do not imply eight new predators; energy flow and life-history details intervene. Lotka-Volterra equations provide one idealized account of such population dynamics, rather than a guarantee that every interacting pair must cycle.

Prey

Words: 55
Predation OurBigBook.com
Prey is an organism consumed by a predator in predation. The name describes the receiving end of that interaction: a small fish can be prey for a large fish while being a predator of zooplankton. In a food web drawn with resource-to-consumer arrows, a feeding arrow goes outward from the prey toward its predator. This convention makes the route of food and energy easy to follow.

Predator

Words: 69
Predation OurBigBook.com
A predator is an organism that consumes prey through predation. A predator need not occupy the highest trophic level of an ecosystem, and the label does not specify its size or guarantee that it has no predators of its own. In the illustrative food chain, the small fish is a predator at level 3 and also prey for the large fish at level 4. Separating these relational labels from species names prevents a misleading division of the world into permanent predator and prey categories.

Protein

Words: 11k Articles: 96
Biology OurBigBook.com
A protein is a biological molecule made of one or more polypeptide chains: ordered amino acid residues joined by peptide bonds. Biological translation assembles a chain in the order specified by messenger RNA codons. Protein folding then brings parts of that chain into spatial relationships that support its function. See Cooper, The Cell: protein composition and structure. These processes can overlap in a biological cell; the sequence-to-shape explanation does not require waiting until biological translation finishes before any folding begins. See Cooper, The Cell: protein folding and processing.
The useful connection is from information to physical work. A protein's protein primary structure records an order; its protein tertiary structure can bring distant amino acid residues together at an active site. An enzyme uses such an arrangement to recognize a substrate and accelerate a chemical reaction. Other proteins serve as receptors, membrane transport proteins or structural material. For example, actin assembles into filaments whose mechanical properties can be described by biopolymer mechanics. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: protein function and binding.
Order matters beyond composition. Let A stand for alanine and M for methionine, and read from the N-terminus to the C-terminus. The illustrative strings AMAMAMAMAMAM and AAAAAAMMMMMM each contain exactly six A and six M amino acid residues. Each has 12−1=11 peptide bonds when made into one unbranched polypeptide chain. In the first string all eleven neighboring pairs have different letters; in the second only the pair at positions 6 and 7 does. A composition histogram therefore loses information about which amino acid residues are neighbors. Their arrangements can affect protein folding and function; these short invented strings neither specify a known functional protein nor establish what shape either would adopt.
Protein structure is a moving arrangement, not a permanently rigid outline. Substrate binding can change an enzyme's shape through induced fit, and a functional protein can include flexible regions. Sequence, surroundings and interacting molecules must therefore be considered together. See Alberts et al.: binding, conformational changes and protein function.

Antibody

Protein OurBigBook.com
An antibody is a protein that recognizes particular molecular targets through binding. Antibodies participate in immunity; laboratory assays such as Western blots exploit their selective binding to detect chosen proteins.
An IgG gives a concrete architecture: two immunoglobulin heavy chains and two immunoglobulin light chains, joined by disulfide bonds. Each arm ends in a paratope assembled from an antibody variable region of each kind of chain. The two paratopes recognize the same epitope in this conventional IgG; the flexible hinge allows different arm separations. The antibody constant regions form the remaining portions. This is an illustrative IgG, rather than the architecture of every antibody format. [ref]
Three questions must be kept separate. Antibody specificity asks which antigens are recognized. Antibody affinity describes one paratope–epitope interaction. Avidity describes the combined attachment when several contacts can cooperate. A selective antibody can have modest antibody affinity, and a monoclonal antibody can still show cross-reactivity. For an assay, the practical question is whether the observed readout identifies the intended antigen under the tested conditions; Western blot antibody specificity controls make that question concrete.

Antibody specificity describes preferential recognition of selected epitopes. It is established relative to tested alternatives and assay conditions, rather than inferred from a reagent's name. Western blot antibody specificity controls distinguish recognition of the proposed protein from retained label caused by other material.

Cross-reactivity occurs when an antibody also recognizes another antigen beyond the one against which it was raised. This may involve related features, but obvious overall similarity is not required. [ref]
For an imagined example, a paratope contacts a small surface patch shared by two otherwise different proteins. Both can bind even though their remaining surfaces differ. Increasing antibody concentration can reveal weak binding that was previously undetectable. Conversely, an extra Western blot band need not prove cross-reactivity: the intended protein may occur in multiple forms, or detection reagents may contribute background. The target-deleted and no-primary antibody comparisons under Western blot antibody specificity controls test different explanations.

A monoclonal antibody preparation derives from one selected antibody-producing biological cell and its descendants, or reproduces their specified antibody sequences. Monoclonal describes the origin and composition of the preparation; it does not guarantee absence of cross-reactivity or establish antibody affinity. [ref]

Antibody OurBigBook.com
Avidity is the combined strength of multivalent attachment. An intact IgG can make two contacts when accessible epitopes have suitable spacing. [ref] If one contact breaks while the other remains, the detached arm stays nearby and can bind again before the whole antibody escapes. That geometric advantage does not require changing either paratope's intrinsic antibody affinity. Two arms binding two separate freely moving antigens do not automatically provide the same tethering advantage. Epitope spacing, accessibility and surface density matter; avidity is not obtained by adding two dissociation constants.

Antibody OurBigBook.com
Antibody affinity concerns one paratope binding one epitope. A Fab fragment supplies a single-site comparison. [ref] In the dilute chemical equilibrium model below, smaller dissociation constant Kd​ means larger antibody equilibrium occupancy at the same free antigen concentration. State the antigen, temperature and buffer solution: a dissociation constant is not a context-free score. It does not alone specify how fast attachment or detachment occurs.
Antibody equilibrium occupancy (θ)
Words: 320
Antibody affinity OurBigBook.com
Antibody equilibrium occupancy counts occupied antibody binding sites, rather than retained assay label. For an original 1:1 model, let A denote an unoccupied site, E free antigen bearing one accessible epitope, and AE their complex. At chemical equilibrium, write
A+E⇌AE,c=[E],Kd​=[AE][A]c​,AT​=[A]+[AE],θ=AT​[AE]​=Kd​+cc​.
(32)
Square brackets mean concentrations. The dissociation constant Kd​ here has concentration units. This is the same independent-site calculation as receptor binding occupancy, now applied to an antibody binding site. The last equality follows by substituting [AE]=[A]c/Kd​ into the occupied fraction and cancelling [A].
Assume identical independent sites, reversible 1:1 binding, dilute chemical solution behavior, fixed temperature and buffer solution, and enough time for chemical equilibrium. Exclude two-arm bridging, cross-reactivity and inaccessible sites from this model. Crucially, c is free antigen concentration; substituting the amount supplied per volume requires negligible depletion by binding. Independent IgG arms could obey this model site by site, but it does not describe avidity from bridging a surface.
Stipulate Kd​=20nM, with 1nM=10−9molL−1. Free antigen concentrations 2, 20 and 200nM give θ=1/11, 1/2 and 10/11. A second stipulated dissociation constant of 200nM instead gives θ=1/11 at c=20nM. Both curves approach one at large c: a nearly saturated readout can conceal an antibody affinity difference. These are invented values, with no universal threshold for a useful antibody.
A Western blot readout additionally depends on Western blot transfer, accessible epitopes, loss during washing and Western blot antibody detection. Western blot response saturation can flatten the final signal even when binding itself remains responsive. An ELISA also reports retained label through an enzyme readout, rather than automatically reporting θ. Thus half of an assay's maximum signal need not occur at c=Kd​. Varying free antigen through concentrations near the candidate dissociation constant, while checking depletion and the readout's response, is more informative than comparing a single saturated point.
Antibody surface plasmon resonance experiment
Words: 164
Antibody affinity OurBigBook.com
A concrete comparison used a Biacore T100 with a CM5 chip bearing the target receptor; unused reactive surface groups were blocked. At 25∘C in a pH 7.4 buffer solution, intact IgG and its Fab fragment were injected for 180s at 5μL/min; dissociation was monitored for 3600s. The optical response tracks changes in refractive index near the surface, rather than counting occupied paratopes directly. A reference surface and blank injections corrected background; association and dissociation responses were fitted with a 1:1 model. The reported intact-IgG detachment was slower than that of the Fab fragment. [ref]
This comparison supports format-dependent attachment, not an intrinsic single-site antibody affinity for intact IgG. The reference and blanks address background, not two-arm avidity, surface accessibility or delivery by diffusion. The paper's fitted 1:1 constants alone cannot distinguish those mechanisms. Its Fab fragment comparison therefore motivates specifying the binding format before interpreting a dissociation constant; a good fit does not establish a unique molecular model.

Western blot

Words: 1k Articles: 12
Protein OurBigBook.com
A Western blot detects selected proteins after their separation and transfer to a membrane, using antibodies. In the yeast cross-species complementation experiment, detection helps distinguish failed protein production from failure of an expressed protein to restore growth.
The useful idea is to preserve where proteins migrated in gel electrophoresis, then ask which positions retain an antibody. Western blot separation, Western blot transfer and Western blot antibody detection answer different questions. A band is evidence of retained label at a position; Western blot band interpretation requires Western blot controls before assigning identity or comparing abundance.

Western blot separation

Words: 62
Western blot OurBigBook.com
In the common SDS-PAGE version, protein denaturation and binding of an anionic surfactant reduce differences due to folded shape and intrinsic electric charge. An electric field drives the resulting protein complexes through the gel; smaller chains generally migrate farther. A lane of reference proteins supplies positions for estimating apparent mass. This estimate depends on the separation conditions: it is not a direct weighing of a molecule, and different proteins can migrate together.

Western blot transfer

Words: 220 Articles: 2
Western blot OurBigBook.com
Western blot transfer moves separated proteins out of the gel onto a Western blot membrane, using an electric field across the gel thickness. Maintaining close contact preserves the lane pattern. Contact gaps, incomplete removal from the gel and passage through the receiving sheet can change how much protein is retained.
The original 1979 experiment pressed a wetted, 0.45μm-pore nitrocellulose Western blot membrane against the gel between scouring pads and plastic pipette-tray grids, held by elastic bands. The urea-gel assembly faced the cathode in acidic solution, with 6V/cm applied for one hour; the SDS-PAGE variant reversed polarity and used a glycine/methanol buffer solution. Stained gel/blot pairs checked pattern preservation. Corresponding labelled ribosome protein spots from two gels were compared through radioactive decay readouts after combustion. The stained gel remaining after transfer supplied a removal check; a second receiving sheet revealed breakthrough on overloading. These tests supported recovery for the examined urea-gel proteins, within experimental variation, while the SDS-PAGE results showed unequal staining recovery. Preserved band positions therefore did not establish universal quantitative transfer. [ref]
Western blot membrane
Words: 51 Articles: 1
Western blot transfer OurBigBook.com
A Western blot membrane is a thin protein-binding support that receives the separated pattern. It is a laboratory support, distinct from a cell membrane. Retaining proteins on its surface makes them accessible for Western blot antibody detection.
Nitrocellulose Western blot membrane
Words: 22
Western blot membrane OurBigBook.com
A nitrocellulose Western blot membrane is a Western blot membrane made from nitrated cellulose. Its retention capacity is finite; the original Western blot transfer experiment tested breakthrough with a second receiving sheet.

Words: 107
Western blot OurBigBook.com
Blocking occupies unused binding sites on the Western blot membrane. The primary antibody is applied, unbound material is washed away, and a labelled secondary antibody detects retained primary antibody. A fluorescence label emits detectable light after excitation; an enzyme-linked label can instead generate a colored product or light. Washing reduces background but does not prove that remaining binding is selective.
In the original experiment, blocking used excess protein. An anti-ribosome-protein serum followed by labelled secondary antibody produced colored or fluorescence bands; preimmune serum supplied comparison strips. The color readout was an enzyme reaction product, rather than a measurement of target enzyme activity. [ref]

Words: 87
Western blot OurBigBook.com
Band position gives an apparent mass, not unique protein identity. Intensity depends on retention, epitope recognition and detection response; it does not establish folded state, enzyme activity or successful protein targeting. Missing bands can reflect missing targets or failed Western blot transfer or Western blot antibody detection. [ref]
The yeast cross-species complementation experiment consequently combines two logically different readouts: Western blot evidence about production of an antibody-recognized protein, and growth evidence about functional complementation. A detectable protein need not perform the biological task required for growth.

Western blot OurBigBook.com
Western blot loading controls ask how much sample entered each lane; Western blot transfer controls ask what reached the receiving sheet; Western blot antibody specificity controls ask what the antibodies recognized. Each closes a different gap in Western blot band interpretation.

Western blot controls OurBigBook.com
A Western blot loading control estimates lane-to-lane sample differences. A reference protein, such as actin, must have stable abundance and detection responsive to amount. Equal saturated bands fail to establish equal loading. [ref]

Words: 50
Western blot controls OurBigBook.com
A Western blot transfer control tests retention after Western blot transfer. Total-protein staining of the Western blot membrane can reveal uneven lanes or blank patches; staining the gel after transfer tests what remained behind. Transferred reference bands check selected positions, not recovery of every target. A pretransfer loading image alone cannot establish the amount retained on the receiving sheet.

Western blot controls OurBigBook.com
A known target-containing sample is a positive comparison for Western blot antibody detection. A matched sample with gene deletion supplies a negative comparison: disappearance of the proposed band supports the assignment, while a persisting band indicates binding unrelated to the deleted target. Deletion must actually remove the recognized protein; changes in other proteins can complicate the comparison. Omitting the primary antibody checks binding or background from the secondary antibody and detection reagents, but cannot exclude binding of the primary antibody to an unintended protein. Independent antibodies recognizing different epitopes add evidence. [ref]

Western blot OurBigBook.com
Total-protein Western blot normalization compares a target-band signal with a signal representing many transferred proteins in that lane. It is distinct from measuring one reference protein, and from measuring the target itself. Its denominator is a loading proxy: normalization estimates target abundance relative to detected total protein, rather than target amount per biological cell. Different sample compositions, selective Western blot transfer losses or unequal stain responses can still matter.
For an original calculation, suppose background-corrected target signals IA​=12, IB​=24 and total-protein signals PA​=30, PB​=60 are in their respective proportional response ranges. Then
IA​/PA​IB​/PB​​=12/3024/60​=1.
(33)
The invented signals double together, so this calculation supplies no evidence for a higher target fraction. With IB​=24 but PB​=30, the same calculation gives 2. These examples assume a common target response and a common total-protein response between lanes, negligible remaining background, and comparable target recovery; they do not equate total-protein staining with target abundance. Multiplying both signals in a lane by the same loading factor cancels in their ratio; a selective target loss does not cancel.

Western blot OurBigBook.com
Western blot response saturation means that increasing target amount no longer increases the recorded signal proportionally. It can arise before imaging, through limited binding or reagent availability, as well as through detector limits. Shortening exposure can address a detector limit without repairing an already unresponsive assay. Test the target and normalization readouts with a dilution series under the actual assay conditions; merely seeing a gray band does not establish a proportional response.
In a 2013 methods experiment, a biological cell extract containing added purified yeast protein was separated on gels, transferred with a Trans-Blot Turbo to polymer membranes, and read with an enzyme-linked secondary antibody. A ChemiDoc MP imager and film recorded the same dilution-series blots. The target and an abundant reference protein had different usable response ranges; transferred total-protein imaging and the reference bands did not track loading equally well. This demonstrates the need for assay-specific response checks, rather than a universal conversion from darkness to amount. [ref]
An illustrative response model separates background b, target amount T, retained fraction q, response scale S and characteristic amount K:
I(T)=b+SK+qTqT​,S,K>0,0<q≤1.
(34)
This is an assumed model, not a fitted Western blot calibration. When qT≪K, I−b≈(Sq/K)T. When qT≫K, I−b approaches S. For two otherwise identical lanes, doubling T gives the background-corrected ratio

At qT=K the ratio is 4/3, despite a true twofold amount change. Thus Western blot normalization cannot recover a lost amount difference merely by dividing two saturated readouts.

The amino acid alpha carbon is the backbone carbon carrying the amino acid side chain in the usual protein amino acid residue. A glutamic acid residue is an amino acid residue represented by Glu or E in polypeptide sequence notation. The name denotes an incorporated chain position, as distinguished from a free amino acid molecule.

Polypeptide OurBigBook.com
A peptide bond is the covalent bond between the carboxyl carbon of one amino acid residue and the amino nitrogen of the next. The displayed group shows the usual linkage, with the central carbon–nitrogen connection being the peptide bond. In an intact unbranched chain of n amino acid residues, adjacent positions supply n−1 peptide bonds. Cutting one internal peptide bond produces two fragments; merely changing the chain's shape need not cut it. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e: peptide bonds and protein structure.

Polypeptide OurBigBook.com
The protein backbone is the repeating chain of chemical atoms that connects successive amino acid residues, including their peptide bonds. The attached groups that distinguish amino acids project from this shared framework. Protein folding changes the framework's spatial arrangement while ordinarily preserving its sequence connectivity. See Cooper: polypeptide backbone and attached groups.

Protein OurBigBook.com
Protein structure describes both the chain's chemical organization and its spatial arrangement. Four levels answer different questions: protein primary structure gives the order; protein secondary structure gives recurring local patterns; protein tertiary structure gives one chain's overall arrangement; protein quaternary structure gives the assembly of multiple chains. These are levels of description, not four mandatory stages that every protein must pass through. See Clark, Douglas and Choi: four levels of protein structure.

A protein domain is a distinguishable structural and functional region of a protein. A catalytic protein domain and a binding protein domain can carry out different tasks within one chain.

An SH2 domain is a protein domain that recognizes a phosphotyrosine residue together with surrounding sequence features. This selective binding recruits a protein to a modified receptor or docking protein; it does not itself imply catalysis.[ref]

Protein primary structure

Protein structure OurBigBook.com
The protein primary structure specifies the ordered amino acid residues of each polypeptide chain, joined through peptide bonds. A chain is conventionally written from its N-terminus to its C-terminus. In the broader chemical sense, a complete protein primary structure also specifies covalent bond crosslinks between chain positions, including protein disulfide bonds; a bare sequence string leaves that information unstated. This describes chemical connectivity rather than the spatial arrangement of protein tertiary structure or protein quaternary structure. See IUPAC Gold Book: primary structure, sequence and chain crosslinking and IUPAC-IUB, 3AA-16: writing residue sequences from the amino end. Some conventions reserve protein primary structure for sequence alone and call the complete chemical connectivity the covalent structure; the distinction should be stated when comparing descriptions. See IUPAC-IUB polypeptide-conformation recommendations, section 6.1: the narrower sequence-only convention.
In this toy example M denotes methionine, A alanine and G glycine. Both polypeptide chains have six amino acid residues, five peptide bonds, an M at the N-terminus and a G at the C-terminus. Their amino acid composition is identical, yet position 2 is A in MAGAMG and M in MMAAGG. There are 6!/(2!2!2!)=90 distinct orders with these counts, a multinomial coefficient. Even fixing those two end residues leaves 4!/(1!2!1!)=12 orders. The counts constrain the answer without determining it.
For multiple polypeptide chains, record each sequence separately and specify any protein disulfide bonds between cysteine positions. Mature insulin, for example, has an A chain of 21 amino acid residues and a B chain of 30 amino acid residues. Their combined 51 residues give (21−1)+(30−1)=49 peptide bonds, rather than the 50 of one unbroken 51-residue chain. See Cooper, The Cell: insulin's two chains and cysteine crosslinks, figure 2.16. A protein disulfide bond joins side groups; it does not concatenate the C-terminus of one chain with the N-terminus of another. The three insulin protein disulfide bonds connect A6 to A11 within the A chain, and A7 to B7 and A20 to B19 between chains. Positions are numbered from each chain's N-terminus. See Replacement of the interchain disulfide bridge-forming amino acids A7 and B7 by glutamate impairs the structure and activity of insulin: native disulfide positions.
Why keep this information? Protein primary structure lets us distinguish changes of chemical identity from changes of shape, and compare corresponding positions between proteins. Protein folding can bring distant amino acid residues together at a protein binding site while preserving their sequence. The attractive idea is that a readable linear record can constrain a complicated three-dimensional object; it is not, by itself, a guarantee of a unique fold in every environment. See protein folding and the ribonuclease A refolding experiment. Merely bending an intact chain preserves its protein primary structure; hydrolysis of a peptide bond, or changing which positions a protein disulfide bond connects, changes its chemical connectivity.

The amino acid composition lists amounts or proportions of the different amino acid residues in a protein or specified polypeptide chain, without giving their order. The toy MAGAMG and MMAAGG each have counts M:2, A:2, G:2, or a proportion 1/3 of each. Knowing composition therefore does not supply protein primary structure. Sanger's account begins by distinguishing the already available composition measurements from the largely unknown residue order. See Sanger's authored 1985 account of the move from composition to terminal-residue analysis.

Amino acid composition OurBigBook.com
Glycine is an amino acid, represented by Gly or G for an incorporated amino acid residue. Its amino acid side chain is a hydrogen chemical atom. It was identified at one insulin N-terminus in Sanger's insulin sequencing experiment. See IUPAC Blue Book, P-103.1: amino-acid names, symbols and structures.
Phenylalanine (Phe, F)

Amino acid composition OurBigBook.com
Phenylalanine is an amino acid, represented by Phe or F for an incorporated amino acid residue. It was identified at the other insulin N-terminus in Sanger's insulin sequencing experiment. See IUPAC Blue Book, P-103.1: amino-acid names and symbols.
Cysteine (Cys, C)
Words: 55
Amino acid composition OurBigBook.com
Cysteine is an amino acid whose amino acid side chain contains sulfur, represented by Cys or C for an incorporated amino acid residue. Two cysteine positions can be joined through a protein disulfide bond. See IUPAC Blue Book, P-103.1: cysteine's structure and symbols and Cooper: cysteine crosslinks in proteins. The C in a sequence means cysteine, whereas the C-end label in the toy diagram means C-terminus.
Sanger's insulin sequencing experiment
Words: 513
Protein primary structure OurBigBook.com
The motivating question was experimental: how could one recover the order in a protein when breaking all its peptide bonds destroys that order? Frederick Sanger and colleagues used complementary tests on portions of insulin. The following is an explanation of their evidence, not a laboratory recipe.
First, mark ends before destroying the chains. Sanger used the colored reagent fluorodinitrobenzene, abbreviated FDNB, to label free amino groups. After acid hydrolysis, the attached label remained on the end-residue products. Separating these derivatives by their different movement through solvents and comparing them with reference derivatives made the labels readable. The N-terminus products identified glycine and phenylalanine. Sanger emphasized that finding a stable label and a way to separate its products were both essential. See Sanger, Citation Classic (1985), discussing The free amino groups of insulin (1945). FDNB also labels suitable free amino groups on amino acid side chains, so a labeled product is not automatically an N-terminus product. See Sanger, The Chemistry of Insulin, Nobel lecture (1958), pp. 546–547.
Next, separate chains and preserve local order. Oxidation with performic acid broke the protein disulfide bonds, allowing A and B chains to be isolated. Partial hydrolysis and enzyme treatments produced fragments; these were separated and their composition and local sequences characterized. Overlaps between different fragment sets linked smaller sequences into longer ones. Many more fragments than minimally necessary were checked for consistency. See Sanger's authored Nobel lecture, pp. 547–552: chain separation, fragment analysis and sequence reconstruction.
The toy fragments make the logic visible. Suppose one cut pattern yields MAG and AMG, and another yields MA, GA and MG. The first set alone permits MAGAMG or AMGMAG. The fragment GA in the second set crosses the MAG–AMG boundary in MAGAMG; it does not occur in AMGMAG. Among concatenations of the first set, therefore, the second set selects MAGAMG. This example assumes intact, correctly identified fragments from one homogeneous chain and known fragment membership in each cut pattern. Repeated stretches, missing fragments or sample mixtures can leave ambiguities; the picture illustrates inference from overlaps, not a universal guarantee of reconstruction.
Finally, determine the protein disulfide bonds separately. Oxidation used to separate whole chains erases their original connections. Sanger and colleagues instead studied fragments still joined by protein disulfide bonds, then oxidized the isolated joined fragments to identify their component pieces and locate the connected chain regions. An important trap was rearrangement of disulfide bonds during treatment: products can acquire connections absent from the starting protein. Their work therefore had to establish conditions that prevented rearrangement before interpreting a linked fragment as evidence. See Ryle and Sanger, A Disulphide Interchange Reaction, Nature 171, 1025–1026 (1953) and Sanger's Nobel lecture, pp. 553–554: preserving and identifying disulfide connections. The result was an experimentally constrained chemical structure rather than a composition list or a photograph of a fold.
Insulin
Words: 573 Articles: 3
Protein primary structure OurBigBook.com
Insulin is a protein hormone. Its mature form has two polypeptide chains; identifying their sequences and protein disulfide bonds provided the motivating example in Sanger's insulin sequencing experiment. See Cooper: insulin as a two-chain hormone, figure 2.16.
A meal illustrates the insulin side of blood glucose homeostasis: rising glucose stimulates beta cells in the pancreatic islets, and released insulin favors uptake and storage of fuel. Alpha cells produce glucagon, while delta cells produce somatostatin, which inhibits release of both insulin and glucagon. The pancreas therefore contains interacting sensor and secretory biological cells, rather than one undifferentiated source of hormones. [ref]
Insulin and glucagon are peptide hormones, built from amino acid residues joined by peptide bonds; glucose is a small carbohydrate molecule. A hormone changes signal transduction, not the identity of the fuel it regulates. Human mature insulin has 51 amino acid residues in two polypeptide chains. Beta cells process proinsulin to insulin and C-peptide, storing the products in secretory granules for exocytosis. Increased glucose metabolism raises the ATP-to-ADP ratio, tending to close ATP-sensitive potassium channels; depolarization and entry of calcium ions then trigger exocytosis. This is an important triggering pathway, with additional amplification and modulatory inputs.[ref]
Binding to the insulin receptor, a receptor tyrosine kinase, starts phosphorylation of the receptor and insulin receptor substrates. Recruitment of phosphoinositide 3-kinase and activation of Akt transmit a major metabolic branch. In skeletal muscle and adipose tissue, that branch helps move GLUT4 to the cell membrane, increasing glucose uptake by facilitated diffusion. GLUT4 is a membrane transport protein, not an insulin receptor. Insulin also favors glycogenesis in skeletal muscle and the liver, and inhibits lipolysis in adipose tissue. In the liver, suppression of glucose output involves enzyme regulation, gene expression, and indirect changes in substrate supply. Its relative direct and indirect contributions are more complex than a single Akt arrow. [ref]
Insulin is not a universal permission slip for glucose entry: red blood cells and much of the nervous system use uptake mechanisms that are not acutely dependent on insulin. Nor does the liver use the same GLUT4 switch as skeletal muscle. This is why reduced insulin action can change blood glucose dramatically without stopping all glucose uptake. [ref]
Diabetes can disrupt production, response, and counterregulation. Type 1 diabetes usually involves destruction of beta cells and severe loss of endogenous insulin; type 2 diabetes combines insulin resistance with insufficient beta cell compensation. High circulating insulin can therefore coexist with impaired insulin action. Inappropriate glucagon release can add to excessive liver glucose output, and the response to low blood glucose can also be impaired: "more glucagon" is not a complete description of diabetes. These distinctions explain mechanisms, rather than prescribe treatment. [ref] [ref]

Glucose clamp technique
Words: 169
Insulin OurBigBook.com
Glucose clamp technique: a method for quantifying insulin secretion and resistance. by R. A. DeFronzo and others separates two questions. In a hyperglycemic clamp, variable glucose infusion holds blood glucose above baseline while sampled insulin reports the response. The 1979 article's abstract reports an early release burst followed by a slower rise. In a euglycemic insulin clamp, infused insulin is held elevated and variable glucose infusion holds blood glucose at baseline. Frequent blood sampling, a glucose analyzer, and controlled infusion apparatus make the imposed concentration a maintained condition rather than an uncontrolled consequence. [ref][ref]
The maintained glucose level controls an important confounder: a change in blood glucose would itself change uptake and hormone release. At a steady state, conservation of mass gives uptake equal to infused supply plus endogenous production, after accounting for losses. Consequently, infusion alone estimates uptake only if endogenous production is negligible and the other balance assumptions hold. Labelled glucose measurements can estimate residual endogenous production; matching infused insulin across comparisons matters. Whole-body uptake cannot by itself identify the responding tissue, and plasma insulin reflects both release and removal. This interpretation uses the accessible 1979 abstract and the later authored methods chapter; the original article's full methods were not available for inspection.[ref]

Protein secondary structure

Words: 874 Articles: 6
Protein structure OurBigBook.com
Protein secondary structure consists of recurring local arrangements of the protein backbone, notably the alpha helix and beta sheet. Backbone hydrogen bonds help stabilize these patterns. A beta sheet can bring together stretches far apart in the protein primary structure; local refers to the pattern of backbone geometry, not necessarily neighboring sequence positions. See Alberts et al.: alpha helices, beta sheets and backbone interactions.
Alpha helix (α)
Words: 86
Protein secondary structure OurBigBook.com
An alpha helix is a coiled protein secondary structure with a repeated pattern of backbone hydrogen bonds. In the standard pattern, the backbone group of amino acid residue i bonds to that of residue i+4: for example, positions 2 and 6. This is an additional spatial interaction, not a replacement peptide bond between those positions. Pauling, Corey and Branson proposed the helical arrangement in their 1951 paper by reasoning from the geometry of small molecules. See Pauling, Corey and Branson, The Structure of Proteins: Two Hydrogen-Bonded Helical Configurations of the Polypeptide Chain, PNAS 37, 205–211 (1951).
Beta sheet (β)
Words: 692 Articles: 3
Protein secondary structure OurBigBook.com
A beta sheet consists of extended stretches of protein backbone lying alongside one another, joined by backbone hydrogen bonds. The stretches can belong to different portions of the same polypeptide chain or to different chains.
Each extended stretch is a beta strand. Neighboring beta strands pack side by side, with repeated backbone hydrogen bonds between their backbone C=O and N−H groups: the oxygen is a hydrogen bond acceptor, and the backbone nitrogen with its attached hydrogen provides a hydrogen bond donor. These are interactions of the shared protein backbone, not merely contacts between amino acid side chains. Unlike an alpha helix, a beta sheet joins adjacent extended stretches rather than coiling one stretch around an axis. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 3.4: backbone groups in secondary structure.
Read each beta strand in the sequence direction from the N-terminus toward the C-terminus, even when it is an internal part of a longer polypeptide chain. In a parallel beta sheet, neighboring beta strands run in the same N→C direction; in an antiparallel beta sheet, they run in opposite N→C directions. A three-strand example can therefore have arrows right–right–right or right–left–right. A beta sheet can also mix the two arrangements. Direction does not identify chain membership: a single polypeptide chain can fold back to supply several beta strands, and different polypeptide chains can contribute to one beta sheet. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: beta-sheet strand arrangements.
The pleated appearance comes from the geometry of the protein backbone. Successive amino acid residues carry amino acid side chains on alternating faces of an ideal beta strand, conventionally drawn above and below the sheet. The attachment positions are the amino acid alpha carbons. Thus a six-position cartoon has groups 1, 3 and 5 on one face and 2, 4 and 6 on the other. This alternation is a spatial pattern, not a rule that alternating positions must contain identical amino acids. See Clark, Douglas and Choi: side chains above and below the pleats.
Real beta sheets commonly twist and curve; pleating does not make them perfectly flat plates. Which beta strands are neighbors, how connecting regions join them, and how their faces pack are features of the three-dimensional protein structure. An alternating pattern in the protein primary structure alone neither establishes a beta sheet nor specifies a unique fold independently of surroundings and interacting molecules. See Breda et al., Protein Structure, Modelling and Applications: extended strands, sheet twist and three-dimensional organization and protein folding.
Why this arrangement is useful: repeated backbone hydrogen bonds organize extended chain regions into a framework that can contribute to the interior of a folded protein. Amino acid side chains and connecting loops give that framework chemical variety and can shape a protein binding site for a ligand. Its attractive feature is the combination of a reusable backbone pattern with variable exposed groups: similar beta sheets can support different recognition surfaces. See Alberts et al.: beta-sheet cores and loops that form binding sites.
Historically, Linus Pauling and Robert B. Corey published The Pleated Sheet, a New Layer Configuration of Polypeptide Chains in PNAS 37, 251–256 (1951). They reasoned from peptide bond geometry and possible backbone hydrogen bonds, proposing an idealized layer rather than measuring every modern beta sheet. Their initial model should not be identified with all present-day beta sheet geometries; they published further pleated-sheet configurations later in 1951. See Pauling and Corey: original 1951 paper and scan, [ref], and Pauling and Corey, Configurations of Polypeptide Chains With Favored Orientations Around Single Bonds: Two New Pleated Sheets, PNAS 37, 729–740 (1951).

A beta strand is an extended segment of protein backbone in the geometry characteristic of a beta sheet. Several beta strands can associate through backbone hydrogen bonds. A beta strand need not be an entire polypeptide chain.

A parallel beta sheet has neighboring beta strands running in the same direction along their amino acid residue sequences, from the N-terminus toward the C-terminus.
Antiparallel beta sheet

An antiparallel beta sheet has neighboring beta strands running in opposite N→C sequence directions. This specifies strand orientation rather than whether the beta strands belong to one polypeptide chain or several.
Backbone hydrogen bond
