Protein secondary structure OurBigBook.com
A backbone hydrogen bond is a hydrogen bond involving groups of the protein backbone, typically a backbone oxygen chemical atom and a hydrogen chemical atom already joined by a covalent bond to backbone nitrogen. It can connect positions that are not adjacent along the polypeptide chain. The peptide bonds still determine which amino acid residues are consecutive. See the original structural argument cited under alpha helix.

Protein tertiary structure

Words: 164 Articles: 2
Protein structure OurBigBook.com
The protein tertiary structure is the overall spatial arrangement of one polypeptide chain. It includes how its protein secondary structures and intervening regions fit together. For example, the schematic under protein places positions 4 and 9 near each other despite their separation in protein primary structure. Such cooperation can help construct an active site; sequence distance and spatial separation answer different questions. Hydrophobicity, backbone hydrogen bonds and other interactions help stabilize folds, and some proteins additionally contain protein disulfide bonds. See Cooper: tertiary structure and interactions between chain regions.
Protein binding site

Protein tertiary structure OurBigBook.com
A protein binding site is a region of a protein structure that interacts with a ligand. Its arrangement of amino acid residues helps determine recognition; connecting loops supported by a beta sheet can contribute to it. An enzyme's active site binds a substrate and accelerates a chemical reaction. See Alberts et al.: protein binding sites and active sites.
Protein disulfide bond (S−S)

Protein tertiary structure OurBigBook.com
A protein disulfide bond is a disulfide bond linking two sulfur chemical atoms carried by suitable amino acid residues. It can connect distant portions of a polypeptide chain or different chains. See Cooper: sulfur-containing residues and disulfide crosslinks. The four internal protein disulfide bonds of ribonuclease A are central to the ribonuclease A refolding experiment; breaking these crosslinks need not break the peptide bonds along its protein backbone.

Protein quaternary structure

Words: 61
Protein structure OurBigBook.com
The protein quaternary structure is the arrangement of multiple polypeptide chains in a functional assembly. A single-chain protein has protein tertiary structure without requiring protein quaternary structure. For an exact bookkeeping example, two intact model chains of twelve amino acid residues each contain 2×12=24 residues and 2×11=22 peptide bonds. Assembly alone adds no peptide bond joining their ends. Stable functional assembly should also be distinguished from protein aggregation. See Alberts et al.: proteins as assemblies of polypeptide subunits.

Protein folding

Words: 268 Articles: 1
Protein OurBigBook.com
Protein folding is the process by which a polypeptide chain acquires an organized spatial arrangement. The interactions of its amino acid residues with one another and the surroundings favor some arrangements over others. Protein folding can bring chemically useful groups together at an active site without changing their order along the protein backbone. Its importance is practical: knowing a sequence alone does not tell us whether a sample has the structure needed for function. See Cooper: acquiring functional protein structure.
The ribonuclease A refolding experiment showed that an isolated protein could recover its native properties without a pre-existing folded template under suitable laboratory conditions. Anfinsen interpreted this through a thermodynamic hypothesis: the native arrangement minimizes the whole system's Gibbs free energy in the appropriate environment. His Nobel lecture was delivered on 11 December 1972 and published in Science in 1973. The specified environment is part of the claim, not a disposable qualification. See Anfinsen, Principles that Govern the Folding of Protein Chains, Science 181, 223–230 (1973): Nobel lecture, especially p. 223.
This does not imply that every protein rapidly folds unaided. Molecular chaperones can assist protein folding and reduce protein aggregation; required partners, surroundings and time still matter. Goloubinoff and colleagues' 1989 reconstitution experiments demonstrated assistance from two molecular chaperones and ATP in recovering an active enzyme from unfolded chains. This is experimental evidence that assistance can matter even when the chains already have their specified sequences. See Goloubinoff, Christeller, Gatenby and Lorimer, 1989: chaperone-assisted reconstitution of an active enzyme.

Chaperone (protein)

Words: 45
Protein folding OurBigBook.com
A molecular chaperone is a protein that assists other proteins in reaching or maintaining useful arrangements, for example by limiting unwanted association during protein folding. Assistance does not rewrite the client's protein primary structure. In a crowded cytoplasm, reducing protein aggregation can make successful protein folding more reliable. See Cooper: molecular chaperones and folding assistance.

Denaturation (biochemistry)

Words: 267 Articles: 1
Protein OurBigBook.com
Protein denaturation is the loss of a protein's native spatial organization, often with loss of biological function. Changes in temperature, pH or surroundings can disrupt protein secondary structure, protein tertiary structure or protein quaternary structure. Protein denaturation ordinarily preserves the peptide bonds and protein primary structure; it is different from cutting the chain. Recovery by protein folding is possible in some cases, but removing the denaturing conditions does not guarantee that every protein recovers. See Clark, Douglas and Choi: denaturation, environmental conditions and loss of function.
In the diagram, unfolding preserves all eleven peptide bonds. Cleaving the connection between positions 6 and 7 leaves two six-residue fragments: each contains five peptide bonds, so there are 5+5=10 in total. Simply cooling or otherwise restoring suitable conditions cannot recover the original chain by protein folding alone; the missing covalent bond would have to be remade. Conversely, protein aggregation can impede recovery without breaking any peptide bond. These distinctions explain why loss of function does not by itself reveal whether a protein unfolded, associated with other chains, or suffered chemical damage.

Protein aggregation

Words: 52
Denaturation (biochemistry) OurBigBook.com
Protein aggregation is the association of proteins into clusters, often involving exposed regions of partly folded or unfolded polypeptide chains. It can prevent recovery of normal function while leaving the protein primary structures intact. It is distinct from both unfolding one chain and the functional assembly described by protein quaternary structure. See Cooper: partly folded chains, aggregation and chaperone protection.

Ribonuclease A

Words: 310 Articles: 1
Protein OurBigBook.com
Ribonuclease A is an enzyme that catalyzes cleavage of RNA. The bovine pancreatic ribonuclease A studied by Anfinsen and colleagues has 124 amino acid residues and four internal protein disulfide bonds. It supplied a particularly informative test of the relationship between protein primary structure, protein folding and biological function: recovery could be measured through restored enzyme activity. See the primary sources under ribonuclease A refolding experiment.

Ribonuclease A refolding experiment

Words: 262
Ribonuclease A OurBigBook.com
Anfinsen, Haber, Sela and White's 1961 experiments began by treating bovine pancreatic ribonuclease A with mercaptoethanol in 8molL−1 urea. Urea promotes unfolding; mercaptoethanol breaks protein disulfide bonds. The peptide bonds along the chain remain intact. After separating the chain from those reagents, the authors allowed its reactive sulfur groups to form protein disulfide bonds in the presence of molecular oxygen, at pH 8.2 and temperature 23–24∘C. They examined protein concentrations of 0.1 and 2.0mgmL−1. Measurements showed recovery of native properties under these conditions; the isolated major component had normal activity toward both RNA and a synthetic substrate. See Anfinsen, Haber, Sela and White, The Kinetics of Formation of Native Ribonuclease during Oxidation of the Reduced Polypeptide Chain, PNAS 47, 1309–1314 (1961), pp. 1309–1311.
The observation supports the sufficiency of that intact sequence to recover native protein structure in the tested surroundings without a folded template. It does not establish that every protein refolds, that the original living biological cell needed no assistance, or that activity always returns immediately. Protein folding, forming protein disulfide bonds and recovering an active site are related processes rather than interchangeable measurements.
Anfinsen's lecture also discusses forming protein disulfide bonds while the chain remains in concentrated urea. This gave mostly inactive material; after removing urea, a small amount of mercaptoethanol permitted rearrangement toward the native form. As an exact combinatorial check, eight labeled reactive sulfur groups have 7×5×3×1=105 ways to be paired into four protein disulfide bonds: choose the partner of one group, then repeat with the unpaired groups. Only one pairing is the native one. Equal counting does not mean that all pairings are equally likely experimentally, nor that actual protein folding searches them uniformly. See Anfinsen's Nobel lecture, 1973 publication: scrambled ribonuclease and the 105 pairings, p. 223.

Lysozyme is a protein enzyme that attacks the peptidoglycan of bacterial cell walls. Its active site is a cleft in the folded protein structure, where a suitable substrate can interact with positioned chemical groups. This illustrates why possessing the right amino acid residues is insufficient if their spatial arrangement is lost. See Alberts et al.: lysozyme as a worked example of protein binding and enzyme function.
A concrete structural example is Cheetham, Artymiuk and Phillips's 1992 study of hen egg-white lysozyme bound to a short carbohydrate that inhibits its action. The bound carbohydrate occupies part of the active site; it is not a reacting substrate in this complex. The study describes specific interactions and changes of shape accompanying binding. Thus a real binding site has chemical interactions and flexibility as well as a geometric outline. See Cheetham, Artymiuk and Phillips, 1992: structure of a lysozyme complex with bound inhibitor and RCSB PDB entry 1HEW: the authors' structure and bound three-unit carbohydrate. Receptor (biochemistry)

Words: 3k Articles: 15
Protein OurBigBook.com
A biochemical receptor is a protein that recognizes a signal and couples its detection to a biological effect. Its binding partner is a ligand; recognition depends on compatible shape and chemical interactions at a binding site within the protein structure. Specificity is selective recognition, not a guarantee that only one ligand can bind. Binding also need not activate the receptor: a competing ligand may occupy it while preventing activation by another ligand. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 4th edition: protein binding and specificity.
Compare a cell-surface receptor, accessible to an extracellular ligand, with an intracellular receptor, whose ligand must reach the interior. A cell-surface receptor can detect a hydrophilic ligand without transporting it through the cell membrane. In contrast, some membrane-permeable signals reach intracellular receptors that regulate gene expression. Location and downstream coupling are separate distinctions: an ionotropic receptor directly gates an ion channel, whereas a metabotropic receptor works through intracellular signal transduction. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 9.1: receptor locations and mechanisms.
Receptor binding occupancy quantifies recognition separately from response. A dissociation constant measures binding in a specified equilibrium model; it does not by itself predict the cellular effect. This separation is useful when comparing signals that bind equally well but produce different responses, or when interpreting a binding experiment alongside a functional measurement.

Ionotropic receptor

Words: 528
Receptor (biochemistry) OurBigBook.com
An ionotropic receptor is a receptor in which binding of a ligand directly gates an ion channel within the same protein complex. The binding site detects the chemical signal; the pore supplies a path across the cell membrane. At a chemical synapse, a neurotransmitter therefore changes synaptic conductance without an obligatory intervening G protein or second messenger. [ref]
A familiar example is the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor of skeletal muscle: acetylcholine binding opens a pore passing cations, including sodium and potassium. The muscarinic acetylcholine receptor instead uses intracellular signal transduction; the same neurotransmitter can engage different mechanisms. Direct gating does not mean that an ionotropic receptor pumps ions: electrochemical gradients drive passage through the open ion channel. Nor does “ionotropic” specify excitation. The reversal potential, initial membrane potential and other conductances determine whether the effect favors an action potential, causes hyperpolarization, or supplies shunting inhibition. [ref]
A concrete electrical approximation separates opening from drive. Let N identical ion channels each have open-channel electrical conductance γ and opening probability p(t). At fixed membrane potential V, with common reversal potential Erev​, the expected value of inward-positive electric current is
Iin​(t)=Nγp(t)(Erev​−V).
(36)
For stipulated values N=100, γ=20pS, p=0.2, V=−60mV and Erev​=0, the mean open count is 20, the population electrical conductance is 0.4nS and Iin​=24pA. One open ion channel carries 1.2pA. These are illustrative values, not measurements. At V=Erev​, the net electric current vanishes despite open ion channels; neither binding nor opening alone determines the readout. The approximation omits changes in ion concentrations and voltage-dependent open-channel electrical conductance.
A motivating experiment made the elementary electrical events visible. As Bert Sakmann recounts, chronically denervated frog muscle fibers had acetylcholine-sensitive receptors spread beyond the original nerve contact. Mild enzyme treatment exposed the cell membrane; a polished glass pipette sealed over a small patch to reduce background noise. Two intracellular electrodes held the local membrane potential through voltage clamp, while the patch pipette recorded tiny electric currents. Applying suberyldicholine, a ligand that activates the acetylcholine receptor and prolongs openings, revealed abrupt, approximately rectangular current events. Their amplitudes agreed reasonably with estimates from whole-membrane current fluctuations. This established discrete opening and closing events; it did not make every ligand response instantaneous. Background noise and finite recording bandwidth concealed sufficiently small or brief events.[ref]
Recording an intact membrane patch alone does not exclude intracellular relays. Tank, Huganir, Greengard and Webb supplied a complementary isolation test in 1983: they purified nicotinic acetylcholine receptors from an electric ray's electric organ, incorporated them into artificial lipid membranes, and fused small vesicles into larger vesicles by freezing and thawing. Sealed glass-pipette recordings from isolated membrane patches resolved functional ion channels with properties resembling those in muscle. Removing the intact cytoplasm and its signaling machinery supports the sufficiency of the receptor complex for channel function; an artificial lipid environment still cannot reproduce every native regulatory interaction.[ref]
Direct gating supports millisecond communication at many chemical synapses. Response duration also depends on neurotransmitter clearance, binding and channel-state transitions. Continued ligand exposure can prolong activity. Classify an ionotropic receptor by its direct connection between recognition and pore gating, rather than a universal duration cutoff. [ref]

Metabotropic receptor

Words: 920 Articles: 3
Receptor (biochemistry) OurBigBook.com
A metabotropic receptor couples ligand recognition to intracellular signal transduction, which can regulate a separate ion channel, alter enzyme activity or change gene expression. In the usual neurotransmitter context, metabotropic receptors are G protein-coupled receptors: receptor activation is relayed by a G protein. There need not be a change in membrane potential at all. [ref]
Two routes should be distinguished. An activated G protein can regulate an ion channel locally at the cell membrane, without an obligatory diffusible second messenger. Alternatively, it can regulate an enzyme that changes the availability of a second messenger, such as cAMP or inositol trisphosphate. Downstream proteins then change channel opening, phosphorylation or other cellular activities. The receptor, G protein, second messenger and final target are distinct components; an activated G protein is a relay protein, rather than itself a small-molecule second messenger.[ref]
Do not turn this useful chemical synapse classification into the claim that every receptor is a GPCR, or that every indirect response must pass through a G protein. For example, the insulin receptor is an enzyme-linked cell-surface receptor whose intracellular catalytic activity initiates protein phosphorylation. Intracellular receptors supply another category. “Metabotropic” commonly names the GPCR branch in neuroscience; the broader idea of biochemical coupling does not make all non-channel receptors structurally identical. [ref]
Separating recognition from execution allows signal amplification and branching. A persistently activated receptor can activate several relay proteins; a regulated enzyme can produce many second messenger molecules. As an explicitly invented count example, suppose one activated receptor activates four relay proteins during one interval, and each relay activates a distinct enzyme that produces fifteen second messenger molecules during the next interval. With sufficient substrates and no loss, this gives 4×15=60 molecules. Those counts do not specify a physiological gain or response duration. A directly gated ion channel also passes many ions while open, so amplification is not an exclusive property of metabotropic receptors: always name the input and output being compared. [ref]
A particularly instructive electrophysiology experiment separated a chemical trigger from the ion channel carrying its eventual electric current. In 1987, Hirono, Ito and Sugiyama injected messenger RNA from rat brain into frog egg cells, then tested acquired responses to neurotensin and muscarinic acetylcholine stimulation. Under voltage clamp at −60mV, neurotensin elicited transient, oscillatory inward electric currents after a delay of several tens of seconds. This delay refers to that response and preparation. Reversal potential measurements implicated increased permeability to chloride anions, rather than a pore specific to the applied ligand. Both neurotensin and acetylcholine responses were inhibited by pertussis toxin, which interferes with susceptible G proteins, and by intracellular EGTA, which binds free calcium. Injecting inositol trisphosphate mimicked the responses; a large prior dose of inositol trisphosphate reduced subsequent responses to either extracellular signal. These interventions implicate a shared intracellular relay and calcium-dependent channel opening.[ref]
The informative comparison with the nicotinic acetylcholine receptor experiment is mechanistic: an extracellular ligand can produce an inward electric current either by directly gating the pore or by mobilizing an intracellular second messenger and stored calcium that activate another pore. Intracellular inositol trisphosphate bypasses reception, whereas EGTA tests the need for free calcium. However, neither inhibition nor mimicry alone identifies every molecular connection: a perturbation can affect several targets, and an injected mediator can activate a pathway without proving that it is the only natural route. The egg cell's endogenous machinery and the mixed messenger RNA preparation also limit extrapolation to an intact neuron. The experiment establishes functional coupling in its preparation, rather than the exact molecular composition or timing of every metabotropic receptor.
Even G protein-dependent channel regulation need not involve a lengthy second messenger cascade. Pfaffinger and colleagues reported in 1985 that acetylcholine-evoked potassium channel activation in embryonic chick atrial cells required intracellular GTP, a guanine-containing nucleotide, and was abolished by pertussis-toxin pretreatment. Changes in cyclic nucleotides, including cAMP, did not account for the channel response. The report discusses intrinsic activation delays of roughly 30–100ms, illustrating relatively rapid metabotropic receptor action. These observations support a G protein coupling step without cyclic-nucleotide second messengers; they do not by themselves exclude every possible intermediary or prove the specific subunit-channel interaction.[ref]
A small timing model makes the extra steps visible without inventing an experimental trace. Let u(t) jump from zero to one at t=0 and remain on. For a direct-gating model output d, one relay variable x, and its downstream output y, take zero initial conditions and
τd​dtdd​=u−d,τx​dtdx​=u−x,τy​dtdy​=x−y.
(37)
All outputs are normalized dimensionless variables; they are neither recorded electric currents nor fitted concentrations. With illustrative time constants τd​=2ms, τx​=20ms and τy​=100ms, their exponential function solutions for t≥0 are
d(t)=1−e−t/τd​,x(t)=1−e−t/τx​,y(t)=1−τy​−τx​τy​e−t/τy​−τx​e−t/τx​​.
(38)
Initially d′(0)=1/τd​, while y′(0)=0 because its relay must first build up. Both outputs eventually approach one. Equal normalized final values do not imply equal biological amplitudes or absence of signal amplification; normalization deliberately removes that question.
The model's useful feature is the delayed buildup created by sequential relaxation, not its arbitrary numbers. Actual kinetics also depend on ligand delivery, relay deactivation, neurotransmitter clearance and the final target. A local G protein route can act promptly, while an ionotropic receptor can remain active during continued exposure or feed a longer-lasting intracellular response. The beauty of metabotropic receptor coupling is its flexibility: the same recognition event can adjust electrical responsiveness and other cellular tasks through different targets. To classify an observed response, combine timing with molecular identity and controlled perturbations.

A receptor tyrosine kinase combines extracellular ligand recognition with an intracellular protein kinase protein domain. A membrane-spanning segment connects these parts across the cell membrane: the signal changes the intracellular machinery without requiring the ligand to enter the cytosol. The protein kinase transfers a phosphate group from ATP to selected tyrosine residues on proteins, including the receptor itself.[ref]
This architecture makes a reception event useful in two ways: it can change catalytic activity and assemble a local group of signaling proteins. Trans-autophosphorylation can create phosphotyrosine residues recognized by SH2 domains. Recruitment positions a downstream enzyme or relay protein near its partners. Neither every modified site nor every recruited protein has the same effect; association is a specific molecular connection, rather than a universal command to activate everything nearby.[ref]
Compare the epidermal growth factor receptor with the insulin receptor. Their common topology does not impose one activation geometry or make assembly equivalent to activity. The receptor phosphorylation assay consequently needs more than evidence that two protein chains associate.

Insulin receptor OurBigBook.com
An insulin receptor substrate is a docking protein phosphorylated by the activated insulin receptor. Its phosphotyrosine residues recruit downstream signaling proteins, including SH2 domain-containing components of phosphoinositide 3-kinase. This connects reception to the pathway described under insulin, rather than making the insulin receptor substrate another extracellular ligand.[ref]
Receptor phosphorylation assay
Words: 543 Articles: 1
Receptor tyrosine kinase OurBigBook.com
A receptor phosphorylation assay asks whether, and how much, a specified receptor is modified by phosphorylation under defined conditions. It is distinct from a binding assay for receptor binding occupancy, a test of protein kinase activity on a supplied substrate, and a test of downstream signal transduction. Those measurements answer related but different questions.
For a Western blot implementation, compare matched samples with ligand omitted or added, detect a specified phosphorylated epitope, and separately detect total receptor abundance. Preserve the sampled state by stopping further enzyme reactions during sample preparation; otherwise protein kinase or protein phosphatase activity after sampling can change the result. A general anti-phosphotyrosine residue antibody recognizes many modified proteins; a site-selective antibody gives a narrower readout, but still needs Western blot antibody specificity controls.
Reason through the controls before interpreting the difference. Loss of the proposed signal after receptor-specific gene deletion supports protein identity. Treatment with a protein phosphatase, alongside preservation of the total-receptor signal, tests phosphate-dependent recognition. Western blot loading controls and Western blot transfer controls address sample recovery; a usable detection range addresses Western blot response saturation. Lower signal after perturbing protein kinase activity supports dependence on that perturbation, but alternative targets and altered receptor abundance can complicate the inference. These are proposed assay comparisons, not outcomes attributed to the historical membrane experiment.
An original idealized measurement model explains the normalization. Let N be the retained number of receptor molecules, f the fraction carrying the selected modified epitope, and cp​,ct​>0 fixed detection gains. After subtracting their respective backgrounds, suppose the phosphorylated and total-receptor signals lie in a linear response range:
A=cp​Nf,B=ct​N,BA​=ct​cp​​f.
(39)
Dividing by total receptor cancels N under these assumptions. It differs from total-protein Western blot normalization, whose denominator includes many other proteins. For invented values cp​=ct​=1, samples with (N,f)=(100,0.2) and (200,0.2) give A=20 and 40, but both give A/B=0.2. Twice the phospho signal here means twice the retained receptor amount, with no change in fractional modification. Unequal recovery, changed epitope accessibility, nonzero uncorrected background or Western blot response saturation invalidates the cancellation. Unknown relative gains prevent reading an absolute modified fraction directly from the ratio.
Ligand-dependent membrane phosphorylation experiment
Words: 203
Receptor phosphorylation assay OurBigBook.com
A motivating experiment used isolated membranes from A-431 biological cells, which supplied abundant EGFR. Separate membrane aliquots were incubated at 0∘C with ATP carrying radioactive phosphorus in its terminal phosphate group, plus magnesium or manganese ions. Radioactivity in material recovered by chemical acid-induced precipitation supplied the readout. Adding EGF beforehand enhanced incorporation relative to the unstimulated preparation; this placed a ligand-dependent biochemical response in a cell-free membrane system.[ref]
The follow-up comparisons separated increased addition from suppressed removal: phosphate removal was rapid but unaffected by EGF, and anti-EGF antibody reversed activation by removing the ligand. These observations support reversible regulation of membrane-associated protein kinase activity.[ref] Total incorporation alone cannot identify which protein or amino acid residue received the label, prove intrinsic receptor catalysis, or predict an intact biological cell's response.
The same account records an instructive identification error: receptor phosphorylation was initially assigned to the wrong amino acid residue because released modified amino acids migrated together in the electrophoretic electric field. Reanalysis identified phosphotyrosine residues. Retained radioactivity is evidence about the assay's separation and detection, not unique chemical identity.[ref]
Reversible receptor phosphorylation model
Words: 171
Receptor tyrosine kinase OurBigBook.com
Protein kinase activity adds modification, while protein tyrosine phosphatase activity can remove it. An original one-site model shows why a receptor phosphorylation assay cannot determine either process from a single modified fraction. Let f(t)∈[0,1] be the fraction of a fixed receptor population carrying one selected phosphotyrosine residue. Stipulate constant effective first-order rate constants k+​,k−​>0, with ATP availability absorbed into k+​, and no receptor synthesis, degradation or trafficking:
dtdf​=k+​(1−f)−k−​f,f∗​=k+​+k−​k+​​,τ=k+​+k−​1​.
(40)
Here f∗​ is the steady state fraction and τ the time constant. The ordinary differential equation has the exponential function solution
f(t)=f∗​+(f(0)−f∗​)e−t/τ.
(41)
The balance equation and a single relaxation step give this result; it is an illustrative model, rather than a fit or a claim about every RTK.
With stipulated rate constants (k+​,k−​)=(2,1)min−1, f∗​=2/3 and τ=1/3min. Doubling both rate constants leaves f∗​=2/3 but changes τ to 1/6min. The balanced phosphate turnover per site,
J∗​=k+​(1−f∗​)=k−​f∗​=k+​+k−​k+​k−​​,
(42)
doubles from 2/3 to 4/3min−1. Identical steady state modification therefore permits different catalytic fluxes. Removing the addition term instead gives f(t)=f(0)e−k−​t; this illustrates why a perturbation that stops protein kinase activity can expose removal dynamics, subject to the model's unchanged-removal assumption. A maintained steady state with ongoing ATP consumption is not chemical equilibrium.

An intracellular receptor recognizes a ligand inside a biological cell, including in the cytoplasm or cell nucleus. Some intracellular receptors regulate transcription after binding a membrane-permeable signal; an intracellular receptor does not universally imply direct control of DNA. See the receptor-location reference under receptor.

Receptor binding occupancy (θ)

Words: 316
Receptor (biochemistry) OurBigBook.com
Receptor binding occupancy is the fraction of binding sites occupied by a ligand. Consider reversible, noncooperative binding at chemical equilibrium, with homogeneous independent sites: every site has the same binding properties, and binding at one site does not change binding at another. Let L denote free ligand, R an unoccupied receptor site and RL the bound complex. In this dilute concentration model,
L+R⇌RL,Kd​=[RL][L][R]​,RT​=[R]+[RL],θ=RT​[RL]​=Kd​+[L][L]​.
(43)
Square brackets denote concentrations; RT​ is the total site concentration. Here the dissociation constant Kd​ has concentration units. Use free ligand in excess so binding negligibly depletes it; only under that approximation may the supplied total ligand concentration substitute for [L]. See Analysis of Receptor–Ligand Interactions: equilibrium binding and saturation.
For an illustrative dissociation constant Kd​=10nM, where 1nM=10−9molL−1, free ligand concentrations 1, 10 and 100nM give θ=1/11≈0.091, θ=1/2=0.5 and θ=10/11≈0.909, respectively. At [L]=Kd​, exactly half the sites are occupied in this model. Raising [L] tenfold from 10 to 100nM raises occupancy from 50% to about 91%, rather than tenfold: the finite pool of sites causes saturation.
A short derivation uses the law of mass action: at chemical equilibrium, association balances dissociation, giving [RL]=[L][R]/Kd​. Substitute this into θ=[RL]/([R]+[RL]) and cancel [R] to obtain the displayed formula. The limiting values follow directly: zero free ligand gives zero occupancy, and increasing [L] far above Kd​ drives occupancy toward one.
Receptor binding occupancy is not automatically the fraction of maximal response. Signal amplification, differing effects of bound ligands, and downstream saturation can change the relationship. Consequently, [L]=Kd​ specifies half occupancy here; it does not universally specify either half-maximal or maximal cellular response. These numbers describe a toy binding model, not measured responses of every receptor. See Higham and Colquhoun, 2024: the affinity–efficacy problem.

This usage concerns protein binding; it is distinct from the coordination-chemistry use of the word. See the protein-binding reference under receptor.

Morphogen

Words: 1k Articles: 2
Biology OurBigBook.com
A morphogen is a signal whose spatial concentration helps specify different biological cell fates or behaviors during biological development. A morphogen gradient provides a positional cue: biological cells at different distances from a source experience different local concentrations and can follow different developmental pathways. A spatial concentration variation alone does not establish that a substance is a morphogen; its graded developmental effects matter. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 4th edition (2002): morphogens as graded developmental signals.
The beautiful idea is that one distributed signal can help organize several regions of a developing body. A continuous morphogen gradient can supply the input for distinct domains of gene expression, rather than requiring a separate signal for every position. A morphogen response threshold is a useful idealization of that interpretation: high, intermediate and low concentrations are assigned different outcomes. The morphogen reaction-diffusion equation describes one way to generate a morphogen gradient; the equation is a model of transport and reaction, while the morphogen is the signal being transported.
Detection and interpretation also depend on the receiving biological cell. For an extracellular morphogen, receptors and signal transduction connect the local concentration to a response; receptor binding occupancy is only one step in that connection. The same morphogen gradient can be interpreted differently in different tissues because their developmental context differs. Thus a morphogen response threshold summarizes a particular response in a particular context, rather than being a universal property of the signal. See Scott F. Gilbert, Developmental Biology, 6th edition (2000): positional information and context-dependent interpretation.
An important experimental example came in 1988. Wolfgang Driever and Christiane Nüsslein-Volhard used antibodies to examine the bicoid protein in early fruit-fly embryos. They reported a concentration profile approximately described by an exponential function, highest at the front, with the protein concentrated in cell nuclei. Their abstract proposed diffusion from localized messenger RNA and dispersed degradation as a likely origin of the morphogen gradient, rather than proving a unique transport mechanism. [ref]
In a companion study, Driever and Nüsslein-Volhard genetically changed the amount and distribution of bicoid messenger RNA, measured the resulting protein morphogen gradient, and compared developmental maps. Increased local bicoid protein levels shifted prospective anterior structures toward the rear; decreased levels shifted them toward the front. This linked a measured concentration profile to positional effects in biological development. The toy calculations below illustrate that logic with arbitrary numbers, not measured bicoid parameters. [ref]

Morphogen gradient (c(x))

Words: 322
Morphogen OurBigBook.com
A morphogen gradient is a spatially varying concentration profile of a morphogen. The profile c(x) specifies the local amount; its mathematical gradient, c′(x) in one dimension, specifies how rapidly that amount changes with position. In the simplest positional interpretation, a biological cell responds to its local concentration, without having to measure the gradient across itself. Production, transport and removal together determine a morphogen gradient.
For a worked example, take a stationary one-dimensional tissue occupying x≥0, constant diffusion coefficient D>0, and uniform first-order reaction removal at rate k>0. At steady state, this specialization of the morphogen reaction-diffusion equation gives the ordinary differential equation and boundary conditions
Ddx2d2c​−kc=0,c(0)=c0​,limx→∞​c(x)=0.
(44)
Here D has units of length squared per time, k has units of inverse time, and c0​ is a prescribed source concentration. The Dirichlet boundary condition fixes the concentration at x=0. It does not prescribe a source flux; any required flux follows from the solution. These assumptions define a toy morphogen gradient, not a universal account of transport during biological development.
Define the diffusion length ℓ=D/k​. Substitution into the ordinary differential equation shows that its general solution is Aex/ℓ+Be−x/ℓ. The vanishing boundary condition at infinity forces A=0, and the source Dirichlet boundary condition forces B=c0​. Hence
c(x)=c0​e−x/ℓ,ℓ=D/k​.
(45)
Over every additional diffusion length, the concentration falls by the same factor e−1. Faster diffusion increases ℓ; faster removal decreases ℓ. This makes the diffusion length a useful bridge between microscopic transport and the spatial reach of a morphogen gradient.
Choose c0​=100 arbitrary concentration units and ℓ=100μm, where 1μm=10−6m. Then c(x)=100e−x/(100μm): at x=0, 100μm and 200μm, the concentrations are 100, approximately 36.79 and approximately 13.53. The following diagram combines this morphogen gradient with the idealized responses calculated under morphogen response threshold.

Morphogen response threshold (θ)

Words: 457
Morphogen OurBigBook.com
A morphogen response threshold is a concentration level used to distinguish developmental responses to a morphogen. In an idealized threshold model, otherwise equivalent biological cells exposed to c≥θ take one response and those exposed to c<θ take another. Two morphogen response thresholds can assign three bands: fate A for c≥50, fate B for 20≤c<50, and fate C for c<20, all in the toy arbitrary concentration units. The A/B/C labels specify a response rule, not named cell types or a claim that every morphogen produces sharp boundaries. See the positional-information model in Gilbert's reference under morphogen.
For the decreasing morphogen gradient c(x)=c0​e−x/ℓ and 0<θ<c0​, solve c(xθ​)=θ using the natural logarithm:
xθ​=ℓln(θc0​​).
(46)
With c0​=100 and diffusion length ℓ=100μm, the morphogen response thresholds 50 and 20 give
x50​=100ln2μm≈69.3147μm,x20​=100ln5μm≈160.9438μm.
(47)
Thus fate A occupies 0≤x≤x50​, fate B occupies x50​<x≤x20​, and fate C occupies x>x20​ in this idealization. The equality convention belongs to the response rule. If θ=c0​, the crossing is at the source; if θ>c0​, that morphogen response threshold is never reached anywhere in the tissue.
Now double the prescribed source concentration from c0​ to 2c0​, keeping D, k, diffusion length ℓ and a fixed morphogen response threshold 0<θ<c0​ unchanged. The whole morphogen gradient doubles, but the boundary moves by an additive distance:
Δxθ​=ℓln(θ2c0​​)−ℓln(θc0​​)=ℓln2.
(48)
For θ=20, the crossing moves from 160.9438μm to 100ln10μm≈230.2585μm, a shift of 69.3147μm. Every fixed morphogen response threshold below the original source concentration shifts by this same distance in the toy model. The example compares two Dirichlet boundary conditions, c(0)=100 and c(0)=200; doubling an experimentally supplied source flux is a different boundary specification.
These calculations are useful because they separate changes in source concentration, diffusion length and response rule. Their limits are equally concrete: growing tissues change the geometry, a transient response can precede steady state, molecular fluctuations can blur a boundary, and signaling feedback or altered transport can change the morphogen gradient or its interpretation. A local instantaneous morphogen response threshold need not capture exposure duration, signaling adaptation or the receiving biological cell's state. Experiments on cultured human biological cells found different responses to the level and rate of change of developmental signals, illustrating why signal dynamics can matter. [ref] Quantitative measurements of bicoid protein and its downstream gene expression also make precision a question for experiment, rather than something guaranteed by drawing threshold lines. [ref] Morphogen gradients provide one mechanism for spatial patterning in biological development, alongside other signals and interactions.

The study of nervous systems, from the properties of individual neurons to circuits, development, behavior and information processing.

Voltage clamp

Words: 64
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
A voltage clamp uses electrical feedback to hold a preparation's membrane potential near a commanded value while measuring the electric current required to maintain it. Holding voltage separates changes in electrical conductance from changes in electrical driving force. Imperfect voltage control and finite recording bandwidth limit the inference. The muscle experiment under ionotropic receptor used separate intracellular electrodes for voltage control and a sealed patch pipette for recording local electric current.[ref]

Extracellular single-unit recording

Words: 33
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Extracellular single-unit recording uses an electrode outside a neuron to detect electrical events attributed to that unit's action potentials. It records a spike train, not the intracellular membrane potential or every input synapse. [ref]

Primary visual cortex (V1)

Words: 2k Articles: 11
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
The primary visual cortex, often abbreviated V1, is an early cortical stage of visual processing. Its neurons have receptive fields: changing a stimulus in a particular part of the visible scene can change their spike trains. Orientation selectivity adds a further distinction: at the same location, a properly aligned bar can evoke a strong response while a rotated bar evokes little. Simple cells make the dependence on local position and visual contrast especially clear. See the original experiments under orientation selectivity and simple cell.
In their 1962 study, David Hubel and Torsten Wiesel recorded from forty cats under thiopental anesthesia, maintained light anesthesia while monitoring cortical electrical activity, and used succinylcholine to stabilize the eyes. White-light patterns were projected onto a screen 1.5m away. Extracellular single-unit recording with tungsten electrodes sampled individual units; receptive fields were mapped separately for each eye. This connected controlled stimulus geometry to individual spike trains. [ref]
These acute, anesthetized-cat recordings do not directly measure human perception or responses during awake behavior. The useful idea is a local description of structure: a population can distinguish where a feature lies, which way it is aligned, and which side is brighter. The signed spatial filter model of a simple cell turns that idea into a computable example. One neuron's preferred stimulus does not establish recognition of an entire object. Likewise, orientation selectivity in one neuron and an orderly map of preferences across primary visual cortex are different findings: rodents can have strong orientation selectivity without the orderly arrangement typical of some other species. [ref] The existing correlation-based development of visual cortical maps and orientation-map self-organization sections describe hypotheses about how organization develops.

Correlation-based development of visual cortical maps

Words: 61
Primary visual cortex OurBigBook.com
Consider afferent activities zi​, cortical activity ya​ and a constrained Hebbian learning rule w˙ai​=ϵ⟨ya​zi​⟩−Λa​. If ya​=∑b,j​Kab​wbj​zj​, then ⟨ya​zi​⟩=∑b,j​Kab​wbj​Cji​, where C is the input correlation matrix. Thus input correlations and lateral interactions select growing weight modes, while synaptic normalization and bounds stop unlimited growth. The model tests how organization can emerge without assigning every final cortical feature in advance.

Complex cell

Words: 169 Articles: 2
Primary visual cortex OurBigBook.com
A complex cell typically responds selectively to an oriented edge or bar over a finite spatial region with less dependence on spatial phase and contrast polarity than a simple cell. It need not have the simple cell's separated linear ON and OFF subregions. Phase tolerance is local, not invariance to arbitrary displacement outside its receptive field.
Quadrature energy model of a complex cell (E=(ke​∗I)2+(ko​∗I)2)
Words: 70
Complex cell OurBigBook.com
Two oriented linear filters in quadrature have responses Acosφ and Asinφ to a suitably matched narrowband grating. Their squared sum is A2, independent of phase φ, while orientation and spatial-frequency selectivity remain. A nonlinear output function or normalization can transform this energy into firing rate. Ideal quadrature gives an exact phase identity for the matched stimulus; finite approximate filter pairs need not have perfect invariance for arbitrary images.
Pooling model of a complex cell
Words: 47
Complex cell OurBigBook.com
Rectify outputs of simple cells with similar orientations and varying phases or positions, then sum or pool them. Opposite-polarity subunits allow response to both light and dark features. Pooling gives approximate phase and position tolerance over the subunit coverage; its extent and contrast dependence depend on the pooling rule.

Ocular dominance column

Primary visual cortex OurBigBook.com
A cortical region whose visual responses preferentially reflect input from one eye. Competitive activity-dependent models can explain segregation of correlated inputs, while anatomical constraints and species differences also matter.
Activity-dependent ocular dominance segregation
Words: 72
Ocular dominance column OurBigBook.com
Two eye-specific afferent populations compete under Hebbian learning and synaptic normalization. In a simplified symmetric two-eye model, the eye-difference mode da​=waL​−waR​ evolves with a linear operator containing Kab​(Csame​−Ccross​)ab​. Dominant spatial modes can produce alternating eye preference, while saturation sets finite contrast. The interaction width, arbor constraints and correlation structure influence the column scale. This is a mechanistic hypothesis whose predictions can be tested, not a unique inference from the existence of columns.

Orientation selectivity

Words: 532 Articles: 2
Primary visual cortex OurBigBook.com
Orientation selectivity is a systematic dependence of a visual neuron's response on the axis of a bar, edge or stripe pattern presented in its receptive field, under specified stimulus conditions. Here the angle θ measures the stripe axis from horizontal: 0∘ is horizontal and 90∘ vertical. An axis has no arrow, so θ and θ+180∘ describe the same orientation. A preference for one direction of movement across that axis is an additional property; the 1962 recordings included both equal and unequal responses to opposite movements. [ref]
A particularly clear experiment using extracellular single-unit recording appears in the 1959 paper, Figures 2–3. A bright 1∘×8∘ slit was centered on the same receptive field and rotated through successive angles; each presentation lasted one second. The vertical slit strongly increased the extracellularly recorded spike train, whereas the horizontal slit was ineffective. Small-spot tests had identified ON and OFF receptive-field subregions, with a central ON region and opposing flanks: rotation illuminated less of the center and more of the flanks. Geometry and location therefore mattered together. These dimensions belong to that recorded unit, not to every neuron. [ref]
An orientation tuning curve summarizes a controlled angle sweep. Keep location, size and visual contrast fixed; for a stripe pattern also specify spatial frequency and phase. The same signed spatial filter model of a simple cell can produce strong orientation selectivity and strong dependence on phase, as the following original toy illustrates. Its smooth curves are calculated predictions, not digitized or invented biological measurements.
Orientation tuning curve (r(θ))
Words: 162
Orientation selectivity OurBigBook.com
An orientation tuning curve plots a specified response against the stimulus-axis angle θ, with the other stimulus variables controlled. A practical count summary for extracellular single-unit recording is
r(θ)=mT1​∑k=1m​Nk​(θ),
(49)
where Nk​(θ) counts action potentials in the same duration T>0 on trial k, and m is the number of repeats at each angle. This estimates spikes per unit time in that window; the window must specify whether it covers onset, sustained stimulation, or both. Record a blank-background response separately, and report whether it has been subtracted. Randomizing angle order and repeating each condition helps separate orientation selectivity from changes over time, including neural adaptation. This is a proposed measurement procedure, not a claim that the original experiments used this estimator.
A simple cell's orientation tuning curve can also change when the stimulus shifts. An angle sweep at fixed phase, a sweep averaging over phase, and a sweep of moving stripes ask different questions. Consequently, a single preferred angle does not specify the whole receptive field. The toy curve under orientation selectivity holds phase fixed and plots dimensionless output, rather than spikes per second.
Orientation-map self-organization
Words: 52
Orientation selectivity OurBigBook.com
Correlation-based learning among spatially arranged ON and OFF inputs, with synaptic competition and lateral interactions, can select elongated simple cell receptive fields. Neighbor interactions coordinate preferred orientations across cortex, while competition allows different orientations to persist. Selectivity within one cell and a spatial map across many cells are separate predictions, and neither follows from unbounded Hebbian learning alone.

Simple cell

Words: 716 Articles: 1
Primary visual cortex OurBigBook.com
A simple cell is a visual cortical neuron whose receptive field has spatially separable ON and OFF receptive-field subregions. Elongated neighboring subregions give a preferred orientation and a sensitivity to the location and polarity of visual contrast. “Simple” describes the response organization; it does not describe a simpler cell body or a particular shape of neuron.
Hubel and Wiesel's 1962 classification emphasized four observations: distinguishable ON and OFF receptive-field subregions, summation within each region, antagonism between regions, and qualitative prediction of responses to differently shaped stimuli from those regions' arrangement. A slit fitting an elongated center was more effective than a smaller spot; a larger patch could invade opposing flanks and lose effectiveness. An edge separating bright and dark regions could be effective when its boundary matched the boundary between subregions. These were observations about spike trains, rather than an assertion of exact linearity. [ref]
The following deliberately coarse signed spatial filter model of a simple cell makes the geometry easy to count. A centered bright bar contributes positively at five sites. Rotating it preserves its area but mixes positive and negative weights; shifting it preserves its orientation but changes which weights it samples. The model is useful because it predicts distinct effects of these three manipulations instead of treating any bright stimulus as equivalent.
A simple cell is not an ideal linear sensor. Its spike train is nonnegative in event count, and neural adaptation can change responsiveness. The signed spatial filter model of a simple cell supplies a useful approximation to spatial drive and an explicit output rule. Comparing predictions with unseen stimuli is more informative than assuming the rule from the name “simple”. In contrast, the existing complex cell models explore tolerance to phase and local displacement.
Signed spatial filter model of a simple cell (D=∑i,j​Kij​Cij​,R=max(0,D))
Words: 388
Simple cell OurBigBook.com
A signed spatial filter model of a simple cell assigns a weight Kij​ to each sampled location and takes its dot product with the visual contrast image Cij​. Positive weights favor bright features; negative weights favor dark features. The signed drive
D=∑i,j​Kij​Cij​,R=max(0,D)
(50)
is a linear function of the image, while the rectified linear unit output R is nonlinear. D and R below are arbitrary model units. To obtain a predicted firing rate one would need a calibrated gain, background response and possibly a different output function. The model does not generate a spike train; a linear-nonlinear-Poisson cascade model adds a stochastic event-generation assumption.
For the first diagram, every one of five rows has weights
(Ki1​,Ki2​,Ki3​,Ki4​,Ki5​)=(−1/20,−1/20,1/5,−1/20,−1/20).
(51)
A bright central column, with Ci3​=1 and zero elsewhere, gives D=5/5=1. A bright middle row gives D=−1/20−1/20+1/5−1/20−1/20=0; a uniformly bright patch also gives D=0, since every row sums to zero. Move the bright column one site right: D=5(−1/20)=−1/4, so R=0. Make that shifted column dark instead: D=1/4 and R=1/4. Thus an OFF-like weight can increase output for darkness. A negative weight is a descriptive sensitivity, not evidence for a particular inhibitory synapse.
For a smooth example use the real, even Gabor filter
K(x,y)=exp(−2σx2​x2​−2σy2​y2​)cos(qx),Cθ,φ​(x,y)=cos(q(xsinθ−ycosθ)+φ).
(52)
The Gaussian function localizes the weights; the cosine supplies alternating polarity. Choose σx​=1/2, σy​=1 and q=π in arbitrary spatial units. The stripes' spatial frequency is q/(2π)=1/2 cycles per unit. Their axis makes angle θ with horizontal, while brightness changes across the perpendicular axis. φ is their spatial phase. Normalize the full-plane integral of KCθ,φ​ by its value at θ=π/2, φ=0. The Gaussian integral and the product identity for cosines give
D(θ,φ)=A(θ)cosφ,R(θ,φ)=max(0,D(θ,φ)),
(53)
where
A(θ)=1+exp(−2σx2​q2)exp[−2q2​(σx2​(sinθ−1)2+σy2​cos2θ)]+exp[−2q2​(σx2​(sinθ+1)2+σy2​cos2θ)]​.
(54)
At φ=0, horizontal stripes give R≈0.004159, 60∘ stripes give R≈0.286741, and vertical stripes give R=1. At the same vertical orientation, φ=π/2 gives D=R=0, while reversing the polarity with φ=π gives D=−1 and R=0. The preferred axis persists while the response changes dramatically with position. Shifting the vertical stripes by a quarter of their wavelength changes phase by π/2 up to sign, without rotating them.
These are two different toy filters, not discretizations of the same fitted receptive field. The discrete filter exactly rejects a uniform contrast patch; this Gabor filter need not reject uniform contrast because its weight integral need not vanish. Neither toy includes stimulus history, recurrent interactions, saturation or a measured response baseline. Their value is a transparent prediction: orientation selectivity can emerge from spatial summation, and it does not by itself imply tolerance to phase.

Neuron

Words: 5k Articles: 40
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
A neuron is a specialized biological cell that receives, integrates and transmits signals. Its shape separates places where inputs arrive from places where outputs reach other biological cells: this functional asymmetry is neuronal polarity. Understanding a neuron therefore means connecting its anatomy to changes in membrane potential, rather than treating it as a wire that merely forwards every input.
In a common multipolar neuron, branching dendrites receive inputs at synapses; the soma contains the cell nucleus and most major organelles; the axon carries signals to distant or nearby targets; and axon terminals form output contacts. All these regions belong to one biological cell enclosed by a continuous cell membrane. An axon can branch, allowing one neuron to influence several receiving biological cells.[ref]
At an input chemical synapse, a neurotransmitter acts on a receptor, changing an electric current directly or through signal transduction.[ref] A resulting synaptic potential contributes to synaptic integration in the dendrites and soma. In many spiking neurons, sufficiently strong depolarization recruits voltage-gated ion channels in the axon initial segment, initiating an action potential that propagates along the axon. At an output chemical synapse, calcium entry through voltage-gated ion channels promotes synaptic vesicle exocytosis, releasing neurotransmitter. An action potential is thus regenerated electrically along a cell membrane; it is not a packet of neurotransmitter travelling from the dendrites to the axon terminals.[ref]
The compartments are specializations, not exclusive jobs. Inputs can contact the soma or axon as well as dendrites; dendrites can support active voltage-gated ion channels. Paired recordings from a pyramidal neuron's soma and dendrite or axon established that an action potential can begin in the axon and propagate back into the dendrites. The usual output direction therefore does not make every electrical signal strictly one-way.[ref] An electrical synapse, which directly couples cytoplasms through gap junctions, also differs from the sending-and-receiving arrangement of a chemical synapse.[ref]
Nor does every neuron have the upper diagram's shape. A bipolar neuron has two main processes, one dendrite and one axon; a multipolar neuron has several dendrites; and a pseudounipolar neuron has a single process from the soma that divides into peripheral and central branches. In the last arrangement, sensory signals can travel past the soma rather than obligatorily through it. These shape categories do not specify every neuron's receptor, connectivity or firing behavior.[ref] Some neurons in the retina communicate through graded changes in membrane potential without generating action potentials.[ref]
Why timing changes the computation. Synaptic integration can combine inputs at different locations, called spatial summation, and inputs arriving at different times, called temporal summation. A minimal example uses the leaky integrate-and-fire model with the illustrative parameters already given there: resting and reset membrane potential −65mV, firing threshold −50mV, electrical resistance R=100MΩ, capacitance C=200pF, time constant τ=RC=20ms and neuronal refractory period 2ms. These are chosen model values, not measured properties of a particular neuron. Before firing, a constant inward electric current I starting from rest gives
V(t)=−65mV+RI(1−e−t/τ).
(55)
The exponential function expresses the competition between charging the cell membrane's capacitance and leakage through its electrical resistance.[ref]
Two 100pA inputs, each lasting 40ms, produce different outputs depending on their timing. Either input alone reaches only −56.3534mV. Applied together, they give I=200pA and reach threshold after 20ln4ms≈27.7259ms, producing one action potential event during the pulse. If instead the second input begins 20ms after the first ends, the earlier depolarization has partly decayed: the second pulse peaks at approximately −55.9229mV and neither pulse produces an action potential. The two-input protocols deliver the same total electric charge, 8pC, yet only the coincident protocol fires. Counting total input alone misses this timing dependence.
This example makes a neuron a detector of sufficiently clustered input, not a perfect logical gate: different parameters change the result. Actual dendrites introduce location-dependent filtering and active responses, and an inhibitory postsynaptic potential or shunting inhibition can change whether another input succeeds. The single-compartment leaky integrate-and-fire model omits these mechanisms.[ref] Across connected neurons, branching axons distribute outputs while converging synapses combine inputs; spike trains can support temporal coding and rate coding, and synaptic plasticity changes the influence of an input. Connectivity and cellular dynamics together determine the computation.[ref][ref]
Testing the connection between structure and function. Whole-cell recording connects anatomy to a measured membrane potential. In a published mouse protocol, a two-photon microscope guides solution-filled glass pipettes to neurons; an amplifier and bath reference electrode complete the electrical recording apparatus. A high-resistance seal forms against the cell membrane, then brief suction opens the membrane patch beneath the tip. In current clamp, the amplifier supplies a chosen electric current and records the resulting membrane potential, unlike voltage clamp, which controls voltage and measures electric current. The investigators used 500ms current steps of several amplitudes to characterize excitability and firing, and negative current pulses to estimate input electrical resistance.[ref]
The observable is a voltage trace, including graded responses and action potentials. Comparing injected electric current with that trace tests how input becomes output; it does not identify every underlying ion channel. The protocol checks access electrical resistance, which can distort voltage and action potential measurements, and includes intervals without stimulation to record spontaneous activity. In a teaching replication, repeated zero-input trials and monitoring baseline drift would provide further controls; these are recommended comparisons, not additional results attributed to the paper. A recording at the soma also cannot establish the local voltage everywhere in a branching dendrite, and this anesthetized preparation does not establish behavior in every awake neuron.[ref]
A complementary experiment used simultaneous whole-cell recordings from the soma and an apical dendrite or axon of the same pyramidal neuron in a brain slice. The relative onset times of action potentials, together with sodium currents in excised dendrite membrane patches, supported axonal initiation followed by active propagation into dendrites. Pairing sites within one neuron is a useful comparison because it avoids confusing differences between cells with differences between compartments. Instrument timing and comparable recording quality would be essential controls when reproducing the inference. Only the published abstract was accessible here, so no unverified timing values, drug controls or channel distributions are supplied.[ref]

Synaptic integration

Words: 2k Articles: 8
Neuron OurBigBook.com
Synaptic integration is the conversion of inputs at a neuron's synapses into a changing membrane potential and, in a spiking neuron, the timing or absence of action potentials. Spatial summation concerns inputs at different locations; temporal summation concerns inputs at different times. A useful question is whether individually ineffective inputs can act together, and whether an inhibitory postsynaptic potential changes that cooperation. The answer depends on location, timing and the receiving neuron's state.
A synaptic potential is a voltage response, whereas synaptic conductance describes activated ion channels. With inward-positive electric current, the contribution of input j is
Ij​(t)=gj​(t)(Ej​−V).
(56)
Here gj​ is its synaptic conductance, Ej​ its reversal potential and V the local membrane potential. The driving force Ej​−V is an electric potential difference. An EPSP generally brings the membrane potential toward a more positive reversal potential, but its driving force shrinks during depolarization. An IPSP need not produce hyperpolarization: a reversal potential above rest but below the neuronal firing threshold can produce depolarization while opposing a larger excursion. At Ej​=V, the added synaptic conductance initially carries zero electric current yet can cause shunting inhibition of another input.[ref]
Two distinct nonlinearities matter. Even a passive cell membrane can show sublinear synaptic integration when added synaptic conductances reduce driving force and effective electrical resistance. Active voltage-gated ion channels and NMDA receptors can instead amplify sufficiently concentrated inputs and produce a dendritic spike. Neither summing prescribed electric currents nor adding separate measured EPSPs is an exact universal rule for a branching neuron.[ref]
Spatial summation
Words: 753 Articles: 2
Synaptic integration OurBigBook.com
Spatial summation combines inputs arriving at different synapses. Location matters because a dendrite has axial electrical resistance and leaky membrane capacitance: a local synaptic potential need not arrive at the soma with its original amplitude or time course. A passive dendritic cable makes this attenuation explicit. The superposition principle applies to fixed electric current inputs in a linear passive model, but adding synaptic conductances changes the model's coefficients. Compare voltage changes relative to the same baseline, rather than adding absolute membrane potentials.
A motivating experiment. A 2004 study used 300–350μm cortical slices from 18–28-day-old rats at 35–36∘C. Somatic whole-cell recordings measured EPSPs in layer-5 pyramidal neurons. Two fine stimulating electrodes were positioned beside imaged dendrites; calcium-sensitive dye localized activation. Each site was stimulated alone, then both together, usually with paired pulses 20ms apart. Comparing the combined voltage trace with the sum of individual changes tested the summation rule. Nearby inputs on one branch showed strong amplification at intermediate strengths; inputs on different branches were approximately linear.[ref]
Blocking both excitatory receptor classes eliminated voltage and calcium responses, checking against direct electrical activation. NMDA receptor blockers eliminated or markedly reduced amplification; comparisons with inhibition intact and blocked addressed inhibitory contributions. These controls support local active integration. Passing axons could still recruit unintended synapses; somatic voltage does not measure every local membrane potential. The study tested subthreshold slice responses and pairs of branches, not arbitrary activity in an intact brain.[ref]
Passive dendritic cable (λ=rm​/ra​​)
Words: 160
Spatial summation OurBigBook.com
A passive dendritic cable models a uniform dendrite with axial electrical resistance, membrane leak and membrane capacitance, excluding active ion channels. Let ra​ be axial electrical resistance per length, rm​ membrane electrical resistance times length, and cm​ membrane capacitance per length. For voltage deviation v=V−EL​ from the leak reversal potential, electric charge conservation gives the partial differential equation
cm​∂t∂v​=ra​1​∂x2∂2v​−rm​v​+i(x,t),τm​=rm​cm​,λ=ra​rm​​​.
(57)
i is imposed inward electric current per length. Units are ra​:Ω/m, rm​:Ωm and cm​:F/m, so τm​ is a time and λ a length. On a source-free semi-infinite cable with imposed v(0)=v0​ and v(x)→0 as x→∞, the steady state is
v(x)=v0​e−x/λ.
(58)
Differentiate twice to verify the ordinary differential equation λ2v′′−v=0. At x=λ, the amplitude is e−1≈0.368 of the boundary amplitude. This is a stationary attenuation law, not the complete waveform of a brief EPSP. Transient passive spread also broadens and delays responses. Finite ends, branch points and the soma's load alter the solution; distance alone cannot specify every real synaptic potential.[ref]

The spatial panel uses two compartments with membrane potentials Vs​,Vd​, one representing the soma and one a dendrite. Set vs​=Vs​−EL​, vd​=Vd​−EL​, with leak reversal potential EL​=−65mV, each membrane capacitance C=100pF, each leak electrical conductance gL​=5nS and axial electrical conductance gc​=10nS. Electric charge conservation gives
Cv˙s​=−(gL​+gc​)vs​+gc​vd​+Is​,Cv˙d​=gc​vs​−(gL​+gc​)vd​+Id​.
(59)
This chosen passive model has two decay time constants, C/gL​=20ms for the equal-voltage mode and C/(gL​+2gc​)=4ms for the voltage-difference mode. Starting from rest, a 100pA step into the soma gives, with u the time since onset,
vs​(u)=10(1−e−u/20)+2(1−e−u/4)mV,
(60)
while the same step into the dendrite gives
vs​(u)=10(1−e−u/20)−2(1−e−u/4)mV.
(61)
u is expressed in ms. Their long-time rises are 12 and 8mV respectively. Applying both inputs gives 20(1−e−u/20)mV exactly: spatial attenuation coexists with linear summation of prescribed electric currents. After the steps end, both modes decay with their respective time constants. This deliberately coarse model is not a reconstructed dendrite or a fit to the experiment above.
The conductance panels use the existing one-compartment synaptic potential equation, with C=200pF, gL​=10nS, EL​=−65mV and excitatory reversal potential Ee​=0mV. For a constant excitatory synaptic conductance ge​, the steady state voltage rise and membrane time constant are
ΔV∞​=gL​+ge​ge​(Ee​−EL​)​,τeff​=gL​+ge​C​.
(62)
Each isolated 2nS input has a limiting rise 130/12≈10.833mV. Adding those isolated rises predicts 21.667mV, but opening both together gives 260/14≈18.571mV. The two conductances share a changing driving force. This is sublinear input summation even though the voltage ordinary differential equation is linear for each prescribed conductance waveform.
Add gi​=20nS with reversal potential Ei​=EL​ to the joint 4nS excitation. The limiting rise becomes 260/34≈7.647mV and the membrane time constant becomes 200/34≈5.882ms. The shunt alone leaves rest unchanged. At the joint-excitation-only steady state V≈−46.429mV, however, its inward electric current would be 20(−65+46.429)≈−371.429pA: it opposes that excursion. The finite 50ms traces in the diagram approach, but need not reach, these limiting voltages. See shunting inhibition for the constant-electric current comparison.
Temporal summation
Words: 473 Articles: 1
Synaptic integration OurBigBook.com
Temporal summation is overlap of responses to inputs arriving at different times. It can occur at one repeatedly activated synapse or across several synapses; it is not defined by reuse of a particular contact. For prescribed electric current inputs in a passive compartment, residual depolarization from earlier pulses changes the voltage reached by later pulses. The membrane time constant sets how rapidly that residual decays, while the duration of synaptic conductance and spatial filtering by a passive dendritic cable can add other timescales.
For the diagram, write v=V−EL​, choose inward-positive imposed electric current I, and use the ordinary differential equation
Cv˙=−gL​v+I(t),τm​=gL​C​=20ms.
(63)
A rectangular pulse of amplitude I0​=300pA and duration d=5ms, starting from rest, ends with
A=gL​I0​​(1−e−d/τm​)=30(1−e−1/4)mV≈6.636mV.
(64)
Afterwards its contribution decays as Ae−(t−d)/τm​. The superposition principle therefore gives, at the end of the third pulse with onset spacing Δ≥d,
vpeak​=A(1+e−Δ/τm​+e−2Δ/τm​).
(65)
For Δ=5ms this is 15.829mV, so the peak membrane potential is −49.171mV. For Δ=30ms it is 8.447mV, giving −56.553mV. Both protocols inject 3I0​d=4.5pC of electric charge; equal charge does not imply equal peak voltage because the leak drains charge while it is delivered.
In the adjacent-pulse case, the illustrative neuronal firing threshold −50mV is crossed at 10+20log2≈23.863ms. A leaky integrate-and-fire model would emit its first event there and reset, so its later trajectory would differ from the passive diagram. The widely spaced train never reaches that threshold. Thus changing input timing alone can change whether an event occurs. A real neuron's neuronal firing threshold is also state-dependent, and synaptic conductance pulses are not prescribed electric current pulses.[ref]
Measured responses to repeated presynaptic action potentials may also change through synaptic plasticity. A larger second response can therefore reflect a stronger second input as well as residual postsynaptic voltage. To isolate passive temporal summation, compare known injected electric current waveforms with their single-pulse responses under stable recording conditions; to test actual synapses, measure whether input efficacy changes. These are proposed discriminating comparisons, not additional controls claimed for the slice experiment.[ref]
Membrane time constant (τm​=C/G)
Words: 82
Temporal summation OurBigBook.com
The membrane time constant of a passive uniform compartment is its membrane capacitance C divided by its total fixed electrical conductance G. After input removal, voltage deviation from the relevant equilibrium undergoes exponential decay; in one membrane time constant it falls to e−1 of its initial value. For leak alone, G=gL​; while fixed synaptic conductances are open, G=gL​+∑j​gj​. Thus shunting inhibition can both reduce voltage responses and shorten the integration window. This is a local passive timescale: a branching dendrite can have several decay modes, and a time-varying synaptic conductance need not admit one constant τm​.
Neuronal firing threshold (ϑ)

Synaptic integration OurBigBook.com
A neuronal firing threshold specifies the condition for initiating an action potential. The leaky integrate-and-fire model uses a prescribed membrane potential ϑ; real initiation involves active voltage-gated ion channels and depends on recent activity and recording site. A threshold drawn on a passive voltage trace is a comparison criterion, not a simulated action potential.

A dendritic spike is a regenerative local voltage event in a dendrite. Its effect at the soma depends on propagation and attenuation; local regeneration does not by itself establish a somatic action potential. It is an active mechanism beyond the passive dendritic cable.

An NMDA receptor is an ionotropic receptor gating an ion channel with voltage-dependent magnesium block. This voltage dependence permits cooperative amplification when inputs produce sufficient local depolarization; calcium can also pass through the open channel.[ref]

Synapse

Words: 2k Articles: 17
Neuron OurBigBook.com
A synapse is a signaling junction between a neuron and another biological cell. The sending side is presynaptic and the receiving side postsynaptic. At a chemical synapse, released neurotransmitter acts on a receptor in the receiving cell membrane. At an electrical synapse, gap junctions provide a direct path for electric current between cells. See 1.1 Elements of Neuronal Systems.
In a common sequence at a chemical synapse, an arriving action potential opens voltage-gated ion channels selective for calcium. Calcium entry triggers fusion of synaptic vesicles with the presynaptic cell membrane, releasing neurotransmitter into the synaptic cleft. Binding to a receptor changes postsynaptic electrical resistance and conductance, directly through an ion channel or through an intracellular signaling pathway. The resulting change in membrane potential is a synaptic potential. See Ion Channels and the Electrical Properties of Membranes.
A useful conductance approximation writes the inward-positive synaptic electric current as
Isyn​=gsyn​(t)(Esyn​−V),
(66)
where gsyn​≥0 describes the activated electrical resistance and conductance, V is the postsynaptic membrane potential, and Esyn​ is the reversal potential, the voltage at which this current vanishes. Opening these channels tends to pull V toward Esyn​; it does not prescribe a current of fixed sign independently of V.
For a worked example, let V=−65mV and gsyn​=1nS. A reversal potential of 0mV gives Isyn​=65pA, an inward electric current that raises membrane potential. A reversal potential of −75mV instead gives −10pA, which lowers membrane potential. These are illustrative calculations, not measurements. A reversal potential of −60mV can raise V from −65mV yet oppose reaching a threshold of −50mV: a depolarizing input need not be excitatory.
An excitatory synapse favors a subsequent action potential, whereas an inhibitory synapse opposes it. The effect depends on the receptor, the permeating ions, their gradients and the reversal potential; a neurotransmitter does not have one fixed excitatory or inhibitory sign in every context. Even with Esyn​=V, an added conductance can reduce responses to other inputs by lowering effective electrical resistance, an effect called shunting inhibition. See Purves and colleagues: excitatory and inhibitory postsynaptic potentials. This dependence matters when translating a biological synapse into a signed weight or an imposed electric current in computational neuroscience.

Synapse OurBigBook.com
Changes in synaptic efficacy over time. Activity-dependent plasticity can support learning and development, but also requires constraints to prevent unbounded growth or competition in simplified models.
Synaptic competition

Synaptic plasticity OurBigBook.com
Constraints or interactions make the strengthening of some inputs limit others. In developmental models, competition together with input correlations can segregate ON and OFF subregions or inputs from the two eyes; correlations alone do not specify the full biological developmental mechanism.
Synaptic normalization

Synaptic competition OurBigBook.com
A learning rule can constrain the sum or norm of incoming synaptic weights to prevent unbounded Hebbian learning. For ∑i​wai​=S, subtracting the mean unconstrained update from each update preserves the sum. Bounds and renormalization may also be needed to keep excitatory weights nonnegative. Normalization of learning weights is distinct from divisive gain control in instantaneous neural responses.
