Synapse OurBigBook.com
A chemical signal released by a neuron that changes a target cell's activity through its receptors. Its effect depends on the receptor and ionic mechanism rather than being intrinsically excitatory or inhibitory in every context.
Acetylcholine (ACh)
Words: 31
Neurotransmitter OurBigBook.com
Acetylcholine is a neurotransmitter that acts through nicotinic ionotropic receptors and muscarinic metabotropic receptors. The receptor and the target cell's machinery determine the response; acetylcholine itself does not specify whether coupling is direct or mediated by intracellular signal transduction. [ref]
Chemical synapse
Words: 950 Articles: 6
Synapse OurBigBook.com
A chemical synapse transmits a signal by releasing neurotransmitter from a presynaptic neuron to act on postsynaptic receptors across a synaptic cleft. The two cell membranes remain separate. A typical fast transmission sequence is:
  • An arriving action potential produces presynaptic depolarization, opening voltage-gated ion channels selective for calcium.
  • Calcium ions enter down their electrochemical gradient. The local rise in calcium concentration activates release machinery, allowing already prepared synaptic vesicles to fuse with the presynaptic cell membrane by exocytosis.
  • Released neurotransmitter crosses the synaptic cleft by diffusion and binds postsynaptic receptors.
  • Ionotropic receptors directly gate an ion channel; metabotropic receptors activate an intracellular signaling pathway that can alter ion channels indirectly. Changed synaptic conductance changes electric current and usually produces a synaptic potential.
See Chemical Synapses and 3.1 Synapses. The fast pathway uses synaptic vesicles prepared near release sites; it does not require a distant synaptic vesicle to travel across the terminal after every action potential. See Basic Neurochemistry: calcium entry and vesicles at release sites. Some chemical synapses release neurotransmitter in response to graded presynaptic membrane potential changes rather than action potentials.
Neurotransmitter clearance limits how long released neurotransmitter remains available. Depending on the neurotransmitter and location, diffusion away, uptake through membrane transport proteins into the sending or neighboring biological cells, and breakdown by enzymes contribute. Receptor binding and unbinding also affect response duration. Recovering synaptic vesicle membrane is a separate recycling task; uptake of released neurotransmitter is not the return of an intact synaptic vesicle. See General Principles of Cell Communication.
This electrical-to-chemical-to-electrical sequence offers several places to adjust a signal: synaptic release probability, receptor availability and neurotransmitter clearance can change its strength or duration. It helps explain why synaptic plasticity can modify communication between neurons, and why an arriving action potential need not cause a postsynaptic action potential.
Otto Loewi's 1936 Nobel lecture describes his 1921 experiment: fluid from a frog heart whose nerves had been stimulated produced the corresponding response when transferred to another heart. The transferable substance established chemical mediation in that preparation. This was evidence for released chemical signaling, not yet an identification of synaptic vesicle fusion and not a claim that every synapse is chemical. See Loewi, The Chemical Transmission of Nerve Action, Nobel lecture, 12 December 1936.
Neurotransmitter clearance
Words: 37
Chemical synapse OurBigBook.com
Neurotransmitter clearance removes released neurotransmitter from the region where it can activate receptors, through diffusion, cellular uptake or enzyme-mediated breakdown. Its routes and rates help delimit a chemical synapse's response in space and time; see the mechanisms and source under chemical synapse.
Synaptic cleft
Words: 23
Chemical synapse OurBigBook.com
The synaptic cleft is the extracellular gap between the sending and receiving cell membranes of a chemical synapse. Released neurotransmitter crosses this gap to reach a receptor. [ref]
Synaptic vesicle
Words: 323 Articles: 2
Chemical synapse OurBigBook.com
A synaptic vesicle is a small membrane-bounded compartment in a presynaptic terminal that stores neurotransmitter for release. Fusion with the cell membrane exposes its contents to the synaptic cleft; the packet supplied by one synaptic vesicle is a quantum of release. Quantal neurotransmitter release refers to these discrete packets, rather than the release of one molecule at a time. The postsynaptic response to a packet can vary with its contents, receptors and recording conditions. See Purves and colleagues: vesicles as the source of transmitter quanta.
The useful cycle is filling, preparation for fusion, calcium-triggered exocytosis, and recovery of membrane and proteins through endocytosis for reuse. Different recovery routes occur; recycling need not preserve a particular synaptic vesicle as an identifiable container throughout. Limited availability of prepared synaptic vesicles can reduce release during repeated stimulation, while changes in synaptic release probability can also change successive responses. See Basic Neurochemistry: secretion machinery and vesicle reuse and 3.1 Synapses.
For an illustrative calculation, assume four release sites, each with one prepared synaptic vesicle, each releasing with synaptic release probability p=0.25 during one presynaptic action potential. Assume independent Bernoulli trials and at most one release per site. The released packet count K has a binomial distribution:
K∼Bin(4,0.25),E[K]=4(0.25)=1,Var(K)=4(0.25)(0.75)=0.75.
(67)
The probability of no release is P(K=0)=0.754=0.31640625; at least one release has probability 0.68359375. An expected value of one packet does not mean that every action potential releases one packet. If each packet contributes a stipulated 0.5nS conductance increment and increments add, the expected value of that increment is 0.5nS, with zero increment on about 31.6% of trials. These assumptions are a teaching model: shared calcium fluctuations, unequal sites, depletion and nonlinear receptor responses can invalidate them.

Quantal neurotransmitter release is release of neurotransmitter in discrete packets associated with individual synaptic vesicles. Packet count and postsynaptic packet response are different quantities; see the binomial distribution example under synaptic vesicle.

Quantal neurotransmitter release OurBigBook.com
Synaptic release probability is the probability of release at a specified site during a specified opportunity, such as one presynaptic action potential. It depends on the site's state and conditions; it is not the probability that the receiving neuron fires. In the example under synaptic vesicle, p refers to one available site, whereas 1−(1−p)4 refers to any of four independent sites releasing.
Shunting inhibition
Words: 223
Chemical synapse OurBigBook.com
Shunting inhibition is suppression of another input's effect through increased synaptic conductance: opening additional ion channels lowers effective electrical resistance, reducing the voltage response to a given added electric current. When the added reversal potential equals the resting membrane potential, there can be no voltage change at rest and still be inhibition of a simultaneous input. See 1.4 Limitations of the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire Model.
Use the passive synaptic potential model below with leak gL​=10nS, EL​=−65mV and capacitance C=200pF. A sustained inward test electric current of Iext​=100pA alone gives a steady voltage increase of Iext​/gL​=10mV, so V∞​=−55mV. Effective electrical resistance is 100MΩ and the time constant is 20ms.
Now hold a shunting conductance gi​=20nS open with Ei​=EL​=−65mV. With no test electric current, rest stays at −65mV. With the same 100pA test electric current, total conductance becomes 30nS, so the steady voltage increase is only 100/30≃3.333mV: V∞​≃−61.667mV. Effective electrical resistance is 33.333MΩ and the time constant is 200/30≃6.667ms. A faster response can therefore be smaller. At the original rest the shunting electric current is zero; at V=−55mV it is 20(−65+55)=−200pA, opposing the voltage excursion.
The factor of three reduction applies to this constant-electric current, constant-conductance example. A finite pulse, conductance-driven input or spatially extended dendrite need not have the same reduction. The interesting feature is conditional action: the shunt can leave a quiet neuron's voltage unchanged yet reshape its response when another input arrives. A model that represents all inhibition as a fixed outward electric current misses this behavior.
Electrical synapse
Words: 203
Synapse OurBigBook.com
An electrical synapse passes ionic electric current directly between neurons through gap junctions, whose paired channels connect the two cytoplasms. It does not require synaptic vesicle release and postsynaptic neurotransmitter binding. Transmission across the junction is very fast; the receiving cell membrane's capacitance and other conductances still determine its voltage response. Electrical coupling can coordinate the timing of activity across neurons. See Purves and colleagues: electrical synapses and gap junctions.
For a passive junction with constant conductance gj​, the inward electric current into cell 2 is
I2←1​=gj​(V1​−V2​),I1←2​=−I2←1​,
(68)
where each Vk​ is the cell's membrane potential, measured against a common extracellular reference. Taking gj​=2nS, V1​=−55mV and V2​=−65mV gives 20pA into cell 2 and the equal opposite electric current into cell 1. Exchanging the voltages reverses the electric current. Both depolarization and hyperpolarization can therefore be transmitted; an electrical synapse is not inherently an excitatory connection.
Many electrical synapses conduct in both directions, but this does not guarantee equal voltage responses: the cells can have different effective electrical resistance and capacitance. Some junctions rectify, meaning they conduct preferentially in one direction, so the constant-gj​ formula is insufficient. A concrete molecular example is the original study [ref]. Bidirectionality is thus a common property with important qualifications, rather than part of the definition.
Synaptic potential
Words: 556 Articles: 3
Synapse OurBigBook.com
A synaptic potential is a postsynaptic change in membrane potential caused by activity at a synapse. Unlike the regenerative action potential, a passive synaptic potential is graded: its size depends on input strength, the initial membrane potential and the receiving cell membrane's properties. Local voltage changes can decay before reaching the soma; their timing and overlap help determine whether an action potential follows. See Ion Channels and the Electrical Properties of Membranes.
Depolarization means that the interior becomes less negative relative to the exterior; hyperpolarization means that it becomes more negative. Excitation and inhibition instead describe whether an input promotes or opposes postsynaptic action potential generation. An inhibitory postsynaptic potential can be depolarizing, and shunting inhibition can occur with no voltage change at rest. The receptor, permeating ions, ionic gradients and reversal potential matter. See Purves and colleagues: excitation, inhibition and depolarizing inhibition.
A worked passive model treats the receiving membrane as one compartment with capacitance C>0, leak conductance gL​>0, and activated synaptic conductances ge​,gi​≥0:
CdtdV​=gL​(EL​−V)+ge​(Ee​−V)+gi​(Ei​−V)+Iext​.
(69)
All electric currents are inward-positive. Each term g(E−V) vanishes at its reversal potential E; nS×mV=pA. With constant parameters, the ordinary differential equation has
G=gL​+ge​+gi​,V∞​=GgL​EL​+ge​Ee​+gi​Ei​+Iext​​,τ=GC​,
(70)
V(t)=V∞​+(V(0)−V∞​)e−t/τ.
(71)
Here G is total conductance, 1/G is effective electrical resistance, V∞​ is the steady state and τ the time constant. Without imposed electric current, V∞​ is a conductance-weighted average of the reversal potentials. This approximation omits spatial structure, changing ionic gradients and active voltage-gated ion channels; it calculates passive voltage responses, not actual action potential waveforms. See 3.1 Synapses for the mechanism behind the terms; the inward-positive convention here reverses that source's synaptic-current sign.
Take the same illustrative leak and capacitance as under shunting inhibition, start at V(0)=−65mV and set Iext​=0. Opening ge​=2nS with Ee​=0mV gives V∞​=−650/12≃−54.167mV and τ≃16.667ms. Its initial inward electric current is 2(0+65)=130pA. Adding gi​=20nS with Ei​=−65mV changes V∞​ to (−650−1300)/32=−60.9375mV and τ=6.25ms. This is shunting inhibition of the same excitatory drive.
For comparison, gi​=20nS with Ei​=−75mV alone gives V∞​≃−71.667mV: hyperpolarization. With Ei​=−60mV instead, it alone gives V∞​≃−61.667mV: depolarization. Yet adding this depolarizing conductance to the ge​=2nS excitatory drive lowers that drive's V∞​ from −54.167 to (−650−1200)/32=−57.8125mV. At an illustrative firing threshold V=−50mV, its electric current is 20(−60+50)=−200pA, opposing threshold approach. The combined trace initially rises faster than the excitatory drive alone, before settling below it. Thus the sign of a voltage change at rest alone does not determine excitation or inhibition; a claim about firing must specify input strength, timing and the neuron's state.
Synaptic conductance (gsyn​)
Words: 57
Synaptic potential OurBigBook.com
Synaptic conductance describes how strongly activated synaptic ion channels conduct electric current for a given driving force. In the passive approximation, Isyn​=gsyn​(Esyn​−V), with inward-positive electric current. It is the electrical conductance contribution of a synapse; its postsynaptic voltage response also depends on the driving force, the other membrane electrical conductances, and the capacitance. The synaptic potential model and shunting inhibition example show why a nonzero synaptic conductance can have zero electric current at rest.
Excitatory postsynaptic potential
Words: 35
Synaptic potential OurBigBook.com
An excitatory postsynaptic potential is a synaptic potential associated with increased likelihood of a postsynaptic action potential. Its size and effect depend on the receiving neuron's state; the definition concerns firing, not a fixed neurotransmitter identity. See synaptic potential for the mechanism and source.
Inhibitory postsynaptic potential
Words: 35
Synaptic potential OurBigBook.com
An inhibitory postsynaptic potential is a synaptic potential associated with decreased likelihood of a postsynaptic action potential. It can involve hyperpolarization or depolarization; an inhibitory conductance can even produce no measurable voltage change at rest. See synaptic potential and shunting inhibition for worked examples and sources.

Action potential

Words: 258 Articles: 1
Neuron OurBigBook.com
An action potential is a brief regenerative excursion of membrane potential, produced by changing electrical resistance and conductance through voltage-gated ion channels. In a typical fast neuronal action potential, sodium entry raises membrane potential, activating further sodium channels. This feedback produces the rapid rising phase. Inactivation of sodium channels and increased conductance to potassium then lower membrane potential again; persisting potassium conductance can produce an undershoot below the resting level. See Purves and colleagues: the ionic basis of action potentials.
For an illustrative electrical calculation, write inward sodium electric current as INa​=gNa​(ENa​−V). At V=−50mV, taking ENa​=60mV and gNa​=10nS gives INa​=1.1nA inward. A potassium current IK​=gK​(EK​−V) with EK​=−80mV and gK​=20nS gives −0.6nA, outward. These illustrative values expose opposing driving forces; a waveform requires the conductances to evolve with membrane potential and time, as in the Hodgkin-Huxley model.
An action potential propagates along an axon because local electric currents bring neighboring regions of cell membrane into the regime where their voltage-gated ion channels regenerate the signal. It is a traveling pattern of excitation, not a packet of sodium ions traversing the entire axon. Regeneration allows an action potential to travel without the passive attenuation of a small local voltage change. See Ion Channels and the Electrical Properties of Membranes.
The neuronal refractory period constrains how soon another action potential can follow. Under comparable conditions, successive action potentials have roughly stereotyped shapes, making event count and timing useful for neural coding; waveform details can nevertheless change with channel state and conditions. The leaky integrate-and-fire model abstracts each action potential to a threshold event and reset. Its reset jump is a mathematical rule, not the actual regenerative waveform produced by sodium and potassium currents.
Neuronal refractory period
Words: 35
Action potential OurBigBook.com
After an action potential, channel inactivation and recovery temporarily suppress subsequent firing. An absolute refractory interval forbids another spike; a relative interval requires stronger excitation. A memoryless Poisson spike model omits this dependence on recent spikes.

Patch clamp

Words: 2k Articles: 16
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Patch clamp connects an electrode to a small area of cell membrane through a solution-filled patch pipette. A gigaohm seal around the rim makes tiny electric currents through ion channels distinguishable from seal leak current. The beautiful change of scale is from a population's average response to individual opening and closing events in single-channel recording.
Separate two questions. The configuration determines which cell membrane is accessible: an intact patch in cell-attached recording, an excised inside-out patch or outside-out patch, or intracellular access in whole-cell recording. The recording mode determines what is commanded and what is observed: voltage clamp commands an electric potential difference and measures electric current; current clamp commands electric current and measures membrane potential. Whole-cell recording supports both modes. A patch can contain several ion channels; a small recording area does not establish that only one is present.
The 1976 article Single-channel currents recorded from membrane of denervated frog muscle fibres describes an extracellular fire-polished pipette with a 3–5μm opening and 2–5MΩ electrical resistance. It contained saline and a channel-activating compound. Two separate intracellular electrodes supplied local voltage clamp of the muscle fibre; the patch amplifier measured local electric current. Cooling to 6–8∘C and hyperpolarization helped resolve elementary events. Figure 2 shows step-like pulses with a 200Hz filter at −120mV and 8∘C. Discrete amplitudes and overlapping events supported individual ion channel openings rather than a smoothly varying population response. This was neither whole-cell recording through the patch pipette nor current clamp. The specialized conditions improved visibility but limit generalization to warmer preparations; filtering can conceal brief openings.[ref]
For a new single-channel recording experiment, useful controls include a matched recording without the activating compound, controlled membrane potential, repeated seal tests, and an explicitly stated filter frequency response. These are proposed controls, not claims that every one was performed in that 1976 figure. Changing membrane potential tests the single-channel current-voltage relation; changing the recording filter tests whether a short pulse's apparent amplitude is an instrument artifact. A flat baseline establishes neither an absence of ion channels nor an absence of very brief events.

Patch pipette

Words: 41
Patch clamp OurBigBook.com
A patch pipette is the tapered glass, solution-filled probe used in patch clamp. Its electrode connects the solution to an amplifier, with another electrode referencing the bath. The open-tip electrical resistance differs from the much larger gigaohm seal electrical resistance. After break-in, a narrow or partly obstructed tip contributes to patch-clamp series resistance.

Gigaohm seal (Rseal​≳109Ω)

Words: 151 Articles: 1
Patch clamp OurBigBook.com
A gigaohm seal is the high electrical resistance contact between the glass rim and cell membrane, also called a gigaseal. It suppresses a bypass route around the membrane patch; it does not make the membrane patch itself impermeable. The 1981 methods used pulled, coated and heat-polished pipettes, a chlorided silver electrode and a pressure connection. Clean glass and suction supported tight seals; coating reduced pipette-to-bath capacitance and recording noise, rather than being required for sealing.[ref]
Seal leak current (Iseal​=Vp​/Rseal​)
Words: 76
Gigaohm seal OurBigBook.com
Seal leak current bypasses the membrane patch through an imperfect seal. For an ideal ohmic seal to a zero-voltage bath, Iseal​=Vp​/Rseal​, positive from pipette to bath. At ∣Vp​∣=50mV and Rseal​=1GΩ its magnitude is 50pA, far larger than the synthetic 0.8pA single-channel step. A stable baseline can be subtracted, but changing leakage can mimic a biological response. Intrinsic membrane leak through ion channels is distinct from this bypass: interpreting both as the same electrical conductance obscures whether the biological cell or the seal changed.

Cell-attached recording

Words: 53
Patch clamp OurBigBook.com
In cell-attached recording, the membrane under the patch pipette remains intact and the cytosol is retained. If bath voltage is zero, cell-interior voltage is Vcell​ and pipette voltage is Vp​, the patch's inside-minus-outside membrane potential is Vcell​−Vp​. Commanding Vp​ alone does not determine that difference when Vcell​ is unknown or changing. This is especially relevant to single-channel current-voltage relations.

Single-channel recording

Words: 126 Articles: 1
Patch clamp OurBigBook.com
Single-channel recording resolves individual ion channel opening events as changes in electric current. The distinction is resolution, not an absolute rule about configuration: rare, sufficiently large events can also be resolved during whole-cell recording. Simultaneously open identical ion channels can give successive current levels; indistinguishable amplitudes alone do not prove a unique channel identity.
Single-channel current-voltage relation (i=g(V−Erev​))
Words: 80
Single-channel recording OurBigBook.com
For an ideal open ion channel with constant electrical conductance g, membrane potential V and reversal potential Erev​, define outward electric current as positive:
i=g(V−Erev​).
(72)
This is an Ohm's law model of the open state, not a universal channel law or a rule for opening probability. In the synthetic figure, g=10pS and Erev​=0mV. Because 1pS⋅1mV=10−3pA, the open-state electric currents at −80 and −40mV are −0.8 and −0.4pA. Zero electric current at the reversal potential does not imply a closed ion channel. Real ion channels can have nonlinear responses, so the straight line is an explicit idealization.

Inside-out patch

Words: 32
Patch clamp OurBigBook.com
An inside-out patch is an excised membrane patch whose cytosol side faces the bath. Bath changes can therefore test effects on the intracellular face of an ion channel, with the extracellular face exposed to pipette solution.

Outside-out patch

Words: 36
Patch clamp OurBigBook.com
An outside-out patch is an excised membrane patch whose extracellular side faces the bath. It can form on withdrawal after whole-cell recording, with the intracellular face exposed to pipette solution. The orientation determines which side a bath-applied substance reaches.

Whole-cell recording

Words: 740 Articles: 5
Patch clamp OurBigBook.com
Whole-cell recording establishes intracellular electrical access by rupturing the membrane under a sealed patch pipette while retaining the gigaohm seal. Under adequate voltage clamp, the measured electric current combines contributions from accessible ion channels, membrane capacitance and seal leak current. Current clamp instead follows membrane potential while supplying a chosen electric current. Whole-cell recording is useful for linking a biological cell's total electrical response to its ion channels, but neither mode automatically controls distant dendrites or preserves the original cytosol.
In the 1981 methods demonstration, a bovine chromaffin biological cell was tested before and after patch rupture. Small voltage clamp steps produced a much larger capacitive transient after break-in. Integrating it gave 5pF for a 13μm cell; its decay indicated patch-clamp series resistance below 20MΩ. Depolarizing commands then revealed ionic electric currents. Separate current clamp recordings showed spontaneous action potentials. The comparison established access to the cell interior, rather than a claim that every pipette command equals membrane potential. Slower transients sometimes indicated incomplete rupture, and these small-cell results do not establish spatial control of a branched neuron.[ref]
Patch-clamp series resistance (Rs​)
Words: 195
Whole-cell recording OurBigBook.com
Patch-clamp series resistance, also called patch-clamp access resistance, is the effective electrical resistance between the pipette's sensed voltage and the cell interior. It includes tip access and any remaining obstruction after break-in. For injected electric current I into the biological cell, an ideal resistive access path gives
Vp​−V=IRs​.
(73)
Thus 1nA through 20MΩ produces a 20mV difference: a substantial possible voltage clamp error. The electric current in this equation is the access-path current, excluding any bypass seal leak current. In current clamp, the same access drop contaminates the pipette voltage during injection. Bridge compensation subtracts an estimated IRs​; an estimate that changes during recording leaves an error.
An independent passive voltage clamp calculation makes both speed and error visible. Write v=V−EL​ and vp​=Vp​−EL​, with fixed leak reversal potential EL​, constant membrane electrical resistance Rm​ and membrane capacitance Cm​. Assume an ideal command at the pipette node and omit seal leak current and pipette capacitance. Electric charge conservation gives
Cm​dtdv​=Rs​vp​−v​−Rm​v​.
(74)
For a step vp​=ΔV from v(0)=0, the ordinary differential equation gives
v(t)=ΔVRs​+Rm​Rm​​(1−e−t/τvc​),τvc​=Cm​Rs​+Rm​Rs​Rm​​.
(75)
With the figure's parameters and ΔV=10mV, the time constant is 0.909ms, the final membrane rise is 9.091mV, and access-path electric current falls from 500 to 45.45pA. Only when Rm​≫Rs​ does the time constant approach Rs​Cm​ and the final voltage approach the command. Actual voltage clamp also depends on amplifier feedback control and the space clamp problem.
Membrane capacitance (Cm​)
Words: 61
Whole-cell recording OurBigBook.com
Membrane capacitance is the capacitance associated with separated electric charge across cell membrane. A local ideal capacitor has charging electric current IC​=Cm​dV/dt. If a known actual membrane voltage change is ΔV, integrating the charging transient after subtracting sustained ionic and leak components gives Cm​=ΔV−1∫IC​dt. Pipette capacitance, finite patch-clamp series resistance and imperfect transient subtraction can bias the estimate. A capacitive transient is not by itself an ion channel opening.
Space clamp
Words: 43
Whole-cell recording OurBigBook.com
The space clamp problem is the failure to maintain the commanded membrane potential throughout a spatially extended biological cell. A soma voltage clamp can coexist with substantial voltage changes in distant dendrites or an axon. Reducing patch-clamp series resistance improves access at the recording site, but does not eliminate electrical separation within the neuron.
Cytosol dialysis
Words: 199
Whole-cell recording OurBigBook.com
Cytosol dialysis is exchange between the cytosol and pipette solution through the opening used in conventional whole-cell recording. Diffusion can change ion concentrations and dilute soluble regulators of ion channels. A diminishing response can therefore reflect the recording's alteration of the biological cell, rather than the experimental treatment.
A direct motivating example is the 1988 article Muscarinic activation of ionic currents measured by a new whole-cell recording method. In rat lacrimal gland biological cells, the acetylcholine response in conventional whole-cell recording lasted about five minutes. With a pore-forming substance in the patch pipette instead of open break-in, the response remained undiminished after one hour. The readout was activation of calcium-activated potassium and Cl− ion electric currents; preserving the response supported a role for retained cytoplasmic components. The authors also tested the substance extracellularly and observed reversible increases in cation electrical conductance. This comparison motivates perforated patch recording, but does not show that every intracellular constituent or every ion channel response is preserved. [ref]
Practical controls are matched pipette and bath compositions, recording elapsed time after break-in, time-matched untreated preparations, and tracking both patch-clamp series resistance and baseline leakage. Comparing conventional whole-cell recording with perforated patch recording can separate loss of soluble components from an intended treatment effect, but only if electrical access is characterized in both. These are controls suggested by the mechanisms above, not a new set of measured results.
Perforated patch recording
Words: 47
Whole-cell recording OurBigBook.com
Perforated patch recording obtains intracellular electrical access through pores in the patch under the patch pipette, with less open exchange of large cytoplasmic components than conventional whole-cell recording. Pore selectivity matters: retaining some components does not guarantee unchanged ion concentrations. Monitor patch-clamp series resistance as access develops and distinguish a perforated patch from accidental full rupture.

Current clamp

Words: 306 Articles: 1
Patch clamp OurBigBook.com
Current clamp prescribes injected electric current while recording membrane potential. A constant command does not force membrane potential to remain constant: a neuron can produce action potentials or synaptic potentials while that command is unchanged. At zero commanded electric current, the amplifier still measures membrane potential; intrinsic ionic electric currents continue. The name concerns current supplied by the instrument, not the cancellation of all currents in the biological cell.
In whole-cell recording, the measured pipette voltage during a current pulse includes the patch-clamp series resistance drop. A modern authored methods article explicitly describes current-pulse protocols and this distortion.[ref] Check the access contribution with small pulses and distinguish the immediate pipette-voltage jump from the slower membrane capacitance response. A zero-input interval measures a baseline, not proof that the instrument has no voltage offset. The passive example below explains these distinctions without asserting any new physiological measurements.
Passive membrane response in current clamp (τm​=Rm​Cm​)
Words: 177
Current clamp OurBigBook.com
Model a spatially uniform cell membrane as a capacitor of membrane capacitance Cm​ in parallel with membrane electrical resistance Rm​ and a fixed leak reversal potential EL​. Exclude active ion channels, seal leak current and pipette capacitance. For electric current I injected into the biological cell, electric charge conservation yields
Cm​dtdV​=I−Rm​V−EL​​.
(76)
Starting at V(0)=EL​ and applying constant I gives the ordinary differential equation solution
V(t)=EL​+IRm​(1−e−t/τm​),τm​=Rm​Cm​.
(77)
The steady state rise is IRm​; the time constant is Rm​Cm​. With I=50pA, Rm​=200MΩ, Cm​=50pF and EL​=−70mV, the rise is 10mV and τm​=10ms. At one time constant the rise is 10(1−e−1)mV≈6.321mV. The figure's uncompensated pipette voltage adds IRs​=1mV for Rs​=20MΩ. The membrane voltage is continuous at step onset in this model, while the pipette voltage immediately acquires that access drop.
Checking the units is instructive: electrical resistance times capacitance has units ΩF=s, and electric current times electrical resistance has units of voltage. Unlike the passive voltage clamp transient under patch-clamp series resistance, this ideal current clamp membrane time constant is set by Rm​Cm​, not Rs​Cm​. Strong current steps can recruit voltage-gated ion channels; the passive model then fails and cannot generate an action potential. Small pulses of both signs, stable access and repeated baseline measurements help test whether the passive approximation is appropriate.

Computational neuroscience

Words: 2k Articles: 19
Neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Mathematical and computational models connect neural mechanisms, measured responses and proposed information-processing functions. Their predictions require comparison with experiments; matching observations does not uniquely identify the biological mechanism.

Gabor filter

Words: 126
Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
A Gabor filter has a kernel formed by multiplying a Gaussian function by a sinusoid or a complex oscillation. In two-dimensional image processing, its orientation and spatial frequency select local image structure; evaluating the kernel's translated dot product with an image is spatial filtering. The real even example under signed spatial filter model of a simple cell uses a cosine.
There is experimental motivation for this family without making every simple cell an exact Gabor filter. Jones and Palmer fitted two-dimensional Gabor filters to measured spatial and spectral response profiles of simple cells in cat cortex and compared independently estimated parameters as a test of spatial linearity. Their reported residuals supported the approximation in that dataset. The chosen parameters and orientation tuning curve in this article are not extracted from their measurements. [ref]

Dynamic clamp

Words: 65
Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
A dynamic clamp measures a real neuron's voltage, updates a conductance model in real time and injects the resulting current, for example I=g(t)(E−V). It implements a virtual conductance without holding the voltage fixed. It can add artificial synapses, couple real neurons into a hybrid network or test how a voltage-dependent conductance affects excitability. Sampling delay and the injection site limit fidelity to spatially distributed biological channels.

Three-neuron ring stability ((1+τλ)3=Γ)

Words: 75
Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
For a directed three-neuron rate ring τx˙i​=−xi​+Wi,i−1​tanh(βxi−1​), the linearization has characteristic equation (1+τλ)3=Γ, where Γ=β3W13​W32​W21​. Positive loop gain has strict linear asymptotic stability for Γ<1. Negative loop gain has it for −8<Γ<0; at Γ=−8 a complex pair crosses the imaginary axis at frequency 3​/τ. The saturating cubic gives a supercritical Hopf bifurcation under an ordinary loop-gain variation. This directed system does not inherit the energy-descent property of a symmetric Hopfield network.

Leaky integrate-and-fire model (CV˙=−gL​(V−EL​)+I(t))

Words: 488 Articles: 1
Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
The leaky integrate-and-fire model combines a passive equation for membrane potential with a firing rule. Between events, inward-positive applied electric current I(t) obeys
CdtdV​=−gL​(V−EL​)+I(t),R=gL​1​,τ=gL​C​=RC,
(78)
where C>0 is membrane capacitance, gL​>0 is the leak conductance, R is the corresponding electrical resistance, and EL​ is the leak reversal potential. Here the leak conductance is constant. The time constant τ describes passive relaxation. When V first reaches a threshold Vθ​ from below, record an action potential event and reset V to Vr​<Vθ​. In the version used here, hold V=Vr​ for a fixed neuronal refractory period tref​, then resume integration. See 1.3 Integrate-And-Fire Models.
For constant I, with t=0 at the start of an integration interval and V(0)=Vinitial​, the exact subthreshold solution is
V(t)=EL​+RI+(Vinitial​−EL​−RI)e−t/τ.
(79)
The equilibrium point of this passive equation is V∞​=EL​+RI. Subtracting V∞​ leaves d(V−V∞​)/dt=−(V−V∞​)/τ, explaining the exponential function. This solution applies only until a threshold event or a change in I. Starting below threshold, constant input produces repeated events if V∞​>Vθ​; if V∞​=Vθ​, the threshold is approached asymptotically and never reached at finite time.
For a worked example, choose
EL​=Vr​=Vinitial​=−65mV,Vθ​=−50mV,τ=20ms,R=100MΩ,tref​=2ms.
(80)
These imply gL​=10nS and C=200pF. All these parameters are illustrative model choices, not measurements from a particular neuron. With I=200pA, Ohm's law gives RI=20mV and hence V∞​=−45mV. Thus
V(t)=−45mV−20mVe−t/(20ms).
(81)
At threshold, e−t/τ=1/4, so the first event occurs after T=20ln4ms≈27.7259ms. Each subsequent cycle includes the 2ms neuronal refractory period, giving
f=T+tref​1​≈33.6407Hz.
(82)
This is the ideal sustained firing rate; the first-event latency is T, not T+tref​.
With I=100pA instead, RI=10mV and V∞​=−55mV. From the same initial state, V(t)=−55mV−10mVe−t/τ stays below −50mV: no events occur, however long this current is held. The critical sustained current is (Vθ​−EL​)/R=150pA; equality gives asymptotic approach rather than finite-time firing.
The leak gives old inputs progressively less influence, while capacitance prevents an ordinary finite electric current step from changing V instantly. This combination makes the leaky integrate-and-fire model useful for exploring input summation, event timing and network activity at low computational cost. Its fixed parameters and reset omit the evolving voltage-gated ion channels of the Hodgkin-Huxley model, spatial integration in dendrites and mechanisms of neural adaptation. Treating a synapse as a prescribed I(t) also omits its voltage-dependent driving force unless a conductance term is added. See 1.4 Limitations of the Leaky Integrate-and-Fire Model and constant-input firing rate of a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron.
Constant-input firing rate of a leaky integrate-and-fire neuron
Words: 56
Leaky integrate-and-fire model OurBigBook.com
For Cm​V˙=−gL​(V−VL​)+I, reset V0​<Vθ​ and no explicit refractory interval, define Ic​=gL​(Vθ​−VL​) and τm​=Cm​/gL​. Constant current gives
r(I)={0,[τm​log((I−gL​(V0​−VL​))/(I−Ic​))]−1,​I≤Ic​,I>Ic​.​
(83)
The threshold is approached only asymptotically at I=Ic​. At large current, r∼I/[Cm​(Vθ​−V0​)]. Adding an absolute neuronal refractory period changes the denominator to T(I)+tref​ and makes the firing rate saturate rather than grow without bound.

Hodgkin-Huxley model

Words: 266
Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
A conductance-based Hodgkin-Huxley model couples membrane potential to voltage-dependent channel-gating variables. It explains generation of action potentials through regenerative and opposing ionic electric currents, while its parameters and channel assumptions determine its biological domain of validity.
In the classical model, m describes sodium activation, h describes availability against sodium inactivation, and n describes potassium activation. Each follows two-state ion-channel gating, with its own voltage-dependent rates. The available electrical conductances are
gNa​=gˉ​Na​m3h,gK​=gˉ​K​n4.
(84)
The barred quantities are maximum electrical conductances. The factors have the interpretation of independent permissive gates in an ion channel: three activation factors and a distinct inactivation-availability factor for sodium, and four identical activation factors for potassium. Large h means availability; small h means inactivation. These are model assumptions, not a literal structural description of every ion channel. See Gerstner, Kistler, Naud and Paninski, Neuronal Dynamics (2014), §2.2: model definition and stochastic opening.
With inward-positive electric current, a single-compartment form is
CdtdV​=Iext​+gNa​(ENa​−V)+gK​(EK​−V)+gL​(EL​−V).
(85)
Here C is membrane capacitance, Iext​ is imposed inward electric current, gL​ is leak electrical conductance, and each E is a reversal potential. Use consistent units, and either whole-compartment quantities throughout or quantities per membrane area throughout. Opening changes electrical conductance; the reversal potential and present membrane potential determine the associated electric current. Coupling this equation to the voltage-dependent gates makes a generally nonlinear system of ordinary differential equations; a gate's fixed-voltage limit alone does not specify its evolving state during an action potential.
The original quantitative account is [ref]. The contrast with the leaky integrate-and-fire model is useful: here an action potential emerges from evolving ionic electric currents, whereas the simpler model records a threshold event and imposes a reset.

Mutually excitatory saturating rate network (τx˙=−x+g(y),g(z)=ma2z2/(σ2+a2z2))

Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
The symmetric two-neuron rate model has nonnegative activity and saturating recurrent input. Every equilibrium has x=y: otherwise monotonicity of g gives a contradiction. With positive parameters it has three distinct equilibria exactly when am>2σ, namely zero and z±​=(m±m2−4σ2/a2​)/2. The lower positive equilibrium is a saddle and the origin and upper equilibrium are stable nodes. The resulting two attracting activity levels model a persistent switch rather than a spiking waveform.

Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
A stimulus passes through a linear temporal or spatial filter, then a nonnegative nonlinear rate function. A conditionally Inhomogeneous Poisson process generates spikes at that rate. The filter and nonlinearity can be fitted from data and tested on held-out trials. Refractoriness and spike-history correlations require extensions beyond this basic cascade.

Linear-nonlinear-Poisson cascade model OurBigBook.com
For a stimulus-conditioned Inhomogeneous Poisson process, the event log-likelihood is the displayed expression. A causal filter expansion λ(t)=exp[b+∑a​wa​(s∗ba​)(t)] can be fitted by maximum likelihood estimation, with a smoothness or size penalty and held-out validation. The integral term penalizes predicted spikes that did not occur; fitting only stimulus values at observed spikes omits this essential part.

Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
Average the stimulus history preceding each observed spike, after removing the stimulus mean. With white Gaussian stimulation and a suitable one-filter encoding model, the result is proportional to the relevant linear filter. An even nonlinearity can make the average vanish despite strong stimulus dependence, so averaging alone is not universally sufficient.

Spike-triggered average OurBigBook.com
For a single linear filter followed by a rate nonlinearity and a Gaussian stimulus-history vector s with covariance C, Gaussian integration by parts gives E[sg(kTs)]∝Ck. Thus a spike-triggered average estimates Ck, rather than k directly, when the stimulus is correlated. Covariance correction, with regularization if necessary, can recover the filter direction. For an even nonlinearity the proportionality factor can vanish; then a one-filter average is insufficient.

Computational neuroscience OurBigBook.com
How neural responses represent variables relevant to an organism. A coding claim specifies both which response features carry information and how a downstream system can use them.
Receptive field
Words: 196 Articles: 2
Neural coding OurBigBook.com
The region and stimulus features whose variation influences a sensory neuron's response. A visual receptive field may include spatially distinct ON and OFF regions; a linear receptive-field kernel is a signed weighting map, while the full response can be nonlinear and depend on stimulus history.
ON and OFF receptive-field subregions
Words: 86
Receptive field OurBigBook.com
ON and OFF receptive-field subregions distinguish locations by response polarity. In the classic mapping experiment, a bright spot in an ON region increased firing during illumination; illumination in an OFF region suppressed maintained firing and/or evoked a discharge when the light disappeared. If maintained firing was very low, suppression could be hard to see. The recorded decrease alone did not distinguish direct inhibition at a synapse from reduced excitation. [ref] These are functional regions in visual space, not compartments of a cell body.

Receptive field OurBigBook.com
For the toy models here, visual contrast means brightness relative to a positive uniform background L0​: C(x,y)=(L(x,y)−L0​)/L0​. Positive values mean brighter than background, negative values darker, and zero unchanged. This convention separates spatial structure from the background level. A sinusoid C=acos(⋯) with 0≤a≤1 keeps L=L0​(1+C) nonnegative. Different experimental conventions for visual contrast require their own definitions; the toy values below do not specify a historical stimulus intensity.

Representation by spike timing, latency, phase or relative timing across neurons, beyond a chosen count summary. Its interpretation requires a timing reference and a decoder capable of resolving the relevant precision.

Representation by a neuron's firing frequency or the expected spike count in a chosen time window. The window length and averaging convention matter; equal counts do not imply equal temporal patterns.

A sequence of action potential times, represented mathematically as a point process or a sum of Dirac deltas. Its event counts, intervals and correlations summarize different aspects of neural activity.

For a correctly specified conditional rate, transformed interspike intervals have independent unit-exponential distributions, apart from observation-boundary censoring. Enzyme

An enzyme is a biological catalyst: it accelerates a chemical reaction and is regenerated after a successful catalytic cycle. Most enzymes are proteins, but catalytic RNA molecules, called ribozymes, also exist. Many reactions needed by a biological cell would proceed too slowly under its ordinary conditions without enzymes. See Cooper, The Cell: the central role of enzymes as biological catalysts.
The biological beauty is selective speed. A biological cell contains many possible reactants; its enzymes help determine which transformations happen on a useful timescale. In metabolism, one step's reaction product can become another step's substrate, so selective catalysts support an organized flow of material.
The ribosome is a striking biological example: the machinery that builds proteins has RNA at its catalytic centre. The complete ribosome contains both RNA and proteins, but its bond-forming active site is built from RNA. Structural evidence established this distinction in Nissen et al., The structural basis of ribosome activity in peptide bond synthesis, Science 289, 920–930 (2000).
Selection occurs at an active site, the region where substrate binding and catalytic chemistry take place. Shape and chemical interactions favour some substrates over others; binding can also reshape the enzyme, an induced fit. Recognition alone is insufficient: holding a substrate extremely tightly need not make it react quickly. Catalysis requires a favourable route through the transition state, the high-barrier configuration between reactants and reaction products. Positioning reactive groups and stabilizing this configuration relative to the bound substrate can lower that barrier. Specificity is often strong, but need not mean exactly one acceptable substrate. See Cooper, The Cell: mechanisms of enzymatic catalysis.
Read the diagram numerically. Its chosen Gibbs free energies are 0 for the reactants and −10kJmol−1 for the reaction products. The uncatalysed peak is 60kJmol−1, whereas the catalysed peak is 40kJmol−1. The forward free-energy barriers are therefore 60 and 40kJmol−1; viewed from the reaction products, the reverse barriers are 70 and 50kJmol−1. Both decrease by 20kJmol−1, while the endpoint difference stays −10kJmol−1. These are constructed values, not measurements of a particular enzyme.
This separates chemical kinetics from chemical equilibrium. An enzyme changes how rapidly the system approaches chemical equilibrium; it does not change the equilibrium constant for the same overall chemical reaction under the same conditions. Faster catalysis therefore supplies no extra driving energy. In a biological cell, continuing supply of reactants and removal of reaction products can nevertheless sustain a net flow: the surroundings keep that system away from chemical equilibrium. See IUBMB, Symbolism and terminology in enzyme kinetics: basic definitions.
Some enzymes require a cofactor, an additional nonprotein component such as a metal ion or a small organic molecule. Organic helpers are often called coenzymes; they can assist transfers that the protein alone cannot readily perform. The cofactor may remain bound or exchange with the surroundings, depending on the system. A coenzyme can be chemically changed in one reaction and regenerated by another: regeneration of the enzyme does not mean every helper is unchanged in that individual reaction. Some enzymes need no additional cofactor. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: small molecules associated with proteins and Alberts et al., activated carriers and their regeneration.
How much faster does adding substrate make a reaction? Enzyme kinetics gives a quantitative answer when a model's assumptions fit. For an illustrative reaction obeying Michaelis-Menten kinetics, use the Michaelis-Menten equation with substrate concentration s, limiting reaction rate Vmax​ and Michaelis constant KM​. At s/KM​=0.1, substitution gives v/Vmax​=0.1/1.1=1/11≈0.0909. At s/KM​=1, it gives 1/2; at s/KM​=10, it gives 10/11≈0.9091. Thus a hundredfold increase in substrate between the first and last examples yields only a tenfold increase in reaction rate.
For a chosen Vmax​=110μMmin−1, those fractions mean reaction rates of 10, 55 and 100μMmin−1. Doubling substrate from 10KM​ to 20KM​ raises the normalized rate only from 10/11 to 20/21≈0.9524, a relative increase of about 4.76%. In this simplest model, the catalytic machinery is already nearly fully occupied. Doubling the amount of active enzyme instead doubles Vmax​ and the predicted reaction rates at fixed free substrate concentration, provided the other conditions are unchanged. This distinction helps decide whether additional substrate or additional catalytic capacity could improve throughput.
The interpretation has limits. The simplest Michaelis-Menten kinetics assumes a single substrate, fixed active enzyme amount, a suitable quasi-steady-state approximation, and initial measurements with negligible reverse reaction from accumulated reaction product. Substantial depletion, interacting binding sites, or inhibition by excess substrate can invalidate this model. Within it, KM​ is the substrate concentration giving half the limiting reaction rate; it is not generally the binding dissociation constant Kd​. See IUBMB, enzyme kinetics: steady-state approximation and substrate dissociation and IUBMB, Michaelis-Menten and non-Michaelis-Menten kinetics. Measuring activity also requires specified temperature, pH and necessary cofactor availability: a weak signal can reflect unsuitable conditions rather than little enzyme. See Brooks et al., Assay Guidance Manual: basics of enzymatic assays for HTS.

Ribozyme

Words: 1k
Enzyme OurBigBook.com
A ribozyme is an RNA molecule whose folded structure provides catalysis of a chemical reaction. A protein enzyme builds its active site from an amino acid chain; a ribozyme builds a working active site from RNA, sometimes with metal ions and associated proteins. Base pairing can help recognize a substrate, but recognition alone does not establish catalysis: the RNA must promote chemical conversion. A passive messenger RNA template being read by a ribosome is not thereby a ribozyme. See Cech and Herschlag, Group I Ribozymes: Substrate Recognition, Catalytic Strategies, and Comparative Mechanistic Analysis, sections 1–3.
The surprise is that an information-bearing polymer can also perform chemistry. Examples include the self-splicing group I intron of Tetrahymena thermophila and the catalytic RNA component of bacterial RNase P, discussed below. The ribosome supplies an everyday example: its peptide bond-forming active site is made of ribosomal RNA, although the complete machine also contains proteins. Nissen and colleagues examined structures of a large ribosome subunit with substrate analogues and found RNA contacting those analogues at the catalytic centre. This supports an RNA active site, not a claim that isolated ribosomal RNA can carry out all of biological translation. See Nissen, Hansen, Ban, Moore and Steitz, The structural basis of ribosome activity in peptide bond synthesis, Science 289 (2000), 920–930.
For the Tetrahymena group I intron, RNA splicing removes the intron and joins its flanking exons. The first chemical step uses the free 3′ hydroxyl group of an external guanosine to attack the phosphodiester bond at the 5′ splice junction. This releases the upstream exon with a free 3′ hydroxyl group and attaches the guanosine to the intron. That newly freed hydroxyl group then attacks the phosphodiester bond at the other splice junction, joining the exons and releasing the linear intron. Each step exchanges one backbone connection for another; it is not simply separation of base pairs. See Cech, Zaug and Grabowski, 1981: the phosphoester-transfer mechanism.
The motivating experiment began with an unexpected control. As Cech recounts, Zaug purified a ribosomal RNA precursor from Tetrahymena using a detergent and phenol extraction, then compared test tubes with and without added cell nucleus extract. Incubation in salts and nucleotides released the same amount of small intron RNA in both cases, detected by gel electrophoresis. Repetition made a missing ingredient or accidental omission less plausible. Activity also survived treatments intended to destroy proteins. Nevertheless, absence of added extract did not by itself exclude a tightly attached, resistant protein, or prove that the small RNA had been newly excised rather than released from an already processed complex. See Thomas R. Cech, 1989 Nobel lecture, pp. 655–659: the unexpected control and alternative explanations.
An independent chemical readout addressed the latter problem. Cech mixed precursor RNA with phosphorus-32-labelled guanosine bearing three phosphate groups (GTP), and used gel electrophoresis followed by exposure to X-ray film to locate the label. Label appeared in the excised intron with magnesium present; it was absent when magnesium was omitted or labelled ATP replaced the labelled guanosine reagent. This experiment is described in Cech, 1989 Nobel lecture, pp. 657–658: labelled-guanosine controls. The 1981 study established attachment through the guanosine 3′ hydroxyl group and showed that guanosine without a triphosphate also supported excision: breaking down the added nucleotide to supply energy was unnecessary. See Cech, Zaug and Grabowski, In vitro splicing of the ribosomal RNA precursor of Tetrahymena, Cell 27 (1981), 487–496: primary abstract. Separately, sequencing and terminal analysis found an extra 5′ guanosine absent from the corresponding DNA sequence. See Zaug and Cech, The intervening sequence excised from the ribosomal RNA precursor of Tetrahymena contains a 5-terminal guanosine residue not encoded by the DNA, Nucleic Acids Research 10 (1982), 2823–2838. Together, incorporation and sequence evidence support a new covalent bond, beyond a change in how RNA associates.
Kruger, Grabowski, Zaug, Sands, Gottschling and Cech's 1982 test removed dependence on a precursor purified from Tetrahymena. They cloned the intron and adjacent exons into a DNA template, made precursor RNA with purified bacterial RNA polymerase under conditions suppressing RNA splicing, and removed proteins by detergent–phenol extraction. Denaturing gel electrophoresis separated precursor species. Purified precursor was then incubated with the guanosine reagent, magnesium and salt; matched samples without this incubation supplied a precursor baseline. Their standard assay used 10mM magnesium chloride, 0.1mM of that guanosine reagent, 100mM ammonium sulfate and a buffer solution at pH 7.5, for 30 minutes at temperature 37∘C, with specified variations in individual experiments. Gel electrophoresis and radioactive-film detection showed excised intron RNA; sequencing verified its 5′ junction. See Kruger et al., Self-Splicing RNA, Cell 31 (1982), 147–157, figures 3–4 and Experimental Procedures.
Excision alone could leave disconnected exons. To test joining, the authors paired labelled RNA with DNA spanning the joined-exon sequence, removed exposed RNA with enzymes, and separated the protected pieces by denaturing gel electrophoresis. Spliced samples yielded protected RNA long enough to span the junction. See Kruger et al., 1982, figure 6: independent evidence for exon ligation. The experimental logic matters: an intron-sized band identifies a candidate product, while sequence and junction assays test its chemical identity.
These controls support sufficiency of the prepared RNA under the assay conditions. They do not show that every RNA self-splices, or that proteins are dispensable inside a biological cell. Many group I introns use proteins to help attain an active fold. See Cech and Herschlag, Group I Ribozymes, section 6: protein facilitation. Nor does a failed assay necessarily identify an inactive nucleotide sequence: unsuitable ions, pH, or temperature can prevent a working active site from forming.
The distinction between self-processing and repeated use became especially clear with bacterial RNase P. In 1983 Guerrier-Takada, Gardiner, Marsh, Pace and Altman separated the RNA and protein components of RNase P from two bacteria. Purified RNA cleaved precursor transfer RNA under conditions containing 60mM magnesium ions, or 10mM magnesium ions plus 1mM spermidine. The protein components alone had no catalytic activity. At 5–10mM magnesium without spermidine, both components were needed. Thus the comparison demonstrated an RNA catalyst while also explaining why protein assistance could matter under other conditions. RNase P produces the mature 5′ end of transfer RNA by removing its leader; it acts on a separate substrate and can be used again. See Guerrier-Takada et al., The RNA moiety of ribonuclease P is the catalytic subunit of the enzyme, Cell 35 (1983), 849–857: primary abstract.
Self-splicing demonstrates RNA chemistry, but one precursor completing one rearrangement is not yet evidence for catalytic turnover: repeated conversion of separate substrates by a regenerated catalyst. The self-splicing precursor changes its own connectivity and incorporates external guanosine. In 1986 Zaug and Cech showed that a shortened Tetrahymena intron RNA could cleave and rejoin separate short RNA substrates in a sequence-dependent reaction. This demonstrated an RNA enzyme acting beyond its own self-processing. See Zaug and Cech, The intervening sequence RNA of Tetrahymena is an enzyme, Science 231 (1986), 470–475: primary abstract.
Read the second figure as a counting argument. In a stipulated model, A denotes unprocessed precursor and Pself​ counts completed self-processing events. Set A(0)=R0​, Pself​(0)=0 and dA/dτ=−A. The exponential function solution gives Pself​/R0​=1−e−τ, never exceeding one. Here guanosine and other necessary reagents are taken to be available in excess; Pself​ counts events, not every separate reaction product molecule.
For a second stipulated model, let an unchanged ribozyme R perform R+S⟶R+P on a separate substrate S. Assume the effective law of mass action dS/dt=−kRS, no reverse reaction, no ribozyme loss and no inhibited or long-lived bound states. Set R=R0​, S(0)=5R0​, P(0)=0 and τ=kR0​t. Then S/R0​=5e−τ and P/R0​=5(1−e−τ), with S+P=5R0​. At τ=1, self-processing gives about 0.632 completed events per initial RNA, whereas the regenerated ribozyme gives about 3.161 reaction product molecules per initial ribozyme. More than one substrate conversion per initial ribozyme, with appropriate background and identity controls, is evidence for turnover. Product accumulation below that threshold alone cannot distinguish a reusable catalyst from one-shot chemistry. These models illustrate that distinction; actual enzyme kinetics can include folding delays, binding, saturation and product release.

This description concerns those bacterial complexes, not every form of RNase P.

Active site

Words: 1k Articles: 3
Enzyme OurBigBook.com
An active site is the region of an enzyme where a substrate binds and undergoes a chemical reaction. In a protein enzyme, it includes the amino acid residues that contact the substrate and those that directly assist catalysis. These roles can overlap: an amino acid side chain can both orient a substrate and participate in chemistry. The active site occupies only part of the folded protein; the remaining amino acid residues help establish its protein structure, stability and movement. An active site need not be a consecutive stretch of protein primary structure: protein folding can bring distant amino acid residues together. A ribozyme instead supplies an RNA active site. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, Protein Function: binding sites and catalytic sites.
Binding and catalysis answer different questions. A protein binding site recognizes shape and chemistry through such interactions as hydrogen bonds, electrostatics and the hydrophobic effect. At an active site, appropriate positioning also helps a substrate reach the transition state of a chemical reaction. Some amino acid side chains transfer a proton; others participate transiently in a covalent bond. The enzyme-substrate complex is the associated enzyme and substrate, before conversion to a reaction product. Merely accumulating this complex does not establish rapid catalysis: stabilizing the bound substrate without sufficiently stabilizing the transition state can leave a large barrier. The important complementarity is chemical as well as geometric. See Geoffrey M. Cooper, The Cell, The Central Role of Enzymes as Biological Catalysts: substrate binding and transition-state stabilization.
The cartoon makes a useful experimental distinction. Changing a contacting amino acid residue might weaken substrate binding, change the reaction rate, or do both. Changing a distant amino acid residue can also disrupt the active site by changing protein folding. Therefore a loss of activity after a mutation alone does not locate a catalytic group: compare binding, protein structure and enzyme kinetics as well. This is an interpretation guide, not a report of a particular mutation experiment.
A concrete example is hexokinase: it transfers the terminal phosphate group of ATP to the 6-position hydroxyl group of a sugar such as glucose. Specificity need not mean only one acceptable substrate: the hexokinase reaction class includes several possible acceptor sugars. Which are used, and at what reaction rates, depends on the particular enzyme and conditions. See Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics, ENZYME entry EC 2.7.1.1: hexokinase reaction and acceptor range.
Bennett and Steitz compared yeast hexokinase A crystallized with glucose against hexokinase B crystallized without glucose. X-rays scattered by the crystals supplied diffraction measurements from which the authors reconstructed protein structure; comparing coordinates located movement, rather than measuring a reaction rate. The glucose-containing cleft was narrower: one lobe was rotated by about 12∘ relative to the other, with some protein backbone displacements reaching 8A˚. This makes the active site a moving arrangement of interacting groups, rather than a permanent hole. See William S. Bennett Jr. and Thomas A. Steitz, Glucose-induced conformational change in yeast hexokinase, PNAS 75 (1978), 4848–4852.
The structural comparison has two explicit limitations: different forms of hexokinase and different crystal environments were compared, and static coordinates do not record the order of binding and movement. Closure is consistent with induced fit, but those structures alone cannot exclude conformational selection. The solution experiment under induced fit addresses whether compaction also occurs outside a crystal.

Induced fit

Words: 668
Active site OurBigBook.com
In induced fit, a substrate binds to an enzyme and the resulting enzyme-substrate complex subsequently changes its protein structure. This adjustment can position interacting groups at the active site for catalysis. The mechanistic claim concerns order: binding precedes the relevant change. In conformational selection, the unbound enzyme already visits an alternative protein structure, which the substrate preferentially binds. Both processes can occur in one system. Let E and E∗ denote two structures of the same enzyme, and S a substrate. The limiting routes are
induced fit:conformational selection:​E+S⇌ES⇌E∗S,E⇌E∗,E∗+S⇌E∗S.​
(86)
The star labels a structure, not a different protein primary structure, and does not by itself mean catalytic activity. Each reversible arrow abbreviates a step, not the whole catalytic cycle. See Gordon G. Hammes, Yu-Chu Chang and Terrence G. Oas, Conformational selection or induced fit: a flux description of reaction mechanism, PNAS 106 (2009), 13737–13741.
A rigid lock-and-key cartoon usefully suggests selective substrate recognition, but it suppresses movement of the protein and chemical changes at the active site. Replacing it with two static drawings, “open” and “closed”, still does not establish induced fit: both routes above can end at E∗S. Also, if complete closure prevents a substrate entering, the pre-existing structure selected in conformational selection might be partly open and undergo further induced fit after binding. The usefulness of the distinction is that it turns an attractive shape story into questions about enzyme kinetics. Relative traffic through the routes depends on populations, rate constants and free substrate concentration, rather than affinity alone. See Hammes, Chang and Oas, 2009: coupled pathways, their concentrations and the limitations of endpoint structures.
For this analytical illustration, hold the free substrate concentration s constant and assume independent waiting times with exponential distributions of constant rates. The law of mass action gives the binding rate a=kon​s; the competing change has rate b. The probability density function for binding to happen first at time t is ae−(a+b)t, because neither event has happened earlier. Its integral is
P(binding first)=∫0∞​ae−(a+b)tdt=a+ba​.
(87)
With the stated invented rate constants, s=0.1,1,10μM gives 1/11,1/2,10/11, respectively. Raising free substrate concentration makes binding more likely to win this initial competition. This probability is deliberately narrower than a full-route fraction: returns to E, later changes and the binding properties of E∗ would all matter for the latter. The illustration explains why timing and concentration must accompany structural evidence, without assigning a binding mechanism to a real enzyme.
A motivating experiment tested the crystal interpretation in solution. McDonald, Steitz and Engelman prepared solutions of monomeric yeast hexokinase B and compared the unbound preparation with sugar-bound preparations. Their apparatus measured small-angle scattering of X-rays; the spatial extent inferred from that readout was the radius of gyration, rather than a catalytic reaction rate. Binding glucose reduced the radius of gyration by 0.95±0.24A˚; binding the phosphorylated glucose product reduced it by 1.25±0.28A˚, as reported by the authors. The glucose change agreed with the reduction calculated from the crystal coordinates. See Robert C. McDonald, Thomas A. Steitz and Donald M. Engelman, Yeast hexokinase in solution exhibits a large conformational change upon binding glucose or glucose 6-phosphate, Biochemistry 18 (1979), 338–342: primary abstract.
The comparison without added substrate supplies a baseline within the same form of hexokinase; the second bound preparation tests another binding condition. Together with the crystal comparison, solution compaction supports closure beyond crystal packing. It still gives an average spatial readout, not a movie of individual binding events, and product-associated compaction does not demonstrate ongoing catalysis. Neither experiment alone proves that binding precedes movement. To distinguish induced fit from conformational selection, structural comparisons must be combined with measurements sensitive to timing and with a model of the relevant populations and enzyme kinetics.

Flow cytometry

Biology OurBigBook.com
Flow cytometry records signals from suspended particles passing an illuminated interrogation region. For a flow cytometric DNA-content assay, a laser excites a DNA-binding dye and a detector records its fluorescence. An event is a recorded passage, not a guarantee that exactly one intact biological cell was measured.

Flow cytometric DNA-content assay

Words: 300
Flow cytometry OurBigBook.com
Under controlled staining and detector settings, integrated fluorescence can be approximately proportional to nuclear DNA amount. A histogram of accepted single-cell events then separates a 2C region, an intermediate region and a 4C region. These are ordinarily assigned to G0 phase/G1 phase, S phase, and G2 phase/M phase respectively in the stated diploid model.
A Cornell protocol fixes a single-cell suspension by adding cold 70% ethanol dropwise while mixing, reducing clumping. After washing, its staining solution contains propidium iodide at 50μg/ml; ribonuclease A removes interfering RNA. It specifies excitation at 488nm and emission around 600nm. The resulting readout is fluorescence per event, not a direct count of chromosomes. [ref]
Useful controls include an unstained sample for background and a reference population with known nuclear DNA amount, processed with identical settings. Two attached 2C biological cells can mimic one 4C event. Comparing signal integral with pulse height or width helps exclude such doublets; a gate selecting intact single particles also limits debris. These are proposed assay checks, not measurements underlying the illustration.
A 4C peak cannot distinguish G2 phase from mitosis; a 2C peak cannot distinguish G1 phase from G0 phase. Mixed ploidy, uneven staining and aggregates can invalidate phase assignments. Peak areas describe the accepted sample at collection, and do not by themselves establish phase durations, division rates or a particular arrest mechanism. A treatment comparison needs matched handling and another readout appropriate to the claimed mechanism.

Biological cell

Words: 7k Articles: 78
Biology OurBigBook.com
A biological cell is a membrane-bounded basic unit of living organization. In a cell-level experiment it can be an experimental unit, provided that treatment assignment and relevant interactions are handled at that level.
The shared architecture of cellular life combines a selective cell membrane, internal cytoplasm, inherited information in DNA, and ribosomes that assemble proteins. Metabolism supplies transformations of matter and energy needed for maintenance and growth. These components form a coupled system: a boundary retains useful molecules, enzymes organize chemical reactions, and inherited information supports rebuilding the machinery. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e: prokaryotic cells.
A worked structural comparison: in a typical prokaryote, DNA occupies a region without a surrounding cell nucleus; in a typical nucleated eukaryote, much of the DNA lies inside a membrane-bounded cell nucleus. Both still have a cell membrane, cytoplasm and ribosomes. The extra boundary compartmentalizes processes; it does not create a different basic principle of living organization. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e: eukaryotic cells.
Shared architecture describes cellular life and its developmental machinery, rather than requiring every specialized biological cell to retain every component. A mature mammalian red blood cell, for example, lacks a cell nucleus, although it develops from nucleated precursors. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e: components of blood. This distinction makes cellular unity compatible with striking specialization.

Cell cycle

Words: 876 Articles: 14
Biological cell OurBigBook.com
The cell cycle is the sequence of events by which a biological cell prepares for and completes division, including DNA replication and distribution of chromosomes. In Saccharomyces cerevisiae, changing bud appearance provides an accessible readout; see the Burgess, Powers and Mell account and Hartwell, Culotti and Reid's primary study cited there.
For a typical cycling diploid eukaryotic biological cell, the order is G1 phase, S phase, G2 phase, then M phase. DNA replication doubles nuclear DNA amount during S phase; mitosis distributes the copies, and cytokinesis separates the daughters. The useful distinction is between copying a library and allocating its copies: DNA replication changes how much material exists, whereas division changes which biological cell contains it.
Gene expression continues to supply RNA and proteins as the biological cell grows; it is different from duplicating the genome. In the yeast cross-species complementation experiment, restored growth requires successful repeated cell cycles, but growth alone does not locate a defect within a phase. Bud appearance in Saccharomyces cerevisiae provides another readout, while a flow cytometric DNA-content assay asks how much nuclear DNA is present and DNA pulse labeling asks whether new DNA was synthesized during an exposure.

Cell-cycle DNA content ((2n,2C)→(2n,4C)→2(2n,2C))

Words: 259
Cell cycle OurBigBook.com
Let n count chromosomes in one complete set, and let C denote the nuclear DNA amount in one unreplicated haploid set of this organism. Ploidy counts sets, whereas C units count material; C is not a universal mass shared by all species. Here we count a paired replicated chromosome as one until its sister chromatids separate. A copied diploid genome is therefore still diploid through S phase: 2n persists even as 2C becomes 4C.
An original bookkeeping example uses a hypothetical diploid biological cell with n=3. Name its three homologous chromosome pairs A,a, B,b and D,d. Assume ordinary nuclear DNA replication, no chromosome loss, and one continuous double-stranded DNA molecule per unreplicated chromosome or replicated chromatid. Count nuclear material only, excluding mitochondrion DNA.
Stage and counting compartmentChromosomesDouble-stranded DNA moleculesNuclear DNA amount
One G1 phase biological cell6 unreplicated62C
One G2 phase biological cell6 replicated12 in 6 pairs of sister chromatids4C
Whole undivided anaphase biological cell12 separated daughter chromosomes124C total
Each completed daughter cell nucleus6 unreplicated62C each
For example, A becomes the paired copies A1​,A2​ during S phase. They remain one replicated chromosome until separation. Each completed daughter receives one A copy and one a copy, and similarly for the other two pairs. Across both daughters, 2×6=12 double-stranded DNA molecules and 2(2C)=4C: division allocates the copied material without another round of DNA replication.
The whole undivided anaphase biological cell transiently contains 4n separately counted daughter chromosomes. This counting change does not establish a four-set ploidy in a completed daughter genome: each pole receives 2n, and each completed daughter cell nucleus is diploid. Always state whether a number refers to one cell nucleus, one pole, or the entire undivided biological cell. Compare meiotic DNA content: after meiosis I, a haploid cell nucleus can contain 2C, so amount alone cannot determine ploidy.

DNA pulse labeling

DNA pulse labeling exposes biological cells to a detectable precursor for a bounded interval. After removal, later sampling can follow the labeled material and descendants. A short pulse asks about synthesis during that interval; overnight labeling instead accumulates evidence across many hours. Detectable synthesis does not by itself prove completion of a cell cycle, and DNA repair can also incorporate precursors.
DNA synthesis labeling with EdU
Words: 172
DNA pulse labeling OurBigBook.com
EdU labeling uses a modified nucleoside, 5-ethynyl-2'-deoxyuridine, incorporated into newly synthesized DNA, then chemically couples it to a fluorescent reporter.
A 2008 experiment injected adult mice with 100μg of this label and inspected intestinal sections 96 hours later. Fixed sections on slides received 10μM Alexa568-azide for 10 minutes. Imaging with a fluorescence microscope combined the reporter image with a Hoechst DNA counterstain and a transmitted-light view. Labeled cell nuclei marked descendants of biological cells synthesizing DNA during exposure, rather than identifying current S phase at collection. [ref]
The same study's cultured-cell controls compared overnight 10μM label, no label, and label with 10mM hydroxyurea. No-label samples had little reporter background; hydroxyurea strongly suppressed incorporation. The camera detected residual signal with a 3-second exposure versus 40 milliseconds under otherwise identical settings, demonstrating why acquisition settings matter. These controls support synthesis-dependent labeling, without proving that every labeled biological cell completes division. [ref]

The cell envelope comprises a biological cell's surrounding boundary layers, including its cell membrane and a cell wall or additional outer structures when present. The term is especially useful when discussing bacteria, where the layers must be distinguished.
