Cell envelope OurBigBook.com
A bacterial outer membrane is an additional membrane outside the peptidoglycan in typical Gram-negative bacteria. It adds a barrier while the inner cell membrane remains the boundary of the cytoplasm.

Cell wall

Words: 954 Articles: 9
Biological cell OurBigBook.com
A cell wall is a supporting structure outside a cell membrane. It helps preserve shape and bears the load when osmosis raises internal pressure. The cell membrane supplies the selective permeability described in its own article; the cell wall supplies mechanical reinforcement. These functions cooperate: a porous supporting layer can restrain expansion without being the boundary that retains dissolved solutes. Turgor pressure makes this cooperation visible in a firm leaf; plasmolysis and a lysozyme wall-removal experiment separate the two functions experimentally.[ref]
The material is not universal. Most bacteria use peptidoglycan, whose linked sugar chains and amino acid cross-links are explained below. A plant cell wall uses cellulose; a fungal cell wall contains chitin and glucans. Animals lack a cell wall, some bacteria are naturally wall-free, and archaea have different wall chemistry. Thus a cell wall is neither a universal cellular component nor one chemical recipe.[ref][ref][ref]
The bacterial outer membrane in typical Gram-negative bacteria is an additional membrane outside the peptidoglycan, not another name for that supporting mesh. The cell envelope includes the boundary layers together. An extra barrier can change access to the peptidoglycan, so response to lysozyme cannot be inferred from the mere presence of a cell wall.[ref]

A plant cell wall provides reinforcement outside the cell membrane, with cellulose as a major structural component. It is a composite rather than a solid sheet of pure cellulose. Wall construction varies with the kind and developmental state of the biological cell.

Turgor pressure (Pin​−Pout​)

Words: 108
Cell wall OurBigBook.com
Turgor pressure is the internal hydrostatic pressure above the external pressure in a biological cell. When water enters a walled biological cell by osmosis, expansion loads the cell wall. Rising pressure can oppose further net entry while the cell membrane retains its selective permeability. Mechanical support therefore does not require the cell wall to block water.
As an original mechanical check, idealize a small flat patch of cell wall of surface area A under uniform turgor pressure ΔP=Pin​−Pout​. Its outward force is F=ΔPA. Doubling A at fixed pressure doubles the load; equal internal and external pressures give zero net pressure load. This is a force balance, not a measured wall strength or a complete model of a curved, growing biological cell. It says nothing about which solutes cross the cell membrane.

Plasmolysis

Words: 145
Cell wall OurBigBook.com
Plasmolysis is withdrawal of the membrane-bounded contents from parts of a cell wall after water loss. A sufficiently concentrated external hypertonic solution, with solutes effectively excluded by the cell membrane over the observation time, can cause this. The cell wall remains; the enclosed material contracts. Plasmolysis is therefore distinct from osmotic lysis, which breaks the cellular boundary during excessive swelling. A return to a less concentrated surrounding chemical solution can reverse plasmolysis if the biological cell remains functional.[ref]

Protoplast

Words: 278 Articles: 1
Cell wall OurBigBook.com
A protoplast is the living contents of a biological cell bounded by its cell membrane after removal of the cell wall. Removing the cell wall need not immediately destroy the cell membrane; stability depends on the preparation and surroundings. Lysozyme acts on susceptible bacterial peptidoglycan, not on cellulose or chitin, so it is not a universal wall-removal enzyme.
Lysozyme wall-removal experiment
Words: 231
Protoplast OurBigBook.com
The 1953 paper The isolation of protoplasts from Bacillus megaterium by controlled treatment with lysozyme by Claes Weibull (pp. 688–690, Figures 2–3) tested Bacillus megaterium strain KM. Apparatus included a Klett-Summerson colorimeter with a red filter and a Spencer no. 8 phase-contrast microscope. Lysozyme in phosphate buffer produced empty residual bodies; adding 0.2M sucrose preserved granular spheres. Diluting their surroundings caused rapid osmotic lysis.
The same study compared untreated, boiled, lysozyme-exposed and sucrose-protected samples. Filled, stoppered tubes reduced damage from air exposure. After centrifugation, a Beckman DU spectrophotometer measured ultraviolet wave absorption of the separated liquid. Protected samples resembled untreated controls in releasing little ultraviolet-absorbing material; boiled and unprotected samples released much more. Later-growth cultures reduced spontaneous breakdown as a confounder.[ref]
Together, the shape and release readouts support removal of mechanical protection while a permeability barrier persists. They do not establish unchanged selective permeability to every solute, long-term viability, or universal susceptibility.
An instructive extension of this experimental logic is a matched comparison: lysozyme present or absent, crossed with osmotic support present or absent. Keep starting material, buffer, observation interval and handling comparable; include a blank to distinguish optical effects of reagents from changes in the biological cells. Then dilute already formed protoplasts as a separate intervention. This separates access and wall removal from failure after removal. These are proposed controls for interpreting the mechanism, not additional reported results from the historical paper. A fall in optical signal alone cannot establish rupture: shape changes also alter scattering of light.

Words: 40
Cell wall OurBigBook.com
Peptidoglycan is a mesh of linked sugar chains cross-linked by short chains of amino acids in the cell walls of most bacteria. Its absence from the cell walls of archaea helps distinguish envelope chemistry without confusing either cell wall with a cell membrane. See OpenStax Microbiology, 3.3: cell walls and peptidoglycan.

Cell membrane

Words: 2k Articles: 21
Biological cell OurBigBook.com
The cell membrane, also called the plasma membrane, is the selective boundary separating a biological cell's cytoplasm from its surroundings. Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes have a cell membrane. Where a cell wall is present, it is a distinct structure outside the cell membrane; the two names are not synonyms. This separation lets a biological cell maintain internal conditions while exchanging material through membrane transport. See NHGRI: cell membrane.
The familiar architecture is a lipid bilayer containing membrane proteins. In a phospholipid-based lipid bilayer, two membrane leaflets face opposite ways: hydrophilic heads face the water on each side, while hydrophobic tails face one another in the interior. The heads are therefore exposed both outside and inside the biological cell. This arrangement combines a water-facing surface with a barrier to many water-soluble solutes; the schematic represents organization rather than an atomistic structure. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: the lipid bilayer.
Selective permeability means that different substances cross at different rates under comparable conditions. Small nonpolar molecules can pass through a lipid bilayer by diffusion, while ions encounter a strong barrier without a suitable route. An ion channel supplies a selective water-filled pathway when open; a carrier protein binds a solute and changes shape to expose it to the other side. These membrane proteins therefore add specific routes to the barrier. An open ion channel permits passive transport, whereas a carrier protein can mediate either passive transport or active transport. See Alberts et al.: principles of membrane transport.
The useful combination is retention plus controlled exchange: a completely impermeable boundary would prevent uptake, whereas unrestricted mixing would erase differences in concentration and membrane potential. The fluid mosaic model connects these functions to an organized but mobile lipid bilayer containing proteins.

Selective permeability means that a cell membrane permits different substances to pass at different rates under comparable conditions. Both the lipid bilayer and the available membrane proteins contribute to this selection.

Ion channel

Words: 434 Articles: 1
Cell membrane OurBigBook.com
An ion channel is a membrane protein that provides a selective pathway for ions across a cell membrane. An open pore permits passive transport down the relevant electrochemical gradient; it does not supply the free energy for uphill transport as a pump involved in active transport does. Two things are needed for a net electric current: an available pathway and an electrochemical potential difference. Opening a pore alone need not produce a net electric current. See Ion Channels and the Electrical Properties of Membranes.
The selective permeability of an ion channel depends on interactions between its pore and the passing ions, not simply on a hole's diameter. Some ion channels strongly favor potassium over sodium; others admit several kinds of positively charged ions. Thus selective does not necessarily mean exclusive to one ion species. See Purves et al., Neuroscience, 2nd edition (2001): molecular structure of ion channels and the mixed-channel example in Purves et al.: principles derived from studies of the neuromuscular junction.
Gating is the opening and closing of an ion channel's pathway. A voltage-gated ion channel responds to membrane potential; an ionotropic receptor can respond to a bound ligand. Gating changes the available electrical conductance, while the electrochemical gradient supplies the drive for passive transport. For a fixed reversal potential in the simple model below, opening more identical ion channels increases the magnitude of the electric current at a fixed nonzero drive, without choosing its sign independently of membrane potential. The two-state ion-channel gating model describes how the open fraction can change. See the Alberts reference above.
For a worked approximation, hold an open population's electrical conductance at g=10nS and its reversal potential at Erev​=−80mV. Use V=Vinside​−Voutside​ for membrane potential and inward-positive conventional current:
Iin​=g(Erev​−V),g≥0.
(88)
At V=−100,−80,−60mV, respectively, the electric currents are +200,0,−200pA, since 1nS×1mV=1pA. Positive electric current means net positive electric charge entering, or net negative electric charge leaving; it does not mean that every ion moves inward. For a pore passing only positive ions, the three results mean net inward passage, no net passage, and net outward passage. These stipulated values describe an illustrative Ohmic approximation, not measured properties of a particular ion channel; see reversal potential for the current plot and limitations.
The useful connection is between a molecular gate and a controllable electric current. A ligand can change electrical conductance through an ionotropic receptor, or membrane potential can change it through a voltage-gated ion channel, connecting recognition and electrical signaling. In a historical landmark, Erwin Neher and Bert Sakmann reported currents from individual ion channels in frog muscle membranes in 1976. See Neher and Sakmann, Single-channel currents recorded from membrane of denervated frog muscle fibres, Nature 260, 799–802 (1976).

Membrane transport

Words: 905 Articles: 11
Cell membrane OurBigBook.com
Membrane transport is the passage of substances across a cell membrane. For the small solutes considered here, distinguish the available route from its driving force: a lipid bilayer, ion channel, or carrier protein determines how passage can occur, while differences in chemical potential and membrane potential determine which direction is energetically downhill. A large driving force cannot make an unavailable route conduct. See Alberts et al.: principles of membrane transport.
For an ideal dilute chemical solution at uniform temperature and pressure, with the same reference molar chemical potential on both sides, the molar electrochemical potential change for transferring a solute from compartment A to B is
Δμ​A→B​=RTln(cA​cB​​)+zF(VB​−VA​).
(89)
Here cA​,cB​ are concentrations, T is absolute temperature, R is the molar gas constant, z is signed ion charge number, F is the Faraday constant, and VB​−VA​ is the electric potential difference. The natural logarithm contains a dimensionless ratio. The electrical term vanishes for an uncharged solute. More generally, use thermodynamic activities in place of the ideal concentration ratio. This combines the ideal-solution chemical potential difference with electrical energy per mole; see IUPAC Gold Book: electrochemical potential. For a biological cell, taking B inside and A outside makes the voltage term use the existing membrane potential convention.
Passive transport
Words: 453 Articles: 7
Membrane transport OurBigBook.com
Passive transport is net movement down the transported substance's electrochemical gradient without coupling that movement to another source of free energy. Facilitated diffusion is passive transport through an ion channel or a passive carrier protein. Providing such a route can speed passage, but does not turn an uphill transfer into a downhill one. For an uncharged solute under the ideal conditions above, net passive transport runs from higher to lower concentration; for an ion, the membrane potential also matters. See Cooper, The Cell: transport of small molecules.
In the figure, stipulate eight neutral solute tracers in A and two in B, with equal fixed volumes, identical surroundings, and no imposed electric potential difference. The concentration ratio is cA​/cB​=8/2=4, so A-to-B transfer has Δμ​=−RTln4≃−1.38629RT, or −3.458kJmol−1 at the assumed temperature T=300K. If this solute can cross, thermodynamic equilibrium has equal expected concentrations: five tracers per side on average. Individual crossings occur in both directions; an observed ten-particle snapshot need not contain exactly five on each side. These stipulated counts illustrate a driving force, not a measured flow rate or a prediction of the time to equilibrate.
For a separate illustrative ion calculation, keep cA​/cB​=4, but assign z=+1 and VA​−VB​=−60mV at 300K. Using R≃8.31446Jmol−1K−1 and F≃96485.33Cmol−1, B-to-A transfer gives RTln4−0.060F≃3.458−5.789=−2.331kJmol−1. Thus an appropriate open ion channel can permit passive transport toward the higher concentration: the electrical contribution outweighs the opposing chemical potential contribution. This stipulated membrane potential is not inferred from the tracer counts.

Passive transport OurBigBook.com
Facilitated diffusion is passive transport through a membrane transport protein, such as an ion channel or carrier protein, down the relevant electrochemical gradient. The protein supplies a route; it does not by itself provide free energy for uphill transfer.

Osmosis is net movement of water across a boundary whose permeability differs for water and relevant solutes. The direction depends on the chemical potential of water, including both dissolved material and pressure. A cell wall can let water reach the cell membrane, yet oppose expansion through turgor pressure. Zero net movement does not mean individual water molecules have stopped crossing.

Osmosis OurBigBook.com
Tonicity describes how a surrounding chemical solution changes cellular volume through osmosis. It depends on which solutes remain effectively excluded on the timescale of interest, not simply on the amount of dissolved material. The following comparisons take a functional cell membrane, an initially unpressurized biological cell, and effectively excluded solutes as the reference; rising turgor pressure can oppose entry in a walled biological cell.
Hypotonic solution

A hypotonic solution favors initial net water entry under the reference conditions above. A susceptible biological cell may undergo osmotic lysis; a sufficiently strong cell wall can instead support turgor pressure.
Hypertonic solution

A hypertonic solution favors initial net water loss under the reference conditions above. In a walled plant cell, enough loss can produce plasmolysis.

An isotonic solution produces no sustained change in cellular volume under the stated comparison conditions. Water can still exchange in both directions.

Osmosis OurBigBook.com
Osmotic lysis is rupture after excessive water entry and swelling. It is an outcome for susceptible biological cells, not an inevitable response of every biological cell to a hypotonic solution. Cell walls can bear the resulting load, and cellular mechanisms can regulate water balance. A protoplast challenge tests a particular preparation under particular conditions.
Active transport
Words: 153
Membrane transport OurBigBook.com
Active transport moves a substance uphill in its electrochemical gradient by coupling the transfer to a downhill process. Some carrier proteins use ATP hydrolysis; others couple uphill transfer of one solute to downhill transfer of another solute, often an ion. The latter mechanism uses a stored electrochemical gradient and need not consume ATP directly at that carrier protein. Maintaining the driving electrochemical gradient still requires a source of energy. See Alberts et al.: carrier proteins and active membrane transport.
For the neutral 8:2 example, B-to-A transfer costs RTln4≃1.38629RT per mole. As an explicitly assumed bookkeeping example, suppose a tightly coupled cycle supplies a downhill free energy change of −2RT per mole of transferred solute. The total is then ΔGcycle​=RTln4−2RT≃−0.61371RT. This makes forward cycling energetically possible under those assumptions; it specifies neither a molecular mechanism nor a rate. Merely adding a carrier protein cannot supply the missing free energy. Conversely, as the transported concentration ratio rises, the required uphill cost rises, so a fixed driving process has a finite thermodynamic limit.
Exocytosis

Membrane transport OurBigBook.com
Exocytosis releases the contents of a membrane-bounded compartment to the extracellular space by fusion with the cell membrane. Synaptic vesicle fusion is an example. Its contents are released, while its membrane becomes connected to the cell membrane; see synaptic vesicle for recovery and reuse.
Endocytosis

Membrane transport OurBigBook.com
Endocytosis takes material into a biological cell by inward budding and separation of part of its cell membrane. At a chemical synapse, it helps recover membrane and proteins after synaptic vesicle exocytosis. This recovery is distinct from uptake of individual neurotransmitter molecules through membrane transport proteins.

Fluid mosaic model

Words: 86
Cell membrane OurBigBook.com
The fluid mosaic model describes a cell membrane as a fluid lipid bilayer with embedded membrane proteins. It connects a continuous barrier to a mosaic of functional components: diffusion within the membrane can coexist with selective passage across it. S. J. Singer and G. L. Nicolson presented the fluid mosaic model in Science in 1972; see Singer and Nicolson, The fluid mosaic model of the structure of cell membranes. The useful picture does not require every protein to move freely: attachments and interactions can restrict movement, as discussed in Cooper, The Cell: structure of the plasma membrane.

Cytoplasm

Words: 312 Articles: 1
Biological cell OurBigBook.com
The cytoplasm is the material inside a cell membrane but outside the cell nucleus, when one is present. It includes the cytosol, the organelles suspended in it, and other structures; it is not just a name for the liquid. In a prokaryote, which has no cell nucleus, the nucleoid and ribosomes are within the cytoplasm. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 4.3: cytoplasm and cytosol and Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 4.2: prokaryotic organization.
Try classifying four positions in the diagram. A point in the pale blue region belongs to both cytosol and cytoplasm. A point inside the mitochondrion belongs to an organelle included in the cytoplasm, but not to the surrounding cytosol. A point on a free ribosome belongs to the cytoplasm, but the ribosome itself is not cytosol. A point inside the cell nucleus belongs to neither cytoplasm nor cytosol. These distinctions prevent the misleading inference that everything outside the cell nucleus shares one undivided liquid environment.
The usefulness of the cytoplasm is this combination of shared surroundings and specialized structures: enzymes in the cytosol carry out many steps of metabolism, while organelles maintain their own internal conditions. A soluble protein made by a free ribosome may work in the cytosol or be transported elsewhere, including into the cell nucleus. Cellular organization therefore combines separation with exchange, rather than assigning each protein permanently to its place of synthesis. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell (2002): traffic between nucleus and cytosol.

Cytosol

Cytoplasm OurBigBook.com
The cytosol is the aqueous part of the cytoplasm surrounding its structures, including organelles. It contains water, ions and dissolved molecules, including many proteins; it is a crowded working environment rather than pure water. The liquid inside a cell nucleus or a membrane-bounded organelle is not the surrounding cytosol.

Nucleoid

Biological cell OurBigBook.com
A nucleoid is the region occupied by chromosome DNA in a prokaryotic biological cell. It has no surrounding nuclear envelope, but its DNA is organized rather than freely spread at random. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 4.2: the nucleoid.

Organelle

Biological cell OurBigBook.com
An organelle is a specialized subcellular structure. Usage varies over whether non-membrane-bounded structures such as ribosomes count as organelles, so explicitly say membrane-bounded organelles when comparing eukaryotic compartmentalization with prokaryotic organization. Mitochondria and chloroplasts are membrane-bounded examples. See OpenStax Microbiology, 3.4: cellular compartments.

A plastid is an organelle of the lineage that includes chloroplasts. A chloroplast is a photosynthetic plastid; the terms are not interchangeable because some plastids are nonphotosynthetic. Endosymbiotic theory connects plastid origins to cyanobacteria, while endosymbiotic gene transfer and organelle protein import explain genetic and functional integration with the host.

Organelle OurBigBook.com
A mitochondrion is an organelle whose inner membrane houses machinery for much of aerobic cellular respiration and ATP production in typical eukaryotic cells. Mitochondria descend from a bacterial endosymbiosis and retain a genome and ribosomes, although many required proteins are encoded by nuclear genes. This combination connects compartmentalized function to evolution. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 23.1: mitochondrial ancestry.

A chloroplast is a compartment in photosynthetic plant and algae biological cells. Its internal thylakoids carry out light-dependent reactions; its surrounding chloroplast stroma contains the enzymes of the Calvin cycle. Cyanobacteria perform oxygenic photosynthesis without chloroplasts. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: chloroplasts and photosynthesis.

Chloroplast stroma

Chloroplast OurBigBook.com
The chloroplast stroma is the fluid compartment inside the chloroplast envelope but outside its thylakoids. The Calvin cycle operates here; the interior of a thylakoid is a separate compartment.

Thylakoid

Chloroplast OurBigBook.com
A thylakoid is a flattened membrane-bounded compartment. In a chloroplast, its membrane contains the machinery for light-dependent reactions, including chlorophyll. Stacks of thylakoids pack membrane area into a small space within the chloroplast; the light-dependent reactions schematic simplifies this architecture.

Cell nucleus

Words: 411 Articles: 3
Biological cell OurBigBook.com
The cell nucleus is a membrane-bounded compartment characteristic of eukaryotic biological cells, containing most of the cellular DNA in a typical nucleated biological cell. Its double nuclear envelope separates this DNA from the surrounding cytoplasm. Most does not mean all: mitochondria and chloroplasts retain their own DNA. Nor does every specialized eukaryotic biological cell retain a cell nucleus: mature mammalian red blood cells have lost theirs. Prokaryotes organize their DNA in a nucleoid without a nuclear envelope, and still have ribosomes. See NHGRI: nucleus, [ref] and Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 40.2: mature mammalian red blood cells.
Follow one nuclear protein-coding gene: its DNA is used in transcription to make RNA; after the appropriate processing, messenger RNA is exported through a nuclear pore complex; a ribosome in the cytoplasm then uses it in biological translation to build an amino acid chain. The DNA remains in the cell nucleus. The RNA is a template, not the material converted into a protein. The ribosome diagram below follows this route; gene expression gives a complementary nucleotide sequence example. See Alberts et al.: selective RNA export and protein import.
This architecture makes gene expression interesting in a spatial way: nuclear transcription and cytoplasmic biological translation are separated by a selective boundary. A messenger RNA can be processed before export and use, while proteins needed for nuclear functions travel inward. Inside the cell nucleus, the cell nucleolus helps assemble ribosome subunits for export. Thus the compartment housing most DNA also helps build the machinery that interprets its messages elsewhere.
Robert Brown described and named the cell nucleus in his account of plant biological cells, read to the Linnean Society in 1831 and published in its Transactions in 1833. This historical observation identified a recurring structure, without establishing its later-understood role in DNA storage or gene expression. See Brown, On the Organs and Mode of Fecundation in Orchideæ and Asclepiadeæ, Transactions 16, 685–738 (1833). This is a documented contribution rather than a claim that no one had observed the structure earlier.

Cell nucleus OurBigBook.com
The nuclear envelope is the double-membrane boundary around a cell nucleus. Regulated passage connects nuclear processes to the surrounding cytoplasm: transcription produces RNA in the cell nucleus, while exported messenger RNA can undergo biological translation on ribosomes outside it. See NHGRI: nuclear membrane.
Nuclear pore complex

Nuclear envelope OurBigBook.com
A nuclear pore complex is an assembly of proteins spanning the nuclear envelope and regulating passage between the cell nucleus and cytosol. It is a selective gateway, not simply an unregulated hole: messenger RNA export and import of nuclear proteins require appropriate transport machinery. See Alberts et al.: nuclear pore complexes.

Nucleolus (biology)

Cell nucleus OurBigBook.com
The cell nucleolus is a region inside a cell nucleus without a surrounding membrane, where much ribosomal RNA is made and processed and ribosome subunits begin to assemble with proteins. The subunits are exported to the cytoplasm; the cell nucleolus is not itself a translating ribosome. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 4.3: nucleolus and ribosomal subunits.

Ribosome

Words: 483
Biological cell OurBigBook.com
A ribosome is the molecular machinery for biological translation: it reads messenger RNA and joins amino acids into a polypeptide that can become a protein. Both prokaryotes and eukaryotes have ribosomes. A ribosome consists of ribosomal RNA and proteins organized into small and large subunits, with no enclosing membrane. Ribosomal RNA contributes to both structure and the active site that forms peptide bonds; a ribosome is therefore not merely a collection of proteins. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 4.3: ribosome composition and Nissen et al., The structural basis of ribosome activity in peptide bond synthesis, Science 289, 920–930 (2000).
For a computed decoding example, choose the reading frame starting at the first displayed nucleotide of 5′-AUG GCU GAA-3′. Under the standard genetic code, AUG specifies methionine (Met), GCU specifies alanine (Ala), and GAA specifies a glutamic acid residue (Glu) in the growing polypeptide. Nine nucleotides divide into three codons, giving the ordered three-amino acid residue segment Met–Ala–Glu. The ribosome reads the messenger RNA 5′→3′, and the chain grows from its N-terminus toward its C-terminus. If synthesis begins at this AUG in an appropriate eukaryotic initiation context, these are the first three amino acid residues before any subsequent processing. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 15.1: standard codon assignments.
For this three-amino acid residue segment, joining the three delivered amino acids requires two peptide bonds, one between Met and Ala and another between Ala and Glu. There is no stop codon in the displayed nucleotide sequence, so this is a growing segment rather than a complete released protein. An isolated nine-nucleotide RNA is not claimed to supply all signals needed for initiation. This small calculation separates three jobs: the messenger RNA specifies order, transfer RNA delivers the amino acids, and the ribosome catalyzes their joining. Each new amino acid residue is added at the C-terminus. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e, 15.5: initiation and chain elongation.
The beauty of a ribosome is its reusable chemistry: the same machinery can assemble many different proteins by following different messenger RNA templates. The genetic code connects an alphabet of nucleotides to an alphabet of amino acids, while transfer RNA links recognition of the message to delivery of building material. Changing the message can therefore change the product without building a different ribosome for every protein.
In 1955 George E. Palade described small particles in the cytoplasm, both free and associated with membranes, in A small particulate component of the cytoplasm, Journal of Biophysical and Biochemical Cytology 1, 59–68. The paper documents the structural observations, rather than the full modern decoding mechanism. Complementary biochemical work by Hoagland, Stephenson, Scott, Hecht and Zamecnik described a soluble RNA intermediate in protein synthesis in 1958, helping establish the role now assigned to transfer RNA; see A soluble ribonucleic acid intermediate in protein synthesis, Journal of Biological Chemistry 231, 241–257. Together, structural observations and biochemical experiments connected visible cellular machinery with its working parts.

Membrane potential OurBigBook.com
A reversal potential Erev​ is a membrane potential at which a specified open ion channel, or specified combination of ion channels, carries zero net electric current, with the surrounding conditions fixed; the electric current changes sign across that voltage. Specifying which current matters: an individual ion contribution and a sum of several contributions can reverse at different voltages. Zero net electric current does not mean that all ions have stopped moving. See Purves et al., Neuroscience, 2nd edition (2001): reversal of a mixed-ion channel current.
Throughout these examples, membrane potential is V=Vinside​−Voutside​, and conventional current is inward-positive. Positive electric current corresponds to net positive electric charge entering or net negative electric charge leaving. Negative electric current corresponds to the reverse charge transfer. A convenient Ohmic approximation is
Iin​=g(Erev​−V),g≥0,
(90)
where g is the available electrical conductance. For fixed g>0, V<Erev​ gives positive electric current, V=Erev​ gives zero, and V>Erev​ gives negative electric current; the line has slope −g. If g=0, the modeled pathway carries zero electric current at every voltage: closing it does not locate its reversal potential. 3.1 Synapses (§3.1: conductance-based synaptic current) uses outward-positive g(V−E); the formula here reverses that sign to match this wiki's inward-positive convention.
For the stipulated single-pathway example from ion channel, Erev​=−80mV and g=10nS give
V (mV)Erev​−V (mV)Iin​ (pA)​−10020200​−8000​−60−20−200​
(91)
The open ion channel carries zero net electric current at −80mV even though g remains positive. Near that point a change of membrane potential changes the electric current, which is why zero current at one voltage does not make an open pathway electrically irrelevant; see shunting inhibition.
For an ion channel passing only one ion species by passive transport, its reversal potential can equal that species' Nernst equilibrium potential, where the chemical and electrical contributions to electrochemical potential balance. At that thermodynamic equilibrium, passage in both directions can continue with no net transport. For an ion channel admitting several ion species, opposing contributions can cancel while each species continues to have net transport. Such a reversal potential is not generally any one species' Nernst equilibrium potential. See the Purves reference above.
To work out that cancellation explicitly, put two Ohmic ion channel populations across the same cell membrane. Stipulate constant electrical conductances and fixed reversal potentials:
gK​=10nS,EK​=−80mV,gNa​=2nS,ENa​=+50mV.
(92)
The potassium and sodium contributions add because both pathways experience the same membrane potential:
Itotal​Eeff​​=gK​(EK​−V)+gNa​(ENa​−V)=(gK​+gNa​)(Eeff​−V),=gK​+gNa​gK​EK​+gNa​ENa​​=12−700​mV≈−58.3333mV.​
(93)
Thus Itotal​=12nS(Eeff​−V). This weighted mean follows simply by expanding and regrouping the two current terms; it assumes additive Ohmic contributions and a positive total electrical conductance. At V=Eeff​, the inward-positive individual electric currents are
IK​=−3650​pA≈−216.6667pA,INa​=+3650​pA≈+216.6667pA.
(94)
The potassium contribution is outward and the sodium contribution inward. Equal and opposite electric currents give Itotal​=0; neither pathway has stopped transporting its ions. The calculation treats two distinct pathways. Applying it to one mixed-species ion channel would additionally require a justified decomposition into independent Ohmic contributions; a general mixed-channel reversal potential cannot be obtained by assuming those hypotheses silently.
This is an instantaneous balance of the specified passive electric currents. It would be the stationary voltage of a passive capacitance model containing only these constant pathways and no applied electric current, but it is not a complete prediction of a living cell's resting membrane potential. Other electric currents, voltage-dependent gating, and pumps involved in active transport can matter. Pumps that transfer net electric charge are electrogenic and contribute their own electric current. See Purves et al.: functional properties of the sodium/potassium pump.
The toy model holds ion concentrations and therefore the stipulated reversal potentials fixed. Continuing inward sodium and outward potassium transport would change finite reservoirs unless active transport or external control maintained them. Transport can be a small fraction of the reservoir's ions over a short interval, making fixed concentrations a useful approximation; it is not a claim that the reservoirs never change. See Gerstner et al., Neuronal Dynamics (2014), §2.1: equilibrium potentials, channel currents and maintained gradients.
A reversal potential makes the effect of opening an ion channel predictable from the present membrane potential. The same open pathway can carry inward or outward electric current as V crosses its reversal potential. The two-pathway example reveals a particularly useful distinction: zero net charge transfer can coexist with continuing exchange of different substances. That distinction connects membrane transport to electric current measurements without mistaking electrical balance for thermodynamic equilibrium.
Nernst equilibrium potential (Eion​=zFRT​ln(ainside​aoutside​​))
Words: 117
Reversal potential OurBigBook.com
The Nernst equilibrium potential is the inside-minus-outside membrane potential at which one ion species has equal electrochemical potential on both sides of a cell membrane. At uniform temperature T, using the same reference chemical potential on both sides, z=0 is the signed ion charge number, R the molar gas constant, F the Faraday constant, and a the dimensionless thermodynamic activity of that ion. For an ideal dilute chemical solution, the activity ratio becomes the concentration ratio. See Purves et al.: the forces that create membrane potentials and the Nernst equation.
The short derivation is to set the outside-to-inside electrochemical potential change from membrane transport to zero: RTln(ainside​/aoutside​)+zFV=0, and solve for V. An open pathway carrying only this species by passive transport then has this reversal potential. A balance of several nonzero ion electric currents does not establish this equilibrium condition for each species.

A membrane channel whose opening depends on membrane potential. Regenerative activation and subsequent inactivation or opposing currents help produce an action potential.
Two-state ion-channel gating (X˙=αX​(V)(1−X)−βX​(V)X)
Words: 831 Articles: 1
Voltage-gated ion channel OurBigBook.com
Two-state ion-channel gating models an individual gate as a random switch between closed and open states. Write p(t) for its open probability; this is the X in the header equation. An individual gate's state is always closed or open, rather than partly open. A population of identical gates can have a fraction open near p(t), and averaging repeated identically prepared trials estimates the same probability. A finite population's observed fraction fluctuates. See Purves and colleagues, Neuroscience, 2nd edition (2001): Ion Channels Underlying Action Potentials for single-channel steps and their population averages.
At fixed membrane potential V, let constant rates α,β>0 govern closed-to-open and open-to-closed transitions respectively, in s−1. This is a two-state continuous-time Markov chain. Over a short interval Δt, an initially closed gate opens with probability αΔt+o(Δt), and an initially open gate closes with probability βΔt+o(Δt). Gain minus loss gives the deterministic ordinary differential equation for the probability:
dtdp​=α(1−p)−βp=τp∞​−p​,p∞​=α+βα​,τ=α+β1​.
(95)
Here p∞​ is the fixed-voltage limiting open probability, and τ is a time constant. The ratio of the rates fixes the limit, while their sum fixes the speed. With initial probability p(0)=p0​∈[0,1],
p(t)=p∞​+(p0​−p∞​)e−t/τ.
(96)
For a short derivation, subtract p∞​: the deviation obeys d(p−p∞​)/dt=−(p−p∞​)/τ, yielding the exponential function. After one time constant, 1/e of the initial deviation remains. The solution stays between p0​ and p∞​, so it remains a valid probability. The rate and time constant formulations are described in Gerstner and colleagues, Neuronal Dynamics, §2.2.2: transition rates and channel kinetics.
For a worked toy condition A, choose α=β=50s−1 and p0​=0.1. Then p∞​=0.5, τ=0.01s=10ms, and
p(10ms)=0.5−0.4e−1≈0.352848.
(97)
In a separately prepared condition B, choose α=200s−1, β=50s−1 and the same p0​=0.1. Now p∞​=0.8, τ=4ms, and p(10ms)=0.8−0.7e−2.5≈0.742540. Condition B approaches a higher limit more quickly. These are two stipulated constant-rate conditions with V held fixed in each experiment, not an empirical function relating rates to voltage or a sequential switch between conditions. The initial p0​=0.1 need not be the limiting probability at the newly imposed voltage.
In the Hodgkin-Huxley model, the rates depend on membrane potential: αX​(V) and βX​(V). Its X∞​(V)=αX​(V)/(αX​(V)+βX​(V)) is the limit for voltage held at that V. During an action potential, changing V changes the rates and gates feed back onto V through ionic electric currents; substituting the present voltage into the constant-rate solution does not solve that coupled system. Gating describes availability of a conducting pathway. Even an open ion channel carries zero net ionic electric current at its reversal potential.
The useful bridge is from abrupt random molecular events to a smooth population prediction. A channel requiring several independent permissive gates in an ion channel has an open probability equal to their product; this can make channel availability much smaller than each gate's availability. The Hodgkin-Huxley model uses gˉ​Na​m3h and gˉ​K​n4 for sodium and potassium electrical conductances, respectively.
Independent permissive gates in an ion channel (Popen​=pq)
Words: 322
Two-state ion-channel gating OurBigBook.com
A permissive gate allows conduction when it is open. Suppose an ion channel conducts only when all q gates are open, where q is a positive integer. If the gate-open events are mutually independent events and each has the same open probability p at the time considered, then
Popen​=∏j=1q​p=pq.
(98)
This follows from the multiplication rule for independent events. Identical transition rates alone do not guarantee independence: the initial gate states must also be independently prepared, and the model must not couple their transitions. Gates sharing a fluctuating membrane potential can be correlated; the simple product requires an appropriate independence assumption, for example independent gates at an externally fixed voltage.
At p=0.5, channels requiring q=1,2,4 permissive gates have open probabilities 0.5, 0.25 and 0.0625. For four independent gates there are 24=16 possible open/closed configurations, equally probable at p=0.5; only the all-open configuration conducts. Thus 0.5 is the gate-open probability, while 0.0625 is the whole-channel open probability. Neither is a fractional state of one observed channel. Among 160 independently prepared identical four-gate channels, the expected value of the open count is 160/16=10, although an actual count fluctuates.
For unequal independent gate-open probabilities pj​, use Popen​=∏j​pj​ rather than pq. This is the distinction behind the Hodgkin-Huxley model's m3h: m and h are different activation and inactivation-availability variables, rather than one common p. Its n4 uses four identical activation factors. Independence and the all-open requirement are model assumptions; correlated gates or alternative conducting configurations require a different calculation. The simple product is useful because a modest gate-open probability can produce sharply suppressed whole-channel availability without any additional gate interaction.

Metabolism

Words: 961 Articles: 18
Biology OurBigBook.com
The network of chemical reactions that maintains a living system, supplies energy and builds or processes its material. Gas emissions can arise as primary metabolic byproducts or secondary metabolic byproducts, with different implications for an atmospheric biosignature gas.
Enzymes make this network operate on biologically useful timescales. Following material through successive substrates and reaction products explains why a single fast enzyme need not make the entire network fast: another step may constrain the flow. Changing enzyme amounts or activity therefore changes which routes can carry material, connecting molecular chemical kinetics to the maintenance and growth of a biological cell. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell: multienzyme complexes and cell metabolism.

Photosynthesis

Words: 453 Articles: 4
Metabolism OurBigBook.com
Photosynthesis captures light energy and transforms it into chemical forms that a biological cell can use. In plants, algae and cyanobacteria, this supports carbon fixation: incorporation of carbon from carbon dioxide into chemical compounds used to build living material. Capturing light and incorporating carbon are distinct processes coupled through metabolism. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 8.1: overview of photosynthesis.
For oxygenic photosynthesis, a simplified net equation writes a six-carbon sugar, glucose, as the representative product:
6CO2​+6H2​O+light⟶C6​H12​O6​+6O2​.
(99)
This is net stoichiometry, not a one-step mechanism. A worked bookkeeping check counts six carbon chemical atoms, twelve hydrogen chemical atoms, and eighteen oxygen chemical atoms on each side: the product side has six oxygen chemical atoms in the sugar and twelve in molecular oxygen. The light label supplies energy, not additional chemical atoms.
Crucially, the released molecular oxygen comes from water, not carbon dioxide. Cancelling water made and consumed in different steps hides this distinction in the net equation. The Calvin cycle supplies a net three-carbon triose phosphate, such as glyceraldehyde 3-phosphate, for subsequent sugar synthesis; it does not directly export glucose. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 8.2: light-dependent reactions and OpenStax Biology 2e, 8.3: using light energy to make organic molecules.
The useful achievement is connecting incoming light to both usable energy and new biological material. ATP is an immediate energy currency; NADPH supplies Electrons for synthesis; carbon dioxide supplies the carbon incorporated into carbohydrates. These roles are complementary. Conservation of energy still holds: photosynthesis transforms energy, never creates it, and some absorbed energy is dissipated as heat. A plant also carries out cellular respiration, including in biological cells that perform photosynthesis. Gas exchange reflects both processes. Oxygenic photosynthesis remains central to interpreting terrestrial molecular oxygen as an atmospheric biosignature gas. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 8.3: photosynthesis and respiration.

Photosynthesis OurBigBook.com
Oxygenic photosynthesis uses water as an Electron source and releases molecular oxygen. Plants, algae and cyanobacteria provide examples. The defining distinction from anoxygenic photosynthesis is molecular oxygen release, not merely capture of light.

Photosynthesis OurBigBook.com
Anoxygenic photosynthesis captures light without producing molecular oxygen. It occurs in some bacteria and uses Electron sources other than water. Whether carbon fixation accompanies this light capture depends on the organism and conditions; photosynthesis does not imply one universal carbon-assimilation pathway. See Alberts et al.: chloroplasts and photosynthetic bacteria.

Photosynthesis OurBigBook.com
In a chloroplast, light-dependent reactions take place at thylakoid membranes. Chlorophyll captures light; Electron transfer helps establish an electrochemical gradient across the thylakoid membrane, enabling formation of ATP. The oxygenic photosynthesis pathway also forms NADPH and releases molecular oxygen from water. ATP and NADPH become available in the chloroplast stroma for the Calvin cycle. See Alberts et al.: chloroplast light reactions.

Light-dependent reactions OurBigBook.com
Chlorophyll is a family of molecules that absorb light for photosynthesis. In chloroplasts, chlorophyll works with proteins in thylakoid membranes; absorbing light initiates energy capture rather than directly constructing a sugar. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 8.2: photosynthetic pigments.

Carbon fixation

Words: 138 Articles: 1
Metabolism OurBigBook.com
Carbon fixation incorporates carbon from carbon dioxide into organic chemical compounds. It identifies a material transformation, rather than a particular source of energy: carbon fixation can be supported by photosynthesis or by other metabolism. The Calvin cycle is one pathway, not the definition of all carbon fixation.

Calvin cycle

Words: 103
Carbon fixation OurBigBook.com
The Calvin cycle couples carbon fixation to use of ATP and NADPH. In a chloroplast it takes place in the chloroplast stroma. Its chemical reactions incorporate carbon dioxide, use NADPH-supplied Electrons, and regenerate the molecules that accept further carbon dioxide.
In the standard Calvin cycle bookkeeping, three carbon dioxide molecules require nine ATP and six NADPH for one net three-carbon triose phosphate. A six-carbon sugar equivalent therefore corresponds to six carbon dioxide, eighteen ATP and twelve NADPH; subsequent sugar synthesis is separate. These are pathway requirements, not a universal measured photosynthesis yield. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 8.3: Calvin cycle bookkeeping.
Calling the Calvin cycle light-independent means its individual chemical reactions do not directly capture light; it does not mean the Calvin cycle runs only at night or independently of the supplies from light-dependent reactions.

Cellular respiration

Words: 31
Metabolism OurBigBook.com
Cellular respiration transfers energy from chemical fuels into usable forms including ATP. Plants carry out cellular respiration as well as photosynthesis; in its aerobic form, cellular respiration consumes molecular oxygen and releases carbon dioxide. See OpenStax Biology 2e, 8.3: energy flow.

Metabolism OurBigBook.com
A compound released through specialized functions such as signaling, defense or stress adaptation rather than the core reactions needed for energy and biomass. Dimethyl sulfide and chloromethane are examples discussed as atmospheric biosignatures. Their specialized origins may improve specificity while lowering the global emission flux.

Primary metabolic byproduct

Words: 38
Metabolism OurBigBook.com
A product released by reactions needed for energy acquisition, growth or biomass construction. Methane from energy-yielding microbial reactions and molecular oxygen from oxygenic photosynthesis are examples. Abiotic chemistry can make some of the same molecules, so production mechanism and environmental abundance matter.

Evolution

Words: 1k Articles: 16
Biology OurBigBook.com
Evolution is descent with inherited modification. Within a population, changes in allele frequencies provide a precise genetic description; over longer histories, branching descent connects populations through common descent. An individual growing larger is biological development, whereas an inherited variant becoming more frequent across generations is evolution. See UC Museum of Paleontology: the definition of evolution.
Mutation supplies new alleles, genetic recombination reshuffles inherited material, natural selection favors variants with greater reproductive contribution in a specified environment, and genetic drift changes frequencies through chance. Gene flow moves variants between populations. Consequently, an increasing allele frequency alone does not identify natural selection. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e: population genetics.
Evidence includes ordered fossils, shared inherited structures and similarities in DNA; phylogenetics uses such observations to infer relationships. A phylogenetic tree is an inferred historical account, with uncertainty about particular branches. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e: evidence of evolution. Evidence also comes from experiments: Blount, Borland and Lenski reported an Escherichia coli lineage able to use citrate with oxygen present by 31,500 generations, and tested historical dependence by replaying evolution from stored ancestors. See Blount, Borland and Lenski, 2008: original experimental report. Such observations constrain explanations; no single frequency equation captures every evolutionary process.

Speciation

Words: 529 Articles: 5
Evolution OurBigBook.com
Speciation is the formation of distinct species through evolution. Detecting a difference between biological populations is a starting observation; its interpretation depends on the stated species concept and the evidence for lasting separation. Reproductive isolation is one important route to limiting gene flow in sexual reproduction.

Reproductive isolation

Words: 494 Articles: 4
Speciation OurBigBook.com
Reproductive isolation consists of barriers that reduce gene flow through sexual reproduction. Distinguish premating isolation from barriers after mating. Barriers before fertilization also include incompatible gametes; barriers after fertilization can reduce offspring survival or fertility. [ref]
An assay should state which step it measures. Observing fewer cross-group matings does not measure offspring fertility; observing fertilization does not demonstrate that the offspring will reproduce. These distinctions make a partial barrier informative without declaring completed speciation.

Premating isolation reduces mating between biological populations. The dietary divergence and mating isolation in Drosophila pseudoobscura assay measures this stage using observed pairings.

Reproductive isolation OurBigBook.com
Postmating reproductive isolation acts after mating. Specify whether the test concerns fertilization, offspring survival, or the offspring's own reproduction; those outcomes are not interchangeable.
Dietary divergence and mating isolation in Drosophila pseudoobscura
Words: 241
Reproductive isolation OurBigBook.com
The 1989 experiment used eight Drosophila pseudoobscura biological populations from one Bryce Canyon population: four maintained on starch medium, four on maltose, in cages at 25∘C. Testing began about a year after establishment. [ref]
Before testing, flies spent one generation on cornmeal–molasses–agar. Virgins aged 3–6 days entered multiple-choice chambers: twelve females from each population, followed by males from both populations introduced nearly simultaneously without anesthesia. Observers scored matings for 60–90 minutes under bright indirect lighting. One group's right wing tips were clipped for identification, with clipping reversed between replicates. [ref]
All sixteen cross-diet comparisons had positive mating assortment contrasts; eleven departed significantly from random mating. Same-diet comparisons did not show significant departures. Common-medium rearing addressed immediate diet conditioning; same-diet controls addressed separation and establishment population bottlenecks. Mate choice was not the selection target; the biological populations were maintained separately. The result supports partial premating isolation accompanying dietary divergence, not completed speciation. [ref]
The causal inference remains limited. A negative same-diet hypothesis test does not prove zero reproductive isolation. One generation under common conditions does not exclude every persistent environmental influence. The chamber readout alone cannot identify a particular gene, establish offspring fertility, or predict gene flow after sustained contact in nature. Further experiments would need to target those questions separately.
Mating assortment contrast (I=(Nsame​−Ncross​)/N)
Words: 147
Reproductive isolation OurBigBook.com
For observed pairings between two labels A,B, let Nsame​=NAA​+NBB​ and Ncross​=NAB​+NBA​, where the first label denotes the female's group and the second the male's. A mating assortment contrast is
I=NNsame​−Ncross​​,N=Nsame​+Ncross​>0.
(100)
It lies between −1 and 1. Positive I describes an excess of same-label pairings over cross-label pairings; whether that is evidence of assortative mating depends on the null mathematical model and the assay. The four counts form a contingency table.
Here is an original scope check. Suppose independently paired females and males have probabilities pf​,pm​ of carrying label A. Then
qsame​=pf​pm​+(1−pf​)(1−pm​),E[I]=2qsame​−1.
(101)
With pf​=pm​=1/2, the expected value is zero. With pf​=pm​=4/5, it is 9/25=0.36, despite pairing being independent of label. This counterexample concerns unequal pool composition; it does not replace the group introductions and contingency table tests in the dietary divergence and mating isolation in Drosophila pseudoobscura experiment. Even with balanced pools, finite observed samples fluctuate: a positive I alone is not a hypothesis test, much less a universal species boundary.

Natural selection

Words: 429 Articles: 2
Evolution OurBigBook.com
Natural selection involves systematic differences in expected reproductive success associated with variation in phenotype. For a continuing evolutionary response, the relevant variation must be inherited: offspring must tend to preserve the differences being favored. Actual offspring counts also fluctuate by chance, producing genetic drift. Survival matters insofar as it affects contribution to future generations. Genotype fitness is therefore contextual, depending on environment and the life cycle being counted, rather than simply measuring strength or longevity. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e: population evolution.
In chapter IV of his 1859 book, Darwin explained natural selection through preservation of favorable variations and greater chances of survival and reproduction. See Darwin, On the Origin of Species, first edition, chapter IV. The beautiful consequence is cumulative change without foresight: inherited differences are filtered repeatedly by present conditions. Natural selection neither generates a needed mutation on demand nor guarantees progress toward a predetermined goal.

Haploid selection recurrence (p′=wp+(1−p)wp​)

Words: 289
Natural selection OurBigBook.com
Consider an explicitly idealized haploid population with two inherited types A,B, one allele per individual at the tracked genetic locus, and discrete, nonoverlapping generations. Assume faithful type transmission, no mutation or gene flow, a constant environment, and reproductive contributions independent of type frequency. Let the expected values of offspring surviving to the next census be mA​,mB​>0, with relative genotype fitness w=mA​/mB​.
For A frequency p, expected offspring contributions are proportional to pmA​ and (1−p)mB​. Normalizing gives the deterministic large-population mathematical model
p′=pmA​+(1−p)mB​pmA​​=wp+(1−p)wp​.
(102)
The denominator is mean relative genotype fitness. For w=1.2 and p0​=0.2, p1​=0.24/1.04=3/13≈0.23077. Equivalently, 200 A and 800 B parents with mA​=1.2,mB​=1 contribute expected counts 240 and 800. Fractional per-parent expected values are averages, not literal fractional offspring. The ratio of these expectations is a deterministic approximation, not generally the expectation of a random ratio.
The odds multiply particularly simply:
1−pt+1​pt+1​​=w1−pt​pt​​,pt​=1−p0​+wtp0​wtp0​​.
(103)
Thus p10​≈0.60753: repeated modest advantage can substantially change composition. For w>1 and 0<p<1, p′−p=(w−1)p(1−p)/(1+(w−1)p)>0. The deterministic boundary p=0 remains unchanged: natural selection needs existing variation.
A distinct stochastic extension fixes N offspring and samples their types independently using a binomial distribution: K∼Binomial(N,q), where q=wp/(wp+1−p), then p′=K/N. Its conditional expected value is q and conditional variance is q(1−q)/N. With w=1, the conditional expected value remains p, yet realized frequencies wander through genetic drift. With w>1, genetic drift can still lower p or lose A entirely. Over several generations, the deterministic curve need not equal the mean stochastic trajectory, because the recurrence is nonlinear.

A phylogenetic tree describes ancestral relationships. In a probabilistic graphical model on a rooted tree, latent variables at ancestral vertices are inferred from observations at leaves using belief propagation.
Felsenstein pruning algorithm
Words: 47
Phylogenetic tree OurBigBook.com
The Felsenstein pruning algorithm computes a site likelihood function by sum-product belief propagation from leaves to root. For a finite-state Markov kernel K, the subtree likelihood function obeys Lv​(a)=∏w child of v​∑b​K(a,b)Lw​(b), with observed-state indicators at leaves. Summing against the root probability distribution gives the site likelihood function. An outward pass gives edge posterior probabilities and expected transition counts for the expectation-maximization algorithm.

Genetics

Words: 11k Articles: 170
Biology OurBigBook.com
Genetics studies how genes are inherited, how their alleles vary, and how that variation contributes to phenotypes. Its central distinction is between an inherited description, the genotype, and what an organism actually expresses, the phenotype. Following alleles through a pedigree answers a family-level question; following allele frequencies through generations leads to population genetics and evolution.
The beauty of Mendelian segregation is that discrete inherited copies can generate predictable statistical patterns without making every offspring identical. A single genetic locus already connects meiosis, probability and observable variation. The Hardy-Weinberg principle then supplies a population baseline: it separates reshuffling inherited copies from processes such as natural selection that change their frequencies. These simple models are useful precisely because their assumptions can be stated and checked.

DNA replication

Words: 521 Articles: 4
Molecular genetics OurBigBook.com
DNA replication copies a double-stranded DNA molecule into two daughter double-stranded DNA molecules. In semiconservative replication, each daughter retains one parental strand and receives one newly synthesized complementary strand. DNA polymerases build the new strands from incoming nucleotides; they do not make RNA or proteins in this copying step. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 4th edition (2002): DNA replication mechanisms.
For a five-base pair example, separate 5′-ATGCC-3′ from its partner 3′-TACGG-5′. Base pairing specifies a new TACGG partner for the old ATGCC strand and a new ATGCC partner for the old TACGG strand. With error-free copying, both daughter DNA molecules have the original nucleotide sequence, but different physical strand histories. One initial duplex contains ten nucleotides; one complete round produces two duplexes containing twenty nucleotides, ten retained and ten newly incorporated.
This is useful for inheritance: both daughter biological cells can receive a copy of the DNA record. The elegant feature is that base pairing lets each strand specify its missing partner. Direction matters too: a replicating DNA polymerase reads its template 3′→5′ and extends the new strand at its 3′ end, so synthesis proceeds 5′→3′. These are opposite directions on antiparallel nucleic acid strands, not two alternative directions of synthesis. The enzyme needs a pre-existing paired strand end to extend; the diagram omits the machinery that starts and coordinates copying. See Alberts et al.: template-directed synthesis and the requirement for a primer.
The strand accounting predicts observable differences between copying mechanisms. In 1958, Meselson and Stahl grew Escherichia coli with the heavier nitrogen isotope 15N, then supplied 14N and measured extracted DNA by density-gradient centrifugation. After one generation their samples contained intermediate-density DNA; after two, intermediate-density and light DNA occurred in equal amounts. This supported semiconservative replication in the tested Escherichia coli culture. It was an isotope assay of sampled DNA, not simultaneous testing of every kind of DNA or direct colored-strand photography. See The replication of DNA in Escherichia coli by Matthew Meselson and Franklin W. Stahl.
Semiconservative replication
Words: 84
DNA replication OurBigBook.com
In semiconservative replication, each daughter duplex retains one strand of its immediate parent. Under complete copying without strand loss or exchange, one starting duplex gives 2n duplexes after n rounds, but still only two original strands. For n≥1, the fraction of duplexes containing an original strand is 2/2n=21−n: all after one round, half after two, a quarter after three. The fraction of all strands that are original is instead 2−n. A strand made in round 1 is parental when round 2 begins.

Gene expression

Words: 1k Articles: 11
Molecular genetics OurBigBook.com
Gene expression uses a gene's information to produce functional RNA or a protein. Transcription makes RNA from a DNA template; for a protein-coding gene, biological translation then uses messenger RNA to specify an amino acid chain. Many genes instead produce functional RNA, including transfer RNA and ribosomal RNA, without a translated protein product. See Alberts et al., Molecular Biology of the Cell, 4th edition (2002): from DNA to RNA.
Follow the chosen coding strand 5′-ATGGCTTAA-3′: transcription of its complementary template gives 5′-AUGGCUUAA-3′ in messenger RNA. In the stated reading frame, its three codons are AUG, GCU and UAA: methionine, alanine and a stop codon. Thus nine nucleotides specify two amino acid residues followed by termination, not three residues. This is an illustrative coding segment embedded in suitable expression and initiation context, not a claim that an isolated nine-nucleotide RNA is sufficient to initiate biological translation.
The distinction between copying and use explains how biological cells can preserve the same DNA yet produce different products. DNA replication duplicates the record; gene expression selects and uses parts of it. Transcription does not use all DNA at once, and gene expression can be controlled at several steps, including transcription, RNA processing and biological translation. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e: regulation of gene expression. The arrows describe template-directed synthesis: the DNA does not physically turn into a protein, and the messenger RNA does not supply the amino acids from which that protein is assembled.

Transcription (biology)
Words: 304 Articles: 2
Gene expression OurBigBook.com
Transcription is synthesis of RNA using one DNA strand as a template by an RNA polymerase. During elongation the RNA polymerase reads that template 3′→5′ while extending RNA 5′→3′. Only the selected region is transcribed; other regions need not be active, and the template strand can differ between genes. See Alberts et al.: RNA polymerase and selection of transcribed DNA regions.
For the displayed example, align these three nucleotide sequences in the same left-to-right positions:
coding DNA:template DNA:RNA product:​5′-ATGGCTTAA-3′,3′-TACCGAATT-5′,5′-AUGGCUUAA-3′.​
(104)
The first template triplet TAC selects AUG: T pairs with A, A with U, and C with G. The next CGA selects GCU, and ATT selects UAA. The coding strand therefore matches the RNA lettering except for T versus U, whereas the template is complementary. Reading that template in its own 5′→3′ direction gives 5′-TTAAGCCAT-3′; orientation cannot be discarded. The gene expression diagram keeps all three rows aligned. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e: template and coding strands in transcription.
This correspondence makes nucleotide sequences interpretable, but replacing T by U is valid only after identifying the coding strand. Moreover, RNA may be processed after transcription, so the initial product and mature messenger RNA need not have identical uninterrupted nucleotide sequences. Transcription also makes functional RNA that will not undergo biological translation. See Alberts et al.: RNA processing and RNA as the final gene product.

Transcription (biology) OurBigBook.com
An RNA polymerase used in transcription is an enzyme that synthesizes RNA from a DNA template. Unlike a replicating DNA polymerase, it can start a new strand without a pre-existing paired strand end; initiation still requires the appropriate DNA signals and associated machinery. See Alberts et al.: RNA polymerase and transcription initiation.
Coding strand
Words: 49
Transcription (biology) OurBigBook.com
For a specified transcription unit, the coding strand is the DNA strand matching the initial RNA product in the 5′→3′ direction, with T in place of U. The opposite DNA strand is the template. The name does not imply that every transcribed gene encodes a protein. See Clark, Douglas and Choi: coding and template strands.
Translation (biology)
Words: 400 Articles: 4
Gene expression OurBigBook.com
Biological translation uses a ribosome to read messenger RNA codons 5′→3′ and assemble the corresponding amino acid chain. Transfer RNA adaptors match codons through base pairing and carry the amino acids; the genetic code supplies the correspondence. The chain grows from the N-terminus toward the C-terminus, by adding each new residue at the C-terminus. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e: ribosomes, transfer RNA and protein synthesis.
In the gene expression diagram, read 5′-AUG GCU UAA-3′ in the chosen reading frame. Under the standard genetic code, AUG specifies methionine and GCU specifies alanine; UAA is a stop codon. The result before any subsequent processing is the two-residue chain N–methionine–alanine–C, followed by termination. The stop codon contributes zero amino acids. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e: the standard genetic code. This example assumes appropriate initiation at the displayed AUG in a suitable context in a eukaryote; the diagram displays the coding segment, not a complete independently translatable messenger RNA.
Initiation establishes the starting position and reading frame, using a ribosome, an initiating transfer RNA and additional factors. At a standard stop codon, a release factor promotes release of the chain rather than delivery of another amino acid by transfer RNA. See Clark, Douglas and Choi: initiation and termination of translation. A short two-residue example illustrates decoding, not the size or folding of a typical functional protein.
The useful connection is between two different alphabets: nucleotides specify the order of amino acids through the genetic code. Base pairing helps select transfer RNA, while the ribosome catalyzes joining the delivered amino acids. The messenger RNA remains a template rather than being consumed as the chain's building material. Separating template, adaptor and product makes clear why transcription and biological translation are distinct mechanisms.
Genetic code
Words: 153 Articles: 3
Translation (biology) OurBigBook.com
The genetic code assigns RNA codons to amino acids or termination signals. Four possible nucleobases at each of three positions give 43=64 codons. In the standard genetic code, 61 specify amino acids and three are stop codons; several codons can specify the same amino acid. Variants exist, so state which genetic code is being used. See Clark, Douglas and Choi: genetic code assignments and variants.

Gene

Genetics OurBigBook.com
A gene is an inherited functional unit of genetic material. In cellular organisms, a gene is a region of DNA whose information produces a functional RNA or contributes to a protein. This connects inheritance to cellular chemistry: a change in a gene can alter the amount or activity of a protein, and thereby a phenotype. See NHGRI: gene.
Alternative inherited versions at a genetic locus are alleles. The distinction matters: two parents can carry the same gene but different alleles, and a genetic locus can have variation outside a gene. Neither the word gene nor a change in DNA alone specifies the resulting phenotype.

Genetics OurBigBook.com
Ascertainment in a genetic study specifies how individuals or families enter a genetic study. If A is the event of inclusion, then P(X∣A)=P(X)P(A∣X)/P(A). Selection on disease phenotype can change an unconditional pedigree likelihood. When comparing genetic marker probabilities conditional on a specified disease pattern, selection depending only on that pattern cancels from the linkage likelihood ratio.

Meiosis

Words: 364 Articles: 3
Genetics OurBigBook.com
Meiosis reduces two sets of chromosomes to one. In the ordinary diploid life cycle, this makes it possible for fertilization of two haploid gametes to restore the diploid state rather than double the number of sets in every generation. Its two divisions perform different tasks: meiosis I separates homologous chromosomes, whereas meiosis II separates sister chromatids. One round of DNA replication precedes both divisions; there is no second round between them. See [ref].
Two homologous chromosomes carry corresponding genetic loci, potentially with different alleles; two sister chromatids originate by DNA replication of one chromosome. After chromosomal crossover between nonsister chromatids, the sister chromatids need not carry identical alleles everywhere. Separating the two relationships explains why a haploid product of meiosis I still contains replicated chromosomes.
The two divisions explain Mendelian segregation; variable orientation of different homologous chromosome pairs connects it to independent assortment. Genetic recombination adds another source of allele combinations. These mechanisms reshuffle inherited material without requiring a new mutation.
The symmetric diagram is useful for counting, but human oogenesis produces one functional ovum rather than four. The polar bodies receive discarded chromosomes and little cytoplasm. See Human Reproductive Anatomy and Gametogenesis (§43.3, Oogenesis and Figure 43.13: unequal divisions and polar bodies).

The first division of meiosis separates replicated homologous chromosomes; their sister chromatids remain associated.

The second division of meiosis separates sister chromatids, without an intervening round of DNA replication.

Meiotic DNA content ((2n,2C)→(2n,4C)→(n,2C)→(n,C))
