Meiosis OurBigBook.com
Ploidy counts sets of chromosomes; DNA amount counts material. Let n be the number of chromosomes in one complete set and C the DNA amount of one unreplicated set. For the ordinary diploid model, read each row per completed cell nucleus, not as a total across all products:
StagePloidyDNA amountChromosome organization
Before DNA replication2n2CTwo unreplicated sets
After DNA replication2n4CTwo sets; each chromosome has two sister chromatids
After meiosis In2COne replicated set
After meiosis IInCOne unreplicated set
In the illustrated n=2 example, the starting biological cell has four chromosomes. DNA replication gives eight chromatids, organized into four replicated chromosomes. Each product of meiosis I has two replicated chromosomes, hence four chromatids; each final product has two unreplicated chromosomes. Across completed products, 2(2C)=4C after meiosis I and 4(C)=4C after meiosis II: division redistributes the replicated DNA. A haploid cell nucleus can therefore have 2C without becoming diploid.

Mendelian segregation (Aa×Aa:41​AA, 21​Aa, 41​aa)

Words: 782 Articles: 2
Genetics OurBigBook.com
In ordinary diploid meiosis, the two copies at a genetic locus separate: each gamete receives one copy. With fair transmission, a heterozygote Aa produces gametes carrying A or a with probability 1/2 each. This is a transmission mechanism conditional on a parental genotype, rather than a statement about how common either allele is in a population.
For the one-locus cross Aa×Aa, assume independent parental transmissions, no new mutation, and no differences in fertilization or survival between the resulting genotypes. Multiplying the two gamete probabilities gives four equally likely ordered outcomes: AA,Aa,aA,aa, each with probability 1/4. Combining the two orders of the heterozygote gives
P(AA)=0.25,P(Aa)=0.50,P(aa)=0.25.
(105)
Only under the additional ideal model of complete dominance of A, complete penetrance, and no environmental changes to the scored characteristic do AA and Aa share the dominant phenotype. Its probability is then 0.25+0.50=0.75. The inheritance calculation alone does not determine a phenotype or predict a generic disease risk.
These are probabilities, not a requirement that every four offspring contain one AA, two Aa and one aa. For 100 independent offspring under the ideal model, the expected values of the three counts are 25,50,25; the aa count has a binomial distribution with standard deviation 100(0.25)(0.75)​≈4.33. Each new transmission keeps the same conditional probabilities given the parental genotypes.
In his paper published in 1866, Mendel reported 5,474 round and 1,850 wrinkled pea seeds: 5474/7324≈0.7474 round, close to the ideal 0.75. Following descendants also distinguished two inherited classes within the round phenotype, illustrating why genotype cannot always be read from appearance.[ref] At several genetic loci, transmission patterns additionally depend on genetic linkage and genetic recombination.

Independent assortment (θ=21​)

Words: 498
Mendelian segregation OurBigBook.com
Independent assortment means that transmission at different genetic loci has conditional independence given the parental genotype. With fair Mendelian segregation, a parent heterozygous at two genetic loci, AaBb, produces AB,Ab,aB,ab gametes with probability 1/4 each. For example,
P(A,B∣AaBb)=P(A∣AaBb)P(B∣AaBb)=21​21​=41​.
(106)
Here AB labels an allele combination; it does not assert that the two genetic loci lie on the same chromosome.
The physical model is stochastic orientation of different homologous chromosome pairs toward the two poles of the spindle apparatus in meiosis I. One pair's orientation does not determine another's. For two pairs, one division can send A,B together and a,b together; another can send A,b together and a,B together. See The Process of Meiosis (§11.1, Metaphase I and Figure 11.5: random orientation of chromosome pairs).
With k distinguishable homologous chromosome pairs, there are 2k choices of parental homologous chromosome origin for a product at a specified pole, each with probability 2−k under this model. For k=3, enumerate MMM,MMP,MPM,MPP,PMM,PMP,PPM,PPP, where M and P mark parental origins. Whole-pole reversal pairs complementary choices, leaving 2k−1 unordered partitions for k≥1. For k=2 there are four choices for a specified pole but only the two relative orientations drawn. This counts possible products across meioses, not eight different products of one division when k=3. Identical alleles at scored genetic loci can also make different parental-origin choices observationally indistinguishable.
Independent assortment of different chromosome pairs does not imply independence of every pair of genes. Nearby genetic loci on the same chromosome can show genetic linkage. Chromosomal crossover can create new haplotypes, but does not automatically erase genetic linkage. See Laws of Inheritance (§12.3, Law of Independent Assortment and Linked Genes Violate the Law of Independent Assortment). In the ordinary fair two-locus model with parental haplotypes AB/ab and recombination fraction r,
P(AB)=P(ab)=21−r​,P(Ab)=P(aB)=2r​.
(107)
Thus r=0 gives only the two parental haplotypes, while r=1/2 gives four equal probabilities. A recombination fraction of 1/2 alone does not establish that the genetic loci lie on different chromosomes.
A motivating experiment appears in Experiments in Plant Hybridization by Gregor Mendel (§9, “The Reproductive Cells of the Hybrids”). In peas, hybrids for round versus wrinkled seeds and yellow versus green seeds were crossed reciprocally with constant wrinkled-green plants. The readout was visible seed shape and color: hybrid seed parents gave 31 round-yellow, 26 round-green, 27 wrinkled-yellow and 26 wrinkled-green; the reciprocal cross gave 24, 25, 22 and 27.
The apparatus was controlled pollination: opening immature flowers, removing stamens with forceps, and applying selected pollen to the stigma. Two-year trials established constant parental characters; greenhouse pots checked interference from insects in outdoor beds. Reciprocal crosses tested both transmission directions. These procedures are described in Experiments in Plant Hybridization by Gregor Mendel (§§2–3).
With complete dominance at both genetic loci, this test cross makes each phenotype report one hybrid gamete combination. The ideal expected values are 110/4=27.5 and 98/4=24.5 per class. The observations support four transmitted combinations, approximately equally frequent. They do not directly image chromosome orientation or prove independence for all genes; failed development and seed germination also limit the inference, as §9 notes.

For two individuals carrying labelled copies (a,b) and (c,d), condensed identity coefficients give the probabilities of nine identity by descent patterns, identifying states that differ only by exchanging the two homologues within either individual. They retain within-individual autozygosity, which three ordinary outbred sharing coefficients omit. One convention is
123456789​abcdab∣cdabc∣d or abd∣cab∣c∣dacd∣b or bcd∣acd∣a∣bac∣bd or ad∣bcone cross-individual pair, two singletonsa∣b∣c∣d​

This follows by conditioning on whether the parents share one ancestral copy and enumerating the four independent Mendelian segregation choices to their two children. Identity-by-descent sharing of inbred full siblings ((P(J=0),P(J=1),P(J=2))=(7/32,17/32,1/4))

Jacquard identity coefficients OurBigBook.com
Let J be the largest number of chromosome copies that can be paired across the two full siblings as identical by descent, counting repeated copies when a child is autozygous. For offspring of otherwise outbred first cousins, with probability 3/4 the parental copies have no common ancestral origin, giving ordinary sibling sharing (1/4,1/2,1/4). With probability 1/4, write the parental copies as (A,B) and (A,C) with three distinct origins. Each child independently has one of AA,AB,AC,BC, equally likely. Among sixteen ordered child pairs, two share no copy, ten share one, and four share two. The mixture gives the displayed probabilities. These three numbers do not determine all Jacquard identity coefficients; the formula ϕ=E[J]/4 is restricted to noninbred individuals and fails here.

First-cousin identity-by-descent probabilities ((k0​,k1​,k2​)=(3/4,1/4,0))

Identity by descent OurBigBook.com
For first cousins in an otherwise outbred pedigree, compare the copies transmitted from their related parents, who are full siblings. These transmissions trace to the same shared grandparent with probability 1/2 and then to the same homologous copy of that grandparent with probability 1/2, giving k1​=1/4. The unrelated parental contributions cannot match, so two shared copies have probability zero. Selecting one random copy from each cousin chooses those two potentially shared copies with probability 1/4, giving kinship coefficient k1​/4=1/16.

Identical-by-descent segment

Words: 78
Identity by descent OurBigBook.com
An identical-by-descent segment is a chromosomal tract inherited from the same ancestral chromosome without an intervening breakpoint in the tracked ancestry. With a specified total number m of independent meioses and a uniform recombination map, the probability that a fixed tract of genetic length d survives without genetic recombination is approximately e−md. Recent common ancestry therefore tends to give longer shared tracts. Lengths of tracts selected by covering a random point are length-biased relative to tracts sampled by their boundaries.

Identity by descent OurBigBook.com

Genetic linkage

Words: 1k Articles: 13
Genetics OurBigBook.com
Why can two individually fair allele transmissions fail to be independent? Genetic loci on the same chromosome can travel together through meiosis. This tendency is genetic linkage; in an ordinary two-locus model, detectable genetic linkage means a recombination fraction below 1/2. A genetic marker can therefore help track a neighboring genetic locus through a pedigree. See Clark, Douglas and Choi, Biology 2e: chromosomal theory and genetic linkage.
Take a diploid individual heterozygous at two genetic loci, with phase-known genotype AB/ab: one homologous chromosome carries alleles A,B, the other a,b. The parental haplotypes are AB,ab; the recombinant haplotypes are Ab,aB. Assume fair Mendelian segregation, equal probabilities within each reciprocal pair of gametes, and no allele-dependent differences in gamete recovery. If the recombination fraction is r=0.2, the gamete probabilities are 0.4,0.4,0.1,0.1 in that order. Each genetic locus still transmits its two alleles equally, but P(AB)=0.4 exceeds P(A)P(B)=0.25: fairness at each genetic locus does not imply independence between genetic loci.
At r=0, only the parental haplotypes occur, each with probability 0.5: this is complete genetic linkage. At r=0.5, all four haplotypes have probability 0.25, giving independent assortment. A recombination fraction near 0.5 alone cannot establish whether the genetic loci lie on different chromosomes or far apart on one chromosome.
Genetic linkage concerns joint transmission through meiosis. Linkage disequilibrium concerns haplotype frequencies in a population, while genetic association compares allele or genotype frequencies with a phenotype. These questions require different observations; pedigrees directly reveal co-transmission.

Words: 539 Articles: 3

A genetic map turns observations of inherited haplotypes into an ordered account of genetic loci along a chromosome. Its distances describe genetic recombination, which makes the map useful for locating a genetic locus relative to known genetic markers. A genetic map measures inheritance separation; separation measured in base pairs describes positions along DNA. Recombination hotspots help explain why equal numbers of base pairs need not give equal genetic map distances. See T. A. Brown, Genomes, 2nd edition (2002), chapter 5: Mapping Genomes.
Write d for the expected value of the number of chromosomal crossovers encountered along one transmitted chromatid between the chosen genetic loci, measured in morgans; 100d is the distance in centimorgans. This counts exchanges along that transmitted chromatid, rather than all exchanges in the four-chromatid meiotic bundle. For a short interval with very few multiple exchanges, the recombination fraction satisfies r≈d: about 1% recombinant gametes then corresponds to about one centimorgan.
For a longer interval, hidden even numbers of chromosomal crossovers make that approximation inaccurate. Under the Haldane mapping function, d=0.2 morgans gives r≈0.164840; conversely r=0.2 gives d≈0.255413 morgans, or 25.5413 centimorgans. Applying the inverse formula to an already specified genetic map distance would confuse a count with a probability.
Genetic map distances add along ordered adjacent intervals because the total exchange count is the sum of its interval counts. For independent random variables describing counts in disjoint intervals of the Haldane mapping function model, the endpoint recombination fraction instead obeys
r12​=r1​(1−r2​)+(1−r1​)r2​=r1​+r2​−2r1​r2​.

Exactly one interval must change parental origin. Thus r1​=r2​=0.2 gives r12​=0.32, although the two genetic map distances add to approximately 0.510826 morgans. The simple composition formula requires the stated independence; crossover interference can invalidate it.

Words: 244
Genetic map OurBigBook.com
The Haldane mapping function connects additive genetic map distance to endpoint recombination fraction in a toy model with no crossover interference. Specify the model directly along a transmitted chromatid: the exchange count N in the interval has a Poisson distribution with expected value d, where d is the distance in morgans. Counts in disjoint intervals are independent random variables. This is the transmitted-chromatid convention; d is not the mean number of exchanges across all four chromatids in meiosis.
An odd exchange count changes parental phase. Summing the odd terms of the Poisson distribution gives
r=P(N is odd)=e−d∑k=0∞​(2k+1)!d2k+1​=21−e−2d​.
(111)
For 0≤r<1/2, the inverse and short-interval approximation are

(112)
Here log is the natural logarithm. At d=0.2, the recombination fraction is 0.16483997698; at r=0.2, the distance is 0.2554128119 morgans, or about 25.5413 centimorgans. The linear approximation r≈d is useful only near zero. The recombination fraction approaches 1/2 as d grows; r=1/2 has no finite inverse in this model.
The model is a useful baseline, not a universal rule for every interval during meiosis. Crossover interference can change the relationship between distance and recombination fraction. For the count convention and assumptions, see Weeks, Tang and Kwon (2009): genetic map functions and exchange-count conventions. Haldane's original paper is bibliographically recorded as The combination of linkage values, and the calculation of distances between the loci of linked factors, Journal of Genetics 8 (1919), 299–309, in Selected Genetics Papers of J. Genetic recombination

Words: 538 Articles: 5
Genetics OurBigBook.com
Genetic recombination rearranges inherited genetic material into new combinations. In the meiosis example considered here, chromosomal crossover exchanges segments between nonsister chromatids of homologous chromosomes. A transmitted chromatid can consequently contain DNA from both parental homologues. This produces new haplotypes without requiring a new mutation at either scored genetic locus. See Meiosis.
For phase-known genotype AB/ab, a single chromosomal crossover between the selected genetic loci can yield Ab and aB on the participating chromatids; the other two chromatids can remain AB and ab. Thus an exchange in the four-chromatid bundle does not mean every resulting gamete is recombinant. Only a chromosomal crossover encountered along the transmitted chromatid within the selected interval affects its two-locus score.
Follow parental origin along the transmitted chromatid from the first genetic locus to the second. Each exchange switches that origin. An odd number of such chromosomal crossovers changes the endpoint combination; an even number restores parental phase. Two exchanges can therefore leave the scored haplotype as AB even though an internal segment came from the other parental homologous chromosome. Recombinant status is relative to the chosen genetic loci, not a complete record of exchanges along the chromosome.
This integer parity distinction connects the physical process of genetic recombination to the observed recombination fraction. It also explains why a long genetic map interval can accumulate many exchanges while its endpoint recombination fraction approaches 1/2 in the Haldane mapping function model.

The breakpoint splits that lineage's ancestral material into two parental contributions. Waiting times are exponential with the sum of the current event rates. At each genomic position, retaining the ancestry at that position gives a marginal phylogenetic tree with the neutral Kingman's coalescent distribution. Different positions have dependent trees because they share parts of the graph.

Linkage disequilibrium means that knowing an allele at one genetic locus changes the probability of an allele at another genetic locus in population haplotypes. It compares their joint probability distribution with the product of their marginal distributions. This is useful because a genetic marker can carry information about another genetic locus: tag SNPs exploit this redundancy, without establishing a causal genetic association.
Consider two genetic loci with alleles A,a and B,b. Sample one haplotype, rather than an unphased diploid genotype. Write its four haplotype frequencies as fAB​,fAb​,faB​,fab​, summing to one, and set the marginal allele frequencies to p=fAB​+fAb​ and q=fAB​+faB​. The linkage disequilibrium coefficient is
D=fAB​−pq=fAB​fab​−fAb​faB​.
(120)
The second expression follows by substituting fab​=1−fAB​−fAb​−faB​. The entire two-locus joint probability distribution is then

(121)
Every row and column sum is unchanged when D varies. Linkage equilibrium means D=0: all four haplotype frequencies equal products of allele frequencies, so the two allele indicators are independent random variables. For p>0, the conditional probability P(B∣A)=q+D/p shows directly how positive D enriches B among copies carrying A, while negative D depletes it. Positive D also enriches ab; negative D enriches Ab and aB. Swapping the labels A and a reverses the sign of D, so neither sign is intrinsically favorable.
For example, fix the allele frequencies at p=0.60,q=0.40. At linkage equilibrium, the haplotype frequencies in the order AB,Ab,aB,ab are (0.24,0.36,0.16,0.24). Positive linkage disequilibrium D=0.12 instead gives (0.36,0.24,0.04,0.36), with P(B∣A)=0.60; negative linkage disequilibrium D=−0.12 gives (0.12,0.48,0.28,0.12), with P(B∣A)=0.20. Counting each allele separately would miss the difference.
Nonnegative haplotype frequencies constrain D. Define the nonnegative bounds L=min(pq,(1−p)(1−q)) and U=min(p(1−q),(1−p)q). The four entries above give
−L≤D≤U,max(0,p+q−1)≤fAB​≤min(p,q).
(122)
Thus ∣D∣≤1/4 globally, but a particular pair of allele frequencies usually permits a smaller, asymmetric interval. The standardized linkage disequilibrium convention used here retains the sign:
D′=⎩⎨⎧​D/U0D/L​D>0,D=0,D<0,​−1≤D′≤1.
(123)
This convention requires 0<p,q<1; if either genetic locus has only one allele in the population, D=0 but normalized measures are undefined. Some presentations report only ∣D′∣. At D′=1 or −1, at least one of the four haplotypes has zero frequency; this alone does not prove that genetic recombination has never occurred.
For the indicator random variables X=1A​ and Y=1B​, their covariance is D, and their variances are p(1−p) and q(1−q). The allelic correlation measure is their squared correlation coefficient,
rLD2​=p(1−p)q(1−q)D2​,0≤rLD2​≤p(1−p)q(1−q)max(L2,U2)​≤1.
(124)
The subscript distinguishes it from the recombination fraction r in linkage-disequilibrium decay under recombination. Squaring loses the association's sign. In the illustrated positive and negative examples, rLD2​=0.25 in both, whereas D′=0.75 and −0.50, respectively. For another original example, take p=0.10,q=0.50,fAB​=0.10: then D=0.05,D′=1, yet rLD2​=1/9. Every A carries B, but most copies carrying B lack A. The frequency constraints and the distinction between these normalizations are analyzed in Mathematical properties of the r² measure of linkage disequilibrium by Jenna M. VanLiere and others (sections 2.1 and 2.5, pp. 131–132 and 135–136).
Genetic linkage describes transmission through meiosis; linkage disequilibrium describes a population's haplotype frequencies. Nearby genetic loci on a chromosome can be in linkage equilibrium. Conversely, mixing populations can create linkage disequilibrium even between genetic loci on different chromosomes. For example, mix equal numbers of independently sampled haplotypes from two populations, each internally at linkage equilibrium, with p=q=0.80 in one and p=q=0.20 in the other. The pooled allele frequencies are p=q=0.50, but fAB​=(0.64+0.04)/2=0.34, giving D=0.09. This is a consequence of population stratification, not a measurement of the recombination fraction.
Measured haplotype frequencies also depend on the sample. Finite sample size, related individuals, genetic-study ascertainment, genotyping error and uncertain haplotype estimation can change an estimate. A missing rare haplotype can give empirical ∣D′∣=1 without demonstrating its absence from the population. Report the sample definition and allele frequencies alongside the association measure; a nonzero sample estimate alone does not establish nonzero population linkage disequilibrium.
A concrete dataset is the 2005 A haplotype map of the human genome by The International HapMap Consortium. The International HapMap Consortium used genotyping platforms including Illumina BeadArray to obtain SNP genotype calls from 269 DNA samples across four collections: 30 parent–offspring trios from Ibadan, 30 trios from Utah, 45 unrelated individuals from Beijing and 44 from Tokyo. Parent–offspring trios and the PHASE algorithm supplied haplotype estimation, rather than direct observation of every chromosome. In Figure 7, 36 SNPs resolve seven haplotypes in a chromosome 2 region in the Utah panel; seven tag SNPs capture the 36 SNPs at rLD2​≥0.8. The readout demonstrates reusable allelic correlation, not causal effects.
Controls required over 80% complete calls, at most one discordance among five duplicate genotypes, at most one Mendelian segregation error per trio panel, and a Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium test with P>0.001; blind reassessment checked performance. Minor allele frequencies of at least 0.05 were targeted, the collections were not population-representative, and inferred haplotypes retain phase uncertainty. These limits restrict extrapolation of linkage disequilibrium.[ref]

Hardy-Weinberg principle (p2,2pq,q2;p+q=1)

Words: 412 Articles: 3
Genetics OurBigBook.com
The Hardy-Weinberg principle describes the genotype proportions produced by independently combining two parental gametes from the same allele pool. For alleles A,a with allele frequencies p,q, where p+q=1, the Hardy-Weinberg proportions are
P(AA)=p2,P(Aa)=2pq,P(aa)=q2.
(126)
The two ordered heterozygote outcomes contribute pq+qp. These proportions sum to (p+q)2=1, and their implied A allele frequency is p2+(2pq)/2=p. Reshuffling copies therefore preserves their frequencies.
For stable Hardy-Weinberg equilibrium across generations, use a large population with random mating, equal allele frequencies in the parental pools, ordinary Mendelian segregation, and no natural selection, mutation, gene flow or genetic drift. Negligible genetic drift is an idealization of large population size. The one-generation random-mating equilibrium needs independent union of gametes; persistence additionally requires processes that change allele frequencies to be absent.
At p=0.70,q=0.30, the predicted genotype proportions are 0.49,0.42,0.09. For 100 sampled individuals the expected values of the counts are 49,42,9, rather than the 25,50,25 of a specified Aa×Aa cross. The latter fixes both parental genotypes; Hardy-Weinberg proportions average over population mating.
An observed population need not have these proportions. For example, 70 AA, no Aa, and 30 aa among 100 individuals still gives p=0.70, but has no heterozygotes. Random mating predicts 0.42 heterozygosity in the next generation under the stated model. A finite sample can also depart by chance, so a discrepancy is a starting point for investigating inbreeding, population stratification or genotyping error, rather than proof of one cause.
Hardy's 1908 note made the conceptual payoff explicit: a dominant phenotype does not by itself make its allele spread. Complete dominance describes expression; changes in frequency require a separate mechanism such as natural selection. See Hardy, Mendelian Proportions in a Mixed Population, Science 28 (1908), 49–50.

This is the two-zygote subtype of a twin.
Dizygotic twins develop from two zygotes and, absent assortative mating and other complications, share one half of additive genetic variation on average.

The ACE model decomposes trait variation into additive genetic effects A, common environmental effects C, and unique environmental effects E.

Falconer's formula estimates narrow-sense heritability from monozygotic and dizygotic twin correlations:
h2=2(rMZ​−rDZ​).
(129)
It relies on equal relevant environments and a dizygotic additive-genetic correlation of one half.

Assortative mating

Quantitative genetics OurBigBook.com
Assortative mating is nonrandom mating in which partners are more or less similar than random pairs for a trait or correlated characteristic. Positive assortment can increase genetic similarity among siblings.

RNA splicing

Words: 110 Articles: 3
Biology OurBigBook.com
Processing of a precursor RNA that removes an intron and joins the flanking exons. The ribozyme experiments show one self-splicing mechanism; RNA splicing need not always be autonomous.

Intron

Words: 58 Articles: 1
RNA splicing OurBigBook.com
A segment represented in a precursor RNA that is removed by RNA splicing; the corresponding segment of a gene is also called an intron. An intron can interrupt ribosomal RNA as well as messenger RNA.

Group I catalytic intron

Words: 30
Intron OurBigBook.com
A class of introns with a conserved RNA catalytic core and a two-step RNA splicing mechanism initiated by external guanosine. Some group I introns self-splice under suitable conditions; others require protein assistance. The ribozyme body explains the Tetrahymena example.

Exon

Words: 29
RNA splicing OurBigBook.com
A segment retained in the mature RNA after RNA splicing, or the corresponding segment of a gene. An exon need not encode a protein: the ribosomal RNA exons in the Tetrahymena ribozyme experiment are an example.

Guanosine

Words: 23
Biology OurBigBook.com
A nucleoside comprising guanine attached to ribose. Its free 3′ hydroxyl group initiates group I intron RNA splicing; guanosine is incorporated into the excised intron, rather than acting as a regenerated catalyst.

Gel electrophoresis

Words: 74 Articles: 1
Biology OurBigBook.com
Separation of charged molecules through a gel in an electric field. Denaturing conditions suppress folded structures, helping compare RNA lengths; matching migration alone does not establish an identical nucleotide sequence or identical covalent bonds. In the ribozyme experiments, labelled RNA was detected after separation by exposing photographic film.

SDS-PAGE

Words: 34
Gel electrophoresis OurBigBook.com
An analytical form of gel electrophoresis using an anionic surfactant and a polymer gel to separate proteins predominantly by chain size under denaturing conditions. Western blot separation often uses SDS-PAGE; the resulting apparent mass and subsequent antibody binding provide complementary, incomplete evidence about identity.

Biology OurBigBook.com

Homeostasis

Words: 2k Articles: 23
Physiology OurBigBook.com
Homeostasis is the maintenance of usable internal conditions despite disturbances. It concerns selected regulated physiological variables, rather than keeping every part of an organism unchanged: core body temperature may remain near its usual range while skin temperature, sweating and blood pressure change. Regulation makes a relatively dependable environment for biological cells out of a changing external world. [ref]
A useful causal description separates a physiological sensor, a physiological integrator and a physiological effector. The return from the physiological effector's action to the sensed regulated physiological variable closes a feedback control loop. In negative feedback, that return opposes the disturbance. The insulin and glucagon articles already trace the blood glucose example; synaptic integration explains how several inputs can jointly influence a neuron. These are implementations and ingredients, not a requirement that every regulatory loop use one anatomical control center. [ref]
Homeostasis is useful precisely because internal activity can change: a nearly steady temperature can conceal a large increase in heat transfer. Conversely, observing a flat trace alone does not identify a regulatory mechanism. The environment might simply be constant, or the measuring instrument too insensitive; a perturbation and an independent response readout provide stronger evidence. The skin-temperature perturbation experiment below makes that distinction tangible.
The historical motivation was the puzzle of stability in changing living material. In his 1932 The Wisdom of the Body, Walter Bradford Cannon emphasized that an organism exchanges material with its surroundings and continually replaces its own structure, yet maintains relatively steady internal conditions. This authored excerpt presents homeostasis as active compensation for external and internal disturbances, rather than a static body. [ref]

Regulated physiological variable

Words: 67 Articles: 2
Homeostasis OurBigBook.com
A regulated physiological variable is a specified internal quantity whose departures elicit actions tending to restore an appropriate range. Examples include core body temperature, blood glucose concentration, blood pressure, and the pH and osmolality of extracellular fluid. Specify the compartment and readout: skin temperature and core body temperature are different quantities, and an insulin concentration is a regulatory message rather than the blood glucose it helps control.

Regulated physiological variable OurBigBook.com
Osmolality counts dissolved particles per mass of solvent; it characterizes a chemical solution, rather than the total amount of water in an organism.

Physiological sensor

Words: 32
Homeostasis OurBigBook.com
A physiological sensor detects a relevant condition and changes a signal. In thermoregulation, temperature-sensitive neurons supply information about internal and skin temperature. Sensing a disturbance and sensing its internal consequence need not be the same operation.

Physiological integrator

Words: 44 Articles: 1
Homeostasis OurBigBook.com
A physiological integrator combines regulatory inputs to select a response; it need not perform the mathematical integral action used in control theory. In thermoregulation, the hypothalamus participates in combining internal and skin signals. The term describes a role, which can be distributed across interacting biological cells, rather than a mandatory single comparator.
Hypothalamus
Physiological integrator OurBigBook.com

Physiological effector

Words: 130 Articles: 1
Homeostasis OurBigBook.com
A physiological effector performs the action that changes the regulated physiological variable. In thermoregulation, sweat glands, changes in skin blood flow, and skeletal muscle shivering contribute different actions. The command, the action and the resulting temperature are three distinct readouts. [ref]
Effector saturation
Words: 92
Physiological effector OurBigBook.com
Effector saturation is a capacity limit beyond which a larger command cannot produce a larger corrective action. In the homeostatic temperature model, take u=min(4x,1/2) during the sustained unit disturbance. Before reaching the cap, x=(1−e−5t)/5. The cap is reached at tc​=log(8/3)/5, when x=1/8. Thereafter
x(t)=21​−83​e−(t−tc​),u(t)=21​.
(130)
The lasting displacement is now 1/2, compared with 1/5 without the cap. The negative feedback command still asks for more cooling, but the action cannot supply it. This illustrates a capacity limit without predicting a human temperature limit. Increasing feedback gain cannot remove a binding cap; integral action cannot overcome inadequate physical capacity either.

Physiological set point

Words: 107
Homeostasis OurBigBook.com
A physiological set point is a reference around which regulation is organized, analogous to a reference signal. An observed average is not automatically a separately encoded target. A range of acceptable values and different response thresholds can be more informative than a single exact number. Negative feedback describes a causal sign; neither perfect constancy nor complete restoration follows from that sign alone.
For core body temperature, circadian rhythms and fever can change the defended level. Thus a response toward the current physiological set point need not restore yesterday's temperature. A drifting target and imperfect tracking of a fixed target are different explanations for a changing readout. [ref]

Homeostatic temperature model (τx˙=d−x−u)

Words: 474
Homeostasis OurBigBook.com
Here is an explicitly synthetic mathematical model of a warming disturbance and its compensatory cooling. It is a teaching analogy for thermoregulation, not a measured human heat budget. Write x=(T−Tr​)/ΔT, where T is a lumped internal temperature, Tr​ is a fixed reference and ΔT>0 is a chosen temperature scale. Let d be an additional heating rate and u an additional cooling rate, both scaled to the same reference rate. All three are dimensionless variables, while τ>0 is a time constant in the chosen time units. The ordinary differential equation is
τx˙=d−x−u,u=kx,k≥0.
(131)
The term −x idealizes increased passive heat transfer with increased internal temperature, around the baseline. The term −u opposes warming through proportional control with feedback gain k. This local signed model does not treat a negative u as negative sweating: it would represent decreased cooling relative to baseline. Changes of the environment and multiple body compartments are omitted.
For a constant disturbance d=D and initial condition x(0)=0, the exponential function solution is
x(t)=1+kD​(1−e−(1+k)t/τ),x∗​=1+kD​,u∗​=1+kkD​.
(132)
Substitution checks the ordinary differential equation directly. Increasing k reduces the lasting offset and, in this instantaneous model, shortens the response time constant to τ/(1+k). It does not make x∗​ zero for a nonzero disturbance and finite k: a persistent cooling command requires a persistent displacement under proportional control. At the equilibrium point, the extra heating is balanced by passive loss x∗​ plus active cooling u∗​. Zero change of temperature means balanced rates, rather than zero rates, consistent with conservation of energy.
The first diagram uses D=1, τ=4, and a pulse from t=2 to t=10, comparing k=0 with k=3. The latter approaches x∗​=1/4 during the pulse, compared with 1 without active feedback control. After the pulse ends, each displacement decays as x(10)e−(1+k)(t−10)/τ. These are computed curves, not physiological measurements. The k=0 curve still has passive loss; it is not a claim that an unregulated body warms without limit.
Real physiological effectors take time to respond. To isolate that issue, set τ=1 and replace the instantaneous command by another ordinary differential equation:
x˙=1−x−u,u˙=4x−u,x(0)=u(0)=0.
(133)
Here the disturbance remains 1 from t=0 onward and the effector time constant is also 1. The equilibrium point is still (x∗​,u∗​)=(1/5,4/5), but the characteristic polynomial is (λ+1)2+4. Its eigenvalues −1±2i give decaying oscillations and asymptotic stability. The exact response is
x(t)=51​+e−t(−51​cos(2t)+52​sin(2t)),u(t)=54​+e−t(−54​cos(2t)−52​sin(2t)).
(134)
In particular, x˙=e−tcos(2t), so the first maximum occurs at t=π/4, with x=1/5+(2/5)e−π/4≃0.3824. The response exceeds its eventual displacement while remaining above its baseline. The return has the same negative sign as before; the extra state changes the timing. A finite effector time constant is distinct from the fixed time lag in the delayed negative feedback model.

Thermoregulation

Words: 345 Articles: 10
Homeostasis OurBigBook.com
Thermoregulation regulates body temperature. Skin signals can anticipate a change of core body temperature, so a response need not wait for an internal error. [ref]
These responses have costs and environmental limits. Shivering consumes metabolic resources; cooling through sweating removes water that must eventually be replaced. High humidity restricts evaporation, so secreted sweat and successful cooling are not interchangeable. Maintaining core body temperature also depends on maintaining circulation: depleted blood volume can compromise skin blood flow and heat transfer. Seeking shade or reducing work changes the disturbance itself, whereas a larger regulatory command merely attempts to counter it. [ref]
Core body temperature (Tc​)
Words: 32
Thermoregulation OurBigBook.com
Core body temperature refers to internal temperature, distinguished from skin temperature. Different measurement sites are proxies with their own limitations, not interchangeable readings of a perfectly uniform interior. [ref]
Skin-temperature perturbation experiment
Words: 194
Thermoregulation OurBigBook.com
Twelve resting volunteers wore a water-perfused suit. Tubes covered the torso, upper arms and legs; the right forearm remained uncovered for laser Doppler blood-flow measurement. Six thermocouples estimated mean skin temperature; a sublingual thermocouple measured oral temperature. A dry-air capsule measured local sweat output from outgoing air moisture. [ref]
After two control scans near 34∘C skin temperature, the suit cooled and then warmed the skin. Mean oral temperature was 36.6∘C during both cooling and early warming; mean skin readings were 30.5 and 38.2∘C. Cutaneous vascular conductance fell during cooling and rose during warming. The inference is that compensatory blood-flow responses can precede an appreciable internal temperature change. [ref]
Repeated baselines controlled comparison within participants; closed mouths reduced oral-probe cooling artifacts. A later control with reduced oral temperature was excluded. Oral temperature is a proxy, local flow is not whole-body heat transfer, and the fixed condition order leaves time effects possible. Brain imaging measured regional blood flow, not direct neuron firing or causal necessity. [ref]

Synthetic insulin-glucagon response model (τI​I˙=I∞​(g)−I,τH​H˙=H∞​(g)−H)

Words: 308
Homeostasis OurBigBook.com
This deliberately synthetic differential equation model illustrates response direction and lag. Every plotted number is chosen for teaching; none is a biological measurement or a fitted human parameter. Let externally prescribed, dimensionless g>0 represent a glucose stimulus relative to a reference. Let I and H be normalized insulin and glucagon response variables, with independently chosen time constants τI​=4 and τH​=6 in arbitrary time units:
I∞​(g)=1+g4g4​,H∞​(g)=1+g41​,τI​I˙=I∞​(g)−I,τH​H˙=H∞​(g)−H.
(135)
Here I∞​ rises and H∞​ falls with g. Their targets add to one by construction; the evolving I+H need not equal one because their time constants differ. Start with g=1 and I=H=1/2. Set g=1.6 from t=10 to 40, g=0.65 from t=40 to 70, and g=1 otherwise. Within a constant-input interval beginning at t0​, the exponential decay solution is
I(t)=I∞​+[I(t0​)−I∞​]e−(t−t0​)/τI​,H(t)=H∞​+[H(t0​)−H∞​]e−(t−t0​)/τH​.
(136)
Each response is a continuous function of time even when the imposed stimulus jumps. The chosen starting values stay between zero and one, since each solution is a weighted arithmetic mean of its interval's starting value and target.
For an illustrative downstream comparison, define release tendency R=0.3+0.6H/(1+I) and uptake tendency U=(0.25+0.5I)g, in the same arbitrary flux units. At the reference target, R=U=0.5. At the high-stimulus targets, R≈0.343 and U≈1.094; at the low-stimulus targets, R≈0.742 and U≈0.212. These chosen functions encode greater uptake with insulin and greater release with glucagon, moderated by insulin; they are not established enzyme kinetics. The g trace is imposed externally, so the figure does not demonstrate self-correction of blood glucose. A closed model would also need a conservation of mass equation, nutrient input, finite glycogen stores, and additional tissue interactions. The qualitative restoring loops are shown separately in the insulin circuit.

Infection

Words: 78
Medicine OurBigBook.com
An infection involves invasion and multiplication of an infectious agent in a host. Bacteria are one possible cause; an agent capable of causing disease is a pathogen. The National Cancer Institute defines infection through invasion and growth in the body. [ref].
In a SIR model, acquiring infection moves a member of the susceptible compartment into the infectious compartment. That immediate transition is a model assumption: the SEIR model instead includes an exposed stage before infectiousness. Specify these states when translating a biological process into compartmental models.

Immunity (medical)

Words: 33
Medicine OurBigBook.com
In infection modelling, immunity is protection against infection or disease, with its strength and duration represented by the chosen host states. A SIR model has a permanently protected recovered state, whereas a SIS model has no lasting post-recovery protection.

Isolation (health care)

Words: 23
Medicine OurBigBook.com
Isolation separates recognized infected or ill individuals from susceptible contacts to limit transmission. Quarantine instead concerns exposed individuals who may or may not be infected.

Psychoactive drug

Words: 145 Articles: 3
Medicine OurBigBook.com
A psychoactive drug is a substance that changes mental activity, mood or perception. In population causal inference, its per-user adverse-event risk and its total population harm are distinct: the latter also depends on how many people use it, for how long, and on substitution between substances.

Mephedrone

Words: 46
Psychoactive drug OurBigBook.com
Mephedrone is 4-methylmethcathinone, a synthetic stimulant psychoactive drug. The chemical identity is described in the EUDA synthetic-cathinone profile. In causal inference, an association between increased use and fewer deaths involving another drug does not itself establish substitution: changes in use, population composition and ascertainment must be distinguished.

MDMA

Words: 30
Psychoactive drug OurBigBook.com
MDMA is 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine, a psychoactive drug commonly called ecstasy. A product's street label does not establish its measured chemical contents. Epidemiological comparisons should distinguish single-substance outcomes from outcomes attributed to several drugs.

Cocaine

Words: 24
Psychoactive drug OurBigBook.com
Cocaine is a stimulant psychoactive drug. Comparisons of its population harm require exposure denominators and consistent definitions of drug-related outcomes, rather than death counts alone.

Medicine OurBigBook.com
Informed consent is voluntary agreement after receiving and understanding relevant information about an intervention or participation in research. In a clinical trial, the participant is informed about the study procedures, potential benefits and risks, alternatives and the option to decline or withdraw. Consent precedes randomization.
